<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
The random graph $G(n,1/2)$ is determined by its generalized spectrum with probability $1-o(1)$, that is,
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr\bigl(G(n,1/2)\text{ is determined by its generalized spectrum}\bigr)=1 .
\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:Ep}
Let $p$ be an odd prime and $d\ge1$. A graph $G$ has a \emph{local failure of degree $d$ at $p$} if some simple $\bar A$-submodule
$U\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p^n$ of dimension $d$ is totally isotropic and orthogonal to $\bar e$. We denote this event by $E_p^{(d)}$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:largedegrees}
The probability that $E_p^{(d)}$ holds for some odd prime $p$ and some $d\ge3\log_2n$ tends to $0$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:smooth}
Fix $\varepsilon\in(0,\frac12)$. Then the probability that some $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$ other than a permutation matrix has a level whose prime factors
are all at most $n^{1/2-\varepsilon}$ tends to $0$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:moderate}
Fix $\varepsilon\in(0,\frac1{10})$. Then the probability that $E_p^{(d)}$ holds for some odd prime $p$ with
$n^{1/2-\varepsilon}<p\le e^{n^{1/10}}$ and some $1\le d<3\log_2n$ tends to $0$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:nofactor}
Fix $\eta\in(0,\frac1{27})$. Then, for all sufficiently large $m$,
\[
\Pr\bigl(\chi_{S_m}\text{ has a monic factor in }\mathbb{Z}[x]\text{ of degree in }[1,m^{\eta}]\bigr)\ \le\ \exp\bigl(-m^{1/9-\eta}/9\bigr).
\]
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:huge}
The probability that $E_p^{(d)}$ holds for some odd prime $p>e^{(\log n)^6}$ and some $d\ge1$ tends to $0$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Put $\varepsilon:=\frac1{20}$ and $G:=G(n,1/2)$. Let $\mathcal A_n$ be the event that $G$ is controllable and that every $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$ other
than a permutation matrix has a level divisible by some prime $p>n^{1/2-\varepsilon}$. By Theorems~\ref{thm:OT} and~\ref{thm:smooth},
$\Pr(\mathcal A_n)\to1$. Let $\mathcal B_n$ be the event that $E_p^{(d)}$ holds for some odd prime $p$ and some $d\ge3\log_2n$, let
$\mathcal C_n$ be the event that $E_p^{(d)}$ holds for some odd prime $p\in(n^{1/2-\varepsilon},e^{n^{1/10}}]$ and some $1\le d<3\log_2n$,
and let $\mathcal D_n$ be the event that $E_p^{(d)}$ holds for some odd prime $p>e^{n^{1/10}}$ and some $d\ge1$. By
Theorems~\ref{thm:largedegrees}, \ref{thm:moderate} and~\ref{thm:huge}, the probabilities of these three events tend to $0$, as
$e^{n^{1/10}}>e^{(\log n)^6}$ for large $n$.

Let $n$ be so large that $n^{1/2-\varepsilon}>2$. Suppose that $\mathcal A_n$ holds and that $\mathcal B_n$, $\mathcal C_n$ and
$\mathcal D_n$ fail, and let $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$. If $Q$ is not a permutation matrix, then by $\mathcal A_n$ some prime $p>n^{1/2-\varepsilon}$ divides
$\ell(Q)$. This prime is odd, so Lemma~\ref{lem:matesfail} shows that $E_p^{(d)}$ holds for some $d\ge1$. Since $\mathcal B_n$ fails we have
$d<3\log_2n$, since $\mathcal C_n$ fails we have $p>e^{n^{1/10}}$, and then $\mathcal D_n$ holds, a contradiction. Hence every $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$ is
a permutation matrix, and $G$ is DGS by Theorem~\ref{thm:wangxu}, since $G$ is controllable. Consequently
\[
\Pr(G\text{ is DGS})\ \ge\ 1-\Pr(\mathcal A_n^c)-\Pr(\mathcal B_n)-\Pr(\mathcal C_n)-\Pr(\mathcal D_n)\ \longrightarrow\ 1 .\qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:wangxu}
Let $G$ be controllable and let $H$ be a graph on $[n]$ with the same generalized spectrum as $G$. Then there is a unique orthogonal matrix
$Q$ with $Qe=e$ and $Q^{\top}A(G)Q=A(H)$, namely $Q^{\top}=W(H)W(G)^{-1}$. In particular $Q$ is rational and $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$. Consequently $G$ is
DGS if and only if every $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$ is a permutation matrix. Moreover, a matrix $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$ is a permutation matrix if and only if
$\ell(Q)=1$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The existence of $Q$ is the theorem of Johnson--Newman~\cite{JN80}. If $Q$ is orthogonal with $Qe=e$ and $Q^{\top}A(G)=A(H)Q^{\top}$,
then $Q^{\top}e=Q^{-1}e=e$, so $Q^{\top}A(G)^ke=A(H)^ke$ for all $k$, that is, $Q^{\top}W(G)=W(H)$. This gives the formula for $Q$ and its
uniqueness, as observed by Wang--Xu~\cite{WX06a}. If $Q$ is a permutation matrix, then $H\cong G$. Conversely, if $H\cong G$ via a
permutation matrix $P$ with $P^{\top}A(G)P=A(H)$, then $P\in\mathcal{Q}_G$, and $Q=P$ by uniqueness. Every $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$ arises in this way, as the
orthogonal matrix attached to some graph $H$ with the same generalized spectrum as $G$. Indeed, $Q^{\top}e=e$ gives $Q^{\top}JQ=J$, so the
graph $H$ with $A(H)=Q^{\top}AQ$ has the same generalized spectrum as $G$, because its adjacency matrix is similar to $A$ and the adjacency
matrix $J-I-A(H)=Q^{\top}(J-I-A)Q$ of its complement is similar to that of the complement of $G$. Hence $G$ is DGS if and only if
every $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$ is a permutation matrix. Finally, $\ell(Q)=1$ if and only if $Q$
is integral. An integral orthogonal matrix is a signed permutation matrix, and $Qe=e$ forces it to be a permutation matrix.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:OT}
With probability $1-o(1)$, the random graph $G(n,1/2)$ is controllable.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:matesfail}
Let $G$ be a graph, let $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$ have level $\ell:=\ell(Q)$, and let $p$ be an odd prime dividing $\ell$. Then the column space
$U_p\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p^n$ of $\ell Q\bmod p$ is a nonzero $\bar A$-stable totally isotropic subspace orthogonal to $\bar e$. In particular
$E_p^{(d)}$ holds for some $d\ge1$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let $B:=Q^{\top}AQ$, which is an integral matrix. Then $AQ=QB$, as $Q$ is orthogonal, so $\bar A$ maps the columns of $\ell Q$ modulo
$p$ into $U_p$, and $U_p$ is $\bar A$-stable.
Since $Q$ is orthogonal, $(\ell Q)^{\top}(\ell Q)=\ell^2I\equiv0\pmod p$, so $U_p$ is totally isotropic. Moreover
$e^{\top}(\ell Q)=\ell(Q^{\top}e)^{\top}={\ell e^{\top}\equiv0\pmod p}$, as $Q^{\top}e=Q^{-1}e=e$. Finally $\ell Q\not\equiv0\pmod p$, since
otherwise $(\ell/p)Q$ would be integral. As $U_p\ne0$ is $\bar A$-stable, it contains a simple $\bar A$-submodule $U$, which is totally
isotropic and orthogonal to $\bar e$, so $E_p^{(\dim U)}$ holds.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:odlyzko}
Let $F$ be a field, let $a,b\in F$ be distinct, and let $V\subseteq F^N$ be a subspace of dimension $k$, or a translate of such a subspace.
Then $V$ contains at most $2^k$ vectors of $\{a,b\}^N$. Hence, if $u$ is uniform on $\{a,b\}^N$, then $\Pr(u\perp U)\le2^{-d}$ for every
subspace $U\subseteq F^N$ of dimension $d$, and a matrix whose $l$ columns are independent copies of $u$ has rank less than $l$ with
probability less than $2^{l-N}$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $V_0$ be the subspace of which $V$ is a translate. There is a set $I$ of $k$ coordinates such that the restriction map $V_0\to F^I$ is
injective, for instance the pivot columns of a basis of $V_0$ in echelon form. Then the restriction map $V\to F^I$ is injective as well, so
the vectors of $\{a,b\}^N$ in $V$ have distinct restrictions to $I$, which lie in the set $\{a,b\}^I$ of size $2^k$. For the second
statement apply this to $V=U^{\perp}$, which has dimension $N-d$. For the third, if the columns $u_1,\dots,u_l$ have rank less than $l$,
then some $u_j$ lies in the span of $u_1,\dots,u_{j-1}$, a subspace of dimension at most $j-1$. Given $u_1,\dots,u_{j-1}$, this has
probability at most $2^{j-1-N}$, and $\sum_{j\le l}2^{j-1-N}<2^{l-N}$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:simple}
Let $p$ be odd, let $M\in M_m(\mathbb{F}_p)$ be symmetric, and let $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_p[x]$ be monic irreducible of degree $d$ with a root
$\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_q$, where $q=p^d$. Put $K_\lambda:=\ker(M-\lambda)\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q^m$ and $g:=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}K_\lambda$, and for
$w\in K_\lambda$ let $U_w:=\{\operatorname{Tr}(cw):\ c\in\mathbb{F}_q\}$, where $\operatorname{Tr}$ acts on vectors coordinatewise.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item The map $w\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}(w)$ is an $\mathbb{F}_p$-linear isomorphism $K_\lambda\to\ker\beta(M)$, which carries multiplication by $\lambda$ to $M$.
The simple $M$-submodules of type $\beta$ are exactly the subspaces $U_w$ with $w\ne0$, one for each $\mathbb{F}_q$-line $\mathbb{F}_qw\subseteq K_\lambda$.
They lie in $\ker\beta(M)$, and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}U_w=d$.
\item For $c,c'\in\mathbb{F}_q$ we have $\operatorname{Tr}(cw)^{\top}\operatorname{Tr}(c'w)=\operatorname{Tr}(cc'\,w^{\top}w)$. Hence $U_w$ is totally isotropic if and only if $w^{\top}w=0$.
\item For $y\in\mathbb{F}_p^m$, $y\perp U_w$ if and only if $y^{\top}w=0$. In particular $\Pr_\xi(\bar\xi\perp U_w)=\Pr_\xi(\xi^{\top}w=0)$.
\item $\beta^2\mid\chi_M$ if and only if $(x-\lambda)^2\mid\chi_M$, and this holds if and only if $g\ge2$, or $g=1$ and $w^{\top}w=0$
for $0\ne w\in K_\lambda$. In particular, if $\beta^2\nmid\chi_M$, then no simple submodule of type $\beta$ is totally isotropic.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
(a) For $w\in K_\lambda$ let $w^{(i)}$ be the vector obtained by applying the Frobenius map $a\mapsto a^{p^i}$ to the coordinates of $w$.
Since $M$ has entries in $\mathbb{F}_p$, the map $w\mapsto w^{(i)}$ is a bijection from $K_\lambda$ onto $K_{\lambda^{p^i}}:=\ker(M-\lambda^{p^i})$,
and $\operatorname{Tr}(w)=\sum_{i<d}w^{(i)}$. Moreover $M\operatorname{Tr}(w)=\operatorname{Tr}(Mw)=\operatorname{Tr}(\lambda w)$ and $\beta(M)\operatorname{Tr}(w)=\operatorname{Tr}(\beta(\lambda)w)=0$, so $w\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}(w)$
is an $\mathbb{F}_p$-linear map $K_\lambda\to\ker\beta(M)$ that carries multiplication by $\lambda$ to $M$. The roots $\lambda^{p^i}$, $0\le i<d$,
of $\beta$ are distinct, so the sum of the spaces $K_{\lambda^{p^i}}$ is direct, and $\operatorname{Tr}(w)=0$ forces $w=0$. Thus the map is injective.
Over $\mathbb{F}_q$, the kernel of $\beta(M)$ is $\bigoplus_iK_{\lambda^{p^i}}$, which has dimension $dg$, and the dimension of a kernel does not
change under field extensions. Hence $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}\ker\beta(M)=dg=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}K_\lambda$, and the map is bijective. So $\ker\beta(M)$, as an
$\mathbb{F}_p[x]$-module, is isomorphic to $K_\lambda$ with $x$ acting as $\lambda$, that is, to an $\mathbb{F}_q$-vector space, as $\mathbb{F}_p[\lambda]=\mathbb{F}_q$. Its
submodules correspond to $\mathbb{F}_q$-subspaces, and the simple ones to the $\mathbb{F}_q$-lines $\mathbb{F}_qw$, whose images are the $U_w$. Every simple
submodule of type $\beta$ is killed by $\beta(M)$, hence lies in $\ker\beta(M)$.

(b) Eigenvectors $y,y'$ of the symmetric matrix $M$ for distinct eigenvalues $\mu\ne\nu$ are orthogonal for the bilinear form, because
$\mu\,y^{\top}y'=(My)^{\top}y'=y^{\top}My'=\nu\,y^{\top}y'$. Expanding the traces, we get
$\operatorname{Tr}(cw)^{\top}\operatorname{Tr}(c'w)=\sum_{i,j}(cw)^{(i)\top}(c'w)^{(j)}=\sum_i(cc'w^{\top}w)^{p^i}=\operatorname{Tr}(cc'w^{\top}w)$. As the trace form
$(c,c')\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}(cc')$ is nondegenerate, $U_w$ is totally isotropic if and only if $w^{\top}w=0$.

(c) For $y\in\mathbb{F}_p^m$ we have $y^{\top}\operatorname{Tr}(cw)=\operatorname{Tr}(c\,y^{\top}w)$, which vanishes for all $c$ if and only if $y^{\top}w=0$.

(d) As $\chi_M$ has coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_p$, applying the automorphism $c\mapsto c^{p^i}$ of $\mathbb{F}_q$ shows that ${(x-\lambda)^2\mid\chi_M}$
if and only if $(x-\lambda^{p^i})^2\mid\chi_M$. Since the roots $\lambda^{p^i}$, $0\le i<d$, of $\beta$ are distinct, this gives the
first equivalence. Next, $(x-\lambda)^2\mid\chi_M$ if and only if $\chi_M(\lambda)=\chi_M'(\lambda)=0$. Put $N:=\lambda I-M$. Then
$\chi_M(\lambda)=\det N$ vanishes if and only if $g\ge1$, and $\chi_M'(\lambda)=\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{adj}N$ by Jacobi's formula.
If $g\ge2$, all minors of order $m-1$ of $N$ vanish, so $\operatorname{adj}N=0$. If $g=1$ and $K_\lambda=\mathbb{F}_qw$, then
$\operatorname{adj}N\ne0$, and $N\operatorname{adj}N=\det(N)I=0$ shows that the columns of $\operatorname{adj}N$ lie in $\mathbb{F}_qw$. As
$\operatorname{adj}N$ is symmetric, like $N$, we get $\operatorname{adj}N=c\,ww^{\top}$ with $c\ne0$, and
$\chi_M'(\lambda)=c\,w^{\top}w$. Hence, if $g\ge1$, then $\chi_M'(\lambda)=0$ if and only if $g\ge2$, or $g=1$ and $w^{\top}w=0$, which
proves the second equivalence. Finally, if $\beta^2\nmid\chi_M$, then $K_\lambda=0$, or
$K_\lambda=\mathbb{F}_qw$ with $w^{\top}w\ne0$, and by (a) and (b) no simple submodule of type $\beta$ is totally isotropic.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:switch}
Let $\Sigma$ be a uniformly random diagonal sign matrix independent of $A$, and put ${S':=\Sigma S\Sigma}$ and $u:=\Sigma e$. Then $S'$ and
$u$ are independent, $S'$ is a uniformly random Seidel matrix, and $u$ is uniform on $\{\pm1\}^n$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
For each fixed diagonal sign matrix $\sigma$ with diagonal entries $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n$, the map $S\mapsto\sigma S\sigma$ multiplies
the entry $(i,j)$ by $\sigma_i\sigma_j$ and is a bijection of the set of Seidel matrices of order $n$. Hence
$(S,\Sigma)\mapsto(\Sigma S\Sigma,\Sigma)$ is a bijection of the product of this set with the set of diagonal sign matrices, and
$(S',\Sigma)$ is uniform on this product, like $(S,\Sigma)$. So $S'$ is uniform and independent of $\Sigma$, and $u=\Sigma e$, the vector
of diagonal entries of $\Sigma$, is uniform on $\{\pm1\}^n$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:Epswitch}
Let $p$ be odd, and let $\Sigma$, $S'$ and $u$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:switch}. Then $E_p^{(d)}$ holds for $G$ if and only if $\bar S'$ has a
totally isotropic simple submodule $U$ of some type $\beta$ with $\deg\beta=d$ and $U\perp\bar u$. In that case $\beta$ is a repeated
factor of $S'$ at $p$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
On $\bar e^{\perp}$ we have $\bar A=-\frac12(I+\bar S)$. So a subspace $U\perp\bar e$ is $\bar A$-stable if and only if it is
$\bar S$-stable, and as the same holds for the subspaces of $U$, it is a simple $\bar A$-submodule if and only if it is a simple
$\bar S$-submodule. The map $\Sigma$ preserves the bilinear form, satisfies $\bar S'\Sigma=\Sigma\bar S$, and maps $\bar e^{\perp}$ to
$\bar u^{\perp}$. So $U\mapsto\Sigma U$ is a type-preserving bijection from the totally isotropic simple $\bar S$-submodules orthogonal to
$\bar e$ onto the totally isotropic simple $\bar S'$-submodules orthogonal to $\bar u$. As a simple submodule has the degree of its type as
its dimension, this proves the equivalence. By Lemma~\ref{lem:simple}(d), a totally
isotropic simple submodule of type $\beta$ exists only if $\beta^2$ divides $\chi_{S'}$ modulo $p$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:border}
Let $F$ be a field, let $L\in F^{r\times r}$ be symmetric with kernel $K$, let $y\in F^r$ and $c\in F$, and put
\[
L^+:=\begin{pmatrix}L&y\\ y^{\top}&c\end{pmatrix}.
\]
We write the vectors of $F^{r+1}$ as pairs $(v,t)$ with $v\in F^r$ and $t\in F$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item If $y\not\perp K$, then $\ker L^+=(K\cap y^{\perp})\times\{0\}$, so that $\operatorname{corank} L^+=\operatorname{corank} L-1$.
\item If $y\perp K$, then $y=Ly_0$ for some $y_0\in F^r$, and $y^{\top}y_0$ does not depend on the choice of $y_0$. If moreover
$c\ne y^{\top}y_0$, then $\ker L^+=K\times\{0\}$, so that $\operatorname{corank} L^+=\operatorname{corank} L$. If $c=y^{\top}y_0$, then
$\ker L^+=\{(v-ty_0,t):\ v\in K,\ t\in F\}$, so that $\operatorname{corank} L^+=\operatorname{corank} L+1$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular $\lvert\operatorname{corank} L^+-\operatorname{corank} L\rvert\le1$, and $\operatorname{corank} L^+\ge\operatorname{corank} L$ if and only if $y\perp K$. If $L$ is invertible, then
$\operatorname{corank} L^+\le1$, with equality if and only if $c=y^{\top}L^{-1}y$, and in that case $\ker L^+$ is spanned by $(L^{-1}y,-1)$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
As $L$ is symmetric, its image is $K^{\perp}$, since it is contained in $K^{\perp}$ and both have dimension $r-\dim K$. A pair $(v,t)$
lies in $\ker L^+$ if and only if $Lv+ty=0$ and $y^{\top}v+tc=0$. (a) If $y\notin K^{\perp}=\operatorname{Im}L$, the first equation
forces $t=0$, and then the two equations say that $v\in K\cap y^{\perp}$, a hyperplane of $K$. (b) If $y=Ly_0$, then $y^{\top}y_0$ does not
depend on $y_0$, as two choices differ by a vector of $K$, which is orthogonal to $y$. The first equation says that $v+ty_0\in K$, and then
$y^{\top}v=y_0^{\top}Lv=-t\,y_0^{\top}Ly_0=-t\,y^{\top}y_0$, so that the second equation reads
$t(c-y^{\top}y_0)=0$. If $c\ne y^{\top}y_0$, this forces $t=0$, so that $\ker L^+=K\times\{0\}$. If $c=y^{\top}y_0$, it holds for every
$t\in F$, so that $\ker L^+$ is the space $\{(v-ty_0,t):\ v\in K,\ t\in F\}$, which has dimension $\dim K+1$. This proves (b), and the
remaining claims follow from (a) and (b), with $K=0$ and $y_0=L^{-1}y$ if $L$ is invertible.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:apriori}
Let $p$ be a prime with $p\nmid a-b$, let $\lambda\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$, and put $g_\lambda(M):=\dim_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p}\ker(\bar M-\lambda I)$. Then
\[
\mathbb{E}\big(2^{g_\lambda(M)^2/4}\big)\le30,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad\Pr\bigl(g_\lambda(M)\ge r\bigr)\le30\cdot2^{-r^2/4}\quad(r\ge0).
\]
Moreover $\mathbb{E}\big(10^{g_\lambda(M)}\big)\le C_0:=1+30\sum_{r\ge1}10^r2^{-r^2/4}<\infty$, for all such $p$ and all $\lambda$ and $m$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
For $1\le k\le m$ let $M_k$ be the leading principal $k\times k$ submatrix of $M$, and put $L_k:=\bar M_k-\lambda I$,
$K_k:=\ker L_k\subseteq\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p^k$ and $r_k:=\dim K_k=g_\lambda(M_k)$. For $k<m$ let $y\in\{a,b\}^k$ be the part of column $k+1$ of
$M$ above the diagonal. It is uniform and independent of $M_k$, and
\[
L_{k+1}=\begin{pmatrix}L_k&\bar y\\ \bar y^{\top}&-\lambda\end{pmatrix}.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:border}, applied over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$ with $L=L_k$, we have $|r_{k+1}-r_k|\le1$, and $r_{k+1}\ge r_k$ only if
$\bar y\perp K_k$. The vectors $z\in\mathbb{F}_p^k$ with $z\perp K_k$ form an $\mathbb{F}_p$-subspace of dimension at most $k-r_k$ (vectors of
$\mathbb{F}_p^k$ that are linearly independent over $\mathbb{F}_p$ remain so over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$, and $K_k^{\perp}$ has dimension $k-r_k$), so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:odlyzko}
\[
\Pr\bigl(r_{k+1}\ge r_k\mid M_k\bigr)\le\Pr\bigl(\bar y\perp K_k\mid M_k\bigr)\le2^{-r_k}.
\]
Put $\Upsilon(r):=2^{r^2/4}$, which is increasing on $r\ge0$. If $r_k\ge3$, the two facts above give
\[
\mathbb{E}\big(\Upsilon(r_{k+1})\mid M_k\big)\le\Upsilon(r_k-1)+2^{-r_k}\Upsilon(r_k+1)=2^{5/4-r_k/2}\,\Upsilon(r_k)\le2^{-1/4}\Upsilon(r_k),
\]
while if $r_k\le2$, then $r_{k+1}\le3$ and $\Upsilon(r_{k+1})\le\Upsilon(3)=2^{9/4}<4.76$. Hence $t_k:=\mathbb{E}(\Upsilon(r_k))$ satisfies
$t_{k+1}\le2^{-1/4}t_k+4.76$, and $t_1\le\Upsilon(1)=2^{1/4}$. By induction $t_k\le4.76/(1-2^{-1/4})<30$ for all $k$. The tail bound
follows by Markov's inequality, and then $\mathbb{E}\big(10^{g_\lambda(M)}\big)\le{\Pr(g_\lambda(M)=0)}+\sum_{r\ge1}10^r\Pr(g_\lambda(M)\ge r)\le C_0$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:kernelpoly}
Let $p$ be a prime with $p\nmid a-b$, and let $d,r\ge1$ be integers. Then, except with probability at most $60\,p^{d-1}2^{-r^2/4}$, every
nonzero $\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_p[x]$ of degree less than $d$ satisfies $\dim\ker\alpha(\bar M)\le(d-1)(r-1)$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The elements $\lambda\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$ of degree less than $d$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ lie in the fields $\mathbb{F}_{p^j}$ with $1\le j<d$, so there are at
most $\sum_{1\le j<d}p^j\le2p^{d-1}$ of them. By Lemma~\ref{lem:apriori} and a union bound, except with probability at most
$60\,p^{d-1}2^{-r^2/4}$, all of them satisfy $g_\lambda(M)\le r-1$. Suppose that this holds, and let $\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_p[x]$ be nonzero of
degree less than $d$. Over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$, $\ker\alpha(\bar M)$ is the direct sum of the spaces $\ker(\bar M-\lambda I)^{k_\lambda}$
over the roots $\lambda$ of $\alpha$, of multiplicities $k_\lambda$, and $\dim\ker N^k\le k\dim\ker N$ for every square matrix $N$ and
every $k\ge1$. As the roots of $\alpha$ have degree less than $d$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ and $\sum_\lambda k_\lambda\le d-1$, we get
$\dim\ker\alpha(\bar M)\le\sum_\lambda k_\lambda g_\lambda(M)\le(d-1)(r-1)$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:suppd}
For all large $m$, with probability at least $1-e^{-m/8}$ the following holds for every prime $p\le e^{m^{1/8}}$ with $p\nmid a-b$, every
$1\le d\le m^{1/4}$, every monic $g\in\mathbb{F}_p[x]$ of degree $d$ and every nonzero $y\in\mathbb{F}_p^m$ with $g(\bar M)y=0$:
$\lvert\operatorname{supp} y\rvert>m/(4(d+1))$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1.}\ We show that a nonzero vector with small support killed by $g(\bar M)$ gives a nonzero kernel vector of a block Krylov
matrix.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $S\subseteq[m]$, $R:=[m]\setminus S$ and $s:=|S|$, and write
\[
\bar M=\begin{pmatrix}\bar M_{S,S}&C^{\top}\\ C&D\end{pmatrix},\qquad C:=\bar M_{R,S},\quad D:=\bar M_{R,R}.
\]
Let $y\ne0$ be supported on $S$ with $g(\bar M)y=0$, where $g=\sum_{k\le d}h_kx^k$ with $h_d=1$, and write
$\bar M^ky=(u_k,w_k)\in\mathbb{F}_p^S\times\mathbb{F}_p^R$. Then $w_0=0$ and $w_{k+1}=Cu_k+Dw_k$, so $w_k=\sum_{j<k}D^{k-1-j}Cu_j$, and the $R$-part of
$g(\bar M)y=0$ reads
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}D^jC\,z_j=0,\qquad z_j:=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1-j}h_{i+j+1}u_i,\qquad z_{d-1}=u_0=y_S\ne0 .
\]
So the block Krylov matrix $K_S:=[\,C\,|\,DC\,|\,\cdots\,|\,D^{d-1}C\,]\in\mathbb{F}_p^{R\times ds}$ has a nonzero kernel vector. It suffices to
show that, with the stated probability, $K_S$ has trivial kernel for all $p$, all $d$ and all $S$ with $1\le s\le m/(4(d+1))$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}\ We show that, except with a very small probability, $\alpha(D)$ has a small kernel for every nonzero $\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_p[x]$ of
degree less than $d$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces The matrix $D$ is the reduction of $M_{R,R}$, a random matrix of the same kind as $M$ of order $m-s$. Put
$r_0:=\lceil m^{0.55}\rceil$, so that $r_0^2\ge m^{1.1}$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:kernelpoly}, applied to $M_{R,R}$ with $r=r_0$, except with
probability at most $60\,p^{d-1}2^{-m^{1.1}/4}$ we have $\dim\ker\alpha(D)\le(d-1)(r_0-1)<\kappa_0:=dr_0$ for all such~$\alpha$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 3.}\ We expose the columns of $C$ one at a time and bound the probability that $K_S$ has a nonzero kernel vector.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces The matrix $D$
and the columns $c_i$, $i\in S$, of $M_{R,S}$ are independent, as they consist of
different entries of $M$, and each $c_i$ is uniform on $\{a,b\}^R$. Fix $D$ with $\dim\ker\alpha(D)<\kappa_0$ for all $\alpha$ as above,
and add the column groups $(\bar c_i,D\bar c_i,\dots,D^{d-1}\bar c_i)$, $i\in S$, one at a time. If $V$ is the span of the groups added so
far, so that $\dim V\le d(s-1)$, the new group fails to add $d$ dimensions if and only if $\alpha(D)\bar c_i\in V$ for some nonzero
$\alpha$ of degree $<d$, which we may take monic (at most $2p^{d-1}$ choices). For a fixed $\alpha$ this says that $\bar c_i$ lies in the
subspace $\alpha(D)^{-1}(V)$, of dimension at most $\dim V+\dim\ker\alpha(D)$, which has probability at most
$2^{d(s-1)+\kappa_0-(m-s)}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:odlyzko}. If every group adds $d$ dimensions, $K_S$ has rank $ds$. So $K_S$ has a nonzero
kernel vector with probability at most
\[
60\,p^{d-1}2^{-m^{1.1}/4}+2s\,p^{d-1}2^{(d+1)s+\kappa_0-m}.
\]

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 4.}\ We take a union bound over the primes $p$, the degrees $d$ and the sets $S$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces There are at most $m^{1/4}e^{m^{1/8}}$ pairs
$(p,d)$, and $p^{d-1}\le e^{m^{3/8}}$ and $\kappa_0\le2m^{0.8}$. As $s\le m/(4(d+1))\le m/8$, for each pair there are at most
$2^{H(1/8)m}\le2^{0.544m}$ sets $S$, and $(d+1)s\le m/4$. Since moreover $m^{1.1}/4\ge m$ for large $m$, both terms of the bound of
Step~3 are at most $e^{o(m)}2^{-0.75m}$. So the total is at most $e^{o(m)}2^{(0.544-0.75)m}\le e^{-m/8}$ for large $m$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:support}
Let $T$ be a uniformly random Seidel matrix of order $m$. With probability ${1-O(2^{-m/8})}$ the following holds: for every odd
prime $p$, every $\lambda\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$ and every nonzero $w\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p^{\,m}$ with $\bar Tw=\lambda w$, one has
$\lvert\operatorname{supp} w\rvert>m/20$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
We may assume that $m$ is large. Put $k:=\lfloor m/20\rfloor\ge1$. Every $w\ne0$ with $\lvert\operatorname{supp} w\rvert\le m/20$ has its support in a set
$I\subseteq[m]$ with $|I|=k$, and there are $\binom mk\le2^{H(k/m)m}\le2^{H(1/20)m}\le2^{0.287m}$ such sets, as $H$ is increasing on
$[0,\frac12]$. For a fixed $I$, if $\operatorname{supp} w\subseteq I$ and $\bar Tw=\lambda w$, then for every $i\notin I$
\[
0=\lambda w_i=(\bar Tw)_i=\sum_{j\in I}T_{ij}w_j ,
\]
so the $(m-k)\times k$ matrix $M:=T_{I^c,I}$ has the nonzero kernel vector $w_I$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$. As the rank does not change
under field extensions, $\operatorname{rank}_pM<k$. The entries of $M$ are independent uniform signs, since none of them lies on the diagonal and no
two of them are symmetric to each other. Let $Y$ consist of the first $N_1:=\lfloor(m-k)/2\rfloor$ rows of $M$, and $Z$ of the
remaining $N_2:=m-k-N_1\ge N_1$ rows. Then $Y$ and $Z$ are independent, and $k-N_2\le k-N_1\le k-\frac{m-k-1}2\le\frac12-0.425m$.

The columns of $Y$ are independent and uniform on $\{\pm1\}^{N_1}$, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:odlyzko} over $\mathbb{Q}$, we have $\operatorname{rank}_\mathbb{Q} Y<k$
with probability at most $2^{k-N_1}$. Suppose that $\operatorname{rank}_\mathbb{Q} Y=k$, and choose, as a function of $Y$, a nonzero $k\times k$ minor $\kappa$
of $Y$. By Hadamard's inequality $|\kappa|\le k^{k/2}$, so $\kappa$ has at most $\frac k2\log_2k$ prime factors, and
$\operatorname{rank}_pM\ge\operatorname{rank}_pY=k$ for every prime $p\nmid\kappa$. For each odd prime $p\mid\kappa$, as $Z$ is independent of $Y$ and is a submatrix
of $M$, Lemma~\ref{lem:odlyzko} over $\mathbb{F}_p$, applied to the reductions of the columns of $Z$, gives
$\Pr(\operatorname{rank}_pM<k\mid Y)\le\Pr(\operatorname{rank}_pZ<k)\le2^{k-N_2}$. Summing over the at most $\frac k2\log_2k$ odd primes $p\mid\kappa$,
and adding the bound $2^{k-N_1}$ for the probability that $\operatorname{rank}_\mathbb{Q} Y<k$, we get
\begin{equation}\label{eq:supportI}
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{rank}_pM<k\text{ for some odd prime }p\bigr)\ \le\ \Big(1+\frac k2\log_2k\Big)2^{\frac12-0.425m}\ \le\ m^2\,2^{-0.425m},
\end{equation}
and a union bound over the sets $I$ shows that the conclusion of the proposition fails with probability at most
$m^22^{(0.287-0.425)m}=O(2^{-m/8})$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:delete}
Let $F$ be a field, $B\in F^{m\times m}$ symmetric with kernel $K$, and $i\in[m]$ such that $w_i\ne0$ for some $w\in K$. Let
$B^{(i)}$ be the matrix obtained from $B$ by deleting row and column $i$, and $b_i\in F^{m-1}$ the $i$th column of $B$ with its $i$th
entry deleted. Then $\dim\ker B^{(i)}=\dim K-1$, $\ker B^{(i)}\subseteq b_i^{\perp}$, and $K\cap e_i^{\perp}$ consists of the vectors
obtained from the vectors of $\ker B^{(i)}$ by inserting a zero in position $i$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
After a simultaneous permutation of the rows and columns we may assume that $i=m$. Then $B=L^+$ in the notation of
Lemma~\ref{lem:border}, with $L:=B^{(m)}$, $y:=b_m$ and $c:=B_{mm}$, and some vector of $K=\ker L^+$ has nonzero last coordinate. This
excludes case (a) of Lemma~\ref{lem:border} and the first case of (b). So $b_m\perp\ker B^{(m)}$, $\dim K=\dim\ker B^{(m)}+1$, and the
vectors of $K$ with last coordinate $0$ are the vectors $(v,0)$ with $v\in\ker B^{(m)}$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:exch}
Let $T$ be a uniformly random Seidel matrix of order $m\ge2$. For $i\in[m]$ let $T^{(i)}$ be the matrix obtained from $T$ by deleting
row and column $i$, and let $t_i\in\{\pm1\}^{m-1}$ be the $i$th column of $T$ with its $i$th entry deleted. Then $(T^{(m)},t_m)$ has the
law of $(S_{m-1},\xi)$, where $\xi$ is uniform in $\{\pm1\}^{m-1}$ and independent of $S_{m-1}$. Let $\Phi$ be a set of pairs consisting
of a Seidel matrix of order $m-1$ and a vector in $\{\pm1\}^{m-1}$, and let $\mathcal F_i$ be the event that $(T^{(i)},t_i)\in\Phi$. Then
$\Pr(\mathcal F_i)=\Pr(\mathcal F_m)$ for all $i$. Moreover, if $\mathcal E$ is an event on which more than $m/20$ indices $i\in[m]$
satisfy $\mathcal F_i$, then
\[
\Pr(\mathcal E)\le20\Pr(\mathcal F_m).
\]
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The matrix $T^{(m)}$ is formed by the entries $T_{jk}$, $j<k<m$, and $t_m$ by the entries $T_{jm}$, $j<m$. These are disjoint sets of
independent uniform signs, which gives the first claim. Fix $i$ and let $\tilde T$ be obtained from $T$ by listing the rows and columns
in the order $1,\dots,i-1,i+1,\dots,m,i$. A simultaneous permutation of rows and columns is a bijection of the set of Seidel matrices of
order $m$, so $\tilde T$ is again uniformly random, and $(\tilde T^{(m)},\tilde t_m)=(T^{(i)},t_i)$. Hence $(T^{(i)},t_i)$ has the law
of $(T^{(m)},t_m)$, and $\Pr(\mathcal F_i)=\Pr(\mathcal F_m)$. Finally, with $N:=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf 1_{\mathcal F_i}$,
\[
\frac m{20}\Pr(\mathcal E)\le\mathbb{E}\big(N;\ \mathcal E\big)\le\mathbb{E}(N)=\sum_{i=1}^m\Pr(\mathcal F_i)=m\Pr(\mathcal F_m).
\qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:Npi}
Let $T$ be a symmetric integer matrix of order $m$, $p$ an odd prime, and $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_p[x]$ monic irreducible. Put
\[
a_\beta(T):=\max_U\Pr_\xi\bigl(\bar\xi\perp U\bigr),
\]
the maximum over the simple $\bar T$-submodules $U\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p^m$ of type $\beta$, with $a_\beta(T):=0$ if there is none. For a set
$\Pi$ of pairs $(p,d)$, $p$ an odd prime and $d\ge1$, put
\[
N_\Pi(T):=\sum_{(p,\beta)}a_\beta(T)\ \in[0,\infty],
\]
the sum running over all pairs $(p,\beta)$ such that $(p,\deg\beta)\in\Pi$ and $\beta$ is a repeated factor of $T$ at $p$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:reduction}
For all sufficiently large $n$ let $\Pi_n$ be a set of pairs $(p,d)$ with $p$ an odd prime and $d\ge1$, and for $m\in\{n-1,n\}$ let
$\mathcal G_m$ be a set of Seidel matrices of order $m$ (equivalently, an event depending only on $S_m$), which may depend on $n$.
Suppose that, for $m\in\{n-1,n\}$,
\[
\Pr(S_m\notin\mathcal G_m)\to0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{E}\big(N_{\Pi_n}(S_m);\ S_m\in\mathcal G_m\big)\to0\qquad(n\to\infty).
\]
Then, for the random graph $G(n,1/2)$, the probability that $E_p^{(d)}$ holds for some $(p,d)\in\Pi_n$ tends to~$0$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Let $n$ be large and put $\Pi:=\Pi_n$. Let $\Sigma$, $S'=\Sigma S\Sigma$ and $u=\Sigma e$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:switch}. Thus $S'$ is a
uniformly random Seidel matrix of order $n$, and $u$ is uniform in $\{\pm1\}^n$ and independent of $S'$. Let $\mathcal S$ be the event
that the conclusion of Proposition~\ref{lem:support} holds for $S'$. Let $\mathcal C$ be the set of pairs $(p,\beta)$ such that
$(p,\deg\beta)\in\Pi$ and $\beta$ is a repeated factor of $S'$ at $p$. For $(p,\beta)\in\mathcal C$ fix a root $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_q$ of
$\beta$, $q=p^{\deg\beta}$, and put $K_\lambda:=\ker(\bar S'-\lambda I)\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q^n$ and $g:=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}K_\lambda$. Note that $g\ge1$,
as $\beta$ divides $\chi_{S'}$ modulo $p$. Let $\mathcal C_1$ be the set of the pairs in $\mathcal C$ with $g=1$, let $\mathcal C_2$ be
the set of the pairs with $g=2$ such that $w^{\top}w\ne0$ for some $w\in K_\lambda$, and let $\mathcal C_3$ be the set of the remaining
pairs, those with $g\ge3$ or with $g=2$ and $w^{\top}w=0$ for all $w\in K_\lambda$.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:Epswitch}, if $E_p^{(d)}$ holds for some $(p,d)\in\Pi$, then there are $(p,\beta)\in\mathcal C$ and a totally
isotropic simple $\bar S'$-submodule $U$ of type $\beta$ with $U\perp\bar u$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:simple}(a),(b), the simple
submodules of type $\beta$ are the subspaces $U_w$, one for each $\mathbb{F}_q$-line $\mathbb{F}_qw\subseteq K_\lambda$, and $U_w$ is totally isotropic
if and only if $w^{\top}w=0$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1.}\ We bound the contribution of the pairs in $\mathcal C_1\cup\mathcal C_2$, which have at most two totally isotropic simple
submodules of type $\beta$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces For a pair in $\mathcal C_1$ there is exactly one simple submodule of type $\beta$. For a pair in
$\mathcal C_2$, choose a basis $w_1,w_2$ of $K_\lambda$. Then
$(\theta_1w_1+\theta_2w_2)^{\top}(\theta_1w_1+\theta_2w_2)=\alpha\theta_1^2+2\gamma\theta_1\theta_2+\alpha'\theta_2^2$ with
$\alpha:=w_1^{\top}w_1$, $\gamma:=w_1^{\top}w_2$ and $\alpha':=w_2^{\top}w_2$, and this binary form is not the zero polynomial, since it
takes a nonzero value. A nonzero binary quadratic form vanishes on at most two points of the projective line, as it is a product of two
linear forms over an algebraic closure. So $K_\lambda$ contains at most two lines $\mathbb{F}_qw$ with $w^{\top}w=0$. In both cases at most two
simple submodules of type $\beta$ are totally isotropic. Since $u$ is uniform and independent of $S'$, each of them is orthogonal to
$\bar u$ with conditional probability at most $a_\beta(S')$ given $S'$. Hence, by a union bound given $S'$, the probability that
$S'\in\mathcal G_n$ and that some $(p,\beta)\in\mathcal C_1\cup\mathcal C_2$ admits a totally isotropic simple submodule $U$ of type
$\beta$ with $U\perp\bar u$ is at most
\[
\mathbb{E}\Bigl(\sum_{(p,\beta)\in\mathcal C}2a_\beta(S');\ S'\in\mathcal G_n\Bigr)=2\,\mathbb{E}\big(N_\Pi(S_n);\ S_n\in\mathcal G_n\big).
\]

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}\ We bound the contribution of the pairs in $\mathcal C_3$ by deleting a coordinate and using exchangeability.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $\mathcal F$
be the event that $\mathcal C_3\ne\emptyset$. This event depends only on $S'$, and we do not use $u$ in this step. The role of the sign
vector is played by a column of $S'$, which we delete together with the corresponding row. For $i\in[n]$ let $T_i$ be the matrix obtained
from $S'$ by deleting row and column $i$, a Seidel matrix of order $n-1$, and let $s_i\in\{\pm1\}^{n-1}$ be the $i$th column of $S'$ with
its $i$th entry deleted, so that $(T_i,s_i)$ is the pair $(T^{(i)},t_i)$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:exch} for $T=S'$. Consider the event
\begin{quote}
$\mathcal F_i$: for some $(p,\beta)$ with $(p,\deg\beta)\in\Pi$, $\beta$ is a repeated factor of $T_i$ at $p$ and
${\bar s_i\perp\ker\beta(\bar T_i)}$.
\end{quote}
On $\mathcal F\cap\mathcal S$ take $(p,\beta)\in\mathcal C_3$, with $\lambda$, $K_\lambda$ and $g$ as above. On $\mathcal S$ every
nonzero $w\in K_\lambda$ has more than $n/20$ nonzero coordinates, so the set $\mathcal I$ of indices $i$ such that $w_i\ne0$ for some
$w\in K_\lambda$ has more than $n/20$ elements. For $i\in\mathcal I$, Lemma~\ref{lem:delete}, applied over $\mathbb{F}_q$ to the symmetric matrix
$B=\bar S'-\lambda I$ (so that $B^{(i)}=\bar T_i-\lambda I$ and $b_i=\bar s_i$), shows that $\dim\ker(\bar T_i-\lambda I)=g-1$, that
$\ker(\bar T_i-\lambda I)\subseteq\bar s_i^{\perp}$, and that inserting a zero in position $i$ maps $\ker(\bar T_i-\lambda I)$ into
$K_\lambda$. Hence $\beta$ is a repeated factor of $T_i$ at $p$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:simple}(d) for $\bar T_i$. Indeed, if $g\ge3$, then
$\dim\ker(\bar T_i-\lambda I)=g-1\ge2$, and if $g=2$, then $\ker(\bar T_i-\lambda I)$ is a line $\mathbb{F}_qw'$ with
$w'^{\top}w'=\hat w^{\top}\hat w=0$, where $\hat w\in K_\lambda$ is obtained from $w'$ by inserting a zero. Moreover, by
Lemma~\ref{lem:simple}(a) every vector of $\ker\beta(\bar T_i)$ has the form $\operatorname{Tr}(v)$ with $v\in\ker(\bar T_i-\lambda I)$, and
$\bar s_i^{\top}\operatorname{Tr}(v)=\operatorname{Tr}(\bar s_i^{\top}v)=0$, as $\bar s_i$ has entries in $\mathbb{F}_p$. So $\bar s_i\perp\ker\beta(\bar T_i)$. Thus, on
$\mathcal F\cap\mathcal S$, the event $\mathcal F_i$ holds for more than $n/20$ indices $i$. As $\mathcal F_i$ is the event that
$(T_i,s_i)$ lies in a fixed set of pairs, Lemma~\ref{lem:exch} (for $T=S'$ and $\mathcal E=\mathcal F\cap\mathcal S$) gives
\[
\Pr(\mathcal F\cap\mathcal S)\le20\Pr(\mathcal F_n).
\]
By the same lemma, $T_n$ is a uniformly random Seidel matrix of order $n-1$, and $s_n$ is uniform in $\{\pm1\}^{n-1}$ and independent of
$T_n$. If $\beta$ is a repeated factor of $T_n$ at $p$, then $\bar T_n$ has an eigenvector for a root of $\beta$, so $\ker\beta(\bar T_n)$
contains a simple submodule $U$ of type $\beta$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:simple}(a)). Then ${\bar s_n\perp\ker\beta(\bar T_n)}$ implies
$\bar s_n\perp U$, which has conditional probability at most $a_\beta(T_n)$ given $T_n$. Summing over the pairs, the conditional
probability of $\mathcal F_n$ given $T_n$ is at most $N_\Pi(T_n)$. As $T_n$ has the law of $S_{n-1}$, we get
\[
\Pr(\mathcal F_n)\le\Pr(S_{n-1}\notin\mathcal G_{n-1})+\mathbb{E}\big(N_\Pi(S_{n-1});\ S_{n-1}\in\mathcal G_{n-1}\big).
\]

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 3.}\ We combine the bounds of Steps~1 and~2 and conclude the proof.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces The event that $E_p^{(d)}$ holds for some $(p,d)\in\Pi$ is
contained in the union of the event $S'\notin\mathcal G_n$, the event bounded in Step~1, the event $\mathcal F\cap\mathcal S$, and
$\mathcal S^c$. Since $S'$ has the law of $S_n$, adding the four bounds gives
\begin{multline*}
\Pr\bigl(E_p^{(d)}\text{ holds for some }(p,d)\in\Pi\bigr)\ \le\ \Pr(S_n\notin\mathcal G_n)+2\,\mathbb{E}\big(N_\Pi(S_n);\ S_n\in\mathcal G_n\big)\\
+20\Bigl(\Pr(S_{n-1}\notin\mathcal G_{n-1})+\mathbb{E}\big(N_\Pi(S_{n-1});\ S_{n-1}\in\mathcal G_{n-1}\big)\Bigr)+\Pr(\mathcal S^c).
\end{multline*}
All terms but the last tend to $0$ by hypothesis, and the last is $O(2^{-n/8})$ by Proposition~\ref{lem:support}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:budget}
Let $T$ be a symmetric integer matrix of order $m$ with $\Delta_T\ne0$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item For every prime $p$, $\sum_\beta\deg\beta\le v_p(\Delta_T)$, the sum running over the repeated factors $\beta$ of $T$ at~$p$.
\item If all eigenvalues of $T$ lie in $[-m,m]$ (for instance, if $T$ is a Seidel matrix), then ${|\Delta_T|\le(2m)^{m(m-1)}}$. Hence, for
every real $P\ge2$, the number of pairs $(p,\beta)$ with $p>P$ prime and $\beta$ a repeated factor of $T$ at $p$ is at most
$m^2\log(2m)/\log P$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
(a) Let $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m$ be the eigenvalues of $T$, and put $\chi:=\chi_T$ and $N:=\chi'(T)\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times m}$. Since
$\chi'(\lambda_i)=\prod_{j\ne i}(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)$, we have
$\det N=\prod_i\chi'(\lambda_i)=\pm\prod_{i<j}(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)^2=\pm\Delta_T$.
By the Smith normal form of $N$, $p^r$ divides $\det N$, where $r:=\dim\ker\bar N$. If $\beta$ is a repeated factor of $T$ at $p$, then
$\beta\mid\bar\chi'$, as $\beta^2\mid\bar\chi$, so $\ker\beta(\bar T)\subseteq\ker\bar N$. Moreover $\ker\beta(\bar T)\ne0$, as the roots
of $\beta$ are eigenvalues of $\bar T$, and $\ker\beta(\bar T)$ is a vector space over the field $\mathbb{F}_p[x]/(\beta)$, with $x$ acting as
$\bar T$, so its dimension is at least $\deg\beta$. Distinct monic irreducible polynomials are coprime, so the sum of the subspaces
$\ker\beta(\bar T)$ over the repeated factors $\beta$ of $T$ at $p$ is direct. Hence $\sum_\beta\deg\beta\le r\le v_p(\Delta_T)$.

(b) The eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m$ of $T$ are real, and $\Delta_T=\prod_{i<j}(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)^2$ with
$|\lambda_i-\lambda_j|\le2m$, so $|\Delta_T|\le(2m)^{m(m-1)}$. (The eigenvalues of a Seidel matrix have absolute value at most its largest
absolute row sum, $m-1$.) By (a), the number of pairs in question is at most
$\sum_{p>P}v_p(\Delta_T)\le\sum_{p>P}v_p(\Delta_T)\frac{\log p}{\log P}\le\frac{\log|\Delta_T|}{\log P}\le\frac{m(m-1)\log(2m)}{\log P}$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:simplespectrum}
$\Pr(\Delta_{S_m}=0)\to0$ as $m\to\infty$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The discriminant $\Delta_{S_m}=\prod_{i<j}(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)^2$, where $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m$ are the eigenvalues of $S_m$,
vanishes if and only if $S_m$ has a repeated eigenvalue. By a theorem of Tao--Vu~\cite[Theorem~1.3]{TV17}, a real symmetric random
matrix whose entries above the diagonal are independent copies of a fixed non-degenerate random variable, and whose diagonal entries
are independent of them (they may be deterministic, and here they are $0$), has simple spectrum with probability $1-O(m^{-C})$ for every
fixed $C>0$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Let $n\ge2$, let $\Pi_n$ be the set of pairs $(p,d)$ with $p$ an odd prime and ${d\ge3\log_2n}$, and for $m\in\{n-1,n\}$ let $\mathcal G_m$ be
the set of Seidel matrices $T$ of order $m$ with $\Delta_T\ne0$. By Theorem~\ref{lem:simplespectrum}, $\Pr(S_m\notin\mathcal G_m)\to0$. Let
$T\in\mathcal G_m$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:budget}(b) with $P=2$, there are at most $m^2\log(2m)/\log2\le n^2\log_2(2n)$ pairs $(p,\beta)$ such
that $p$ is an odd prime and $\beta$ is a repeated factor of $T$ at $p$. By~\eqref{eq:abetaodl}, each of them that is counted in
$N_{\Pi_n}(T)$ contributes $a_\beta(T)\le2^{-\deg\beta}\le2^{-3\log_2n}=n^{-3}$. Hence $N_{\Pi_n}(T)\le\log_2(2n)/n$, so
$\mathbb{E}(N_{\Pi_n}(S_m);\ S_m\in\mathcal G_m)\to0$ for $m\in\{n-1,n\}$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:reduction} proves the theorem.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:form}
For $f,g\in R_\mathbb{Q}$ we have $\iota(f)^{\top}\iota(g)=\operatorname{Tr}_{R_\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Q}}\bigl(fg\,\psi/\varphi'\bigr)$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Since $e=\sum_i\alpha_iv_i$, we have $\iota(f)=\sum_i\alpha_if(\lambda_i)v_i$, so by~\eqref{eq:loc-psi}
\[
\iota(f)^{\top}\iota(g)=\sum_i\alpha_i^2f(\lambda_i)g(\lambda_i)=\sum_if(\lambda_i)g(\lambda_i)\,
\frac{\psi(\lambda_i)}{\varphi'(\lambda_i)}=\operatorname{Tr}_{R_\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Q}}\bigl(fg\,\psi/\varphi'\bigr).\qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:D}
We have $C^*=\iota(\psi^{-1}R)$, and $f\mapsto\iota(f/\psi)+C$ induces an isomorphism of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$-modules
\[
\mathcal T=\mathbb{Z}[x]/(\varphi,\psi)\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ D ,
\]
where $x$ acts on $D$ as $A$. Moreover $|\mathcal T|=|D|=(\det W)^2$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
By Euler's lemma (see Serre (1979)~\cite[Ch.~III, \S6]{Serre}, whose proof applies to every monic separable $\varphi$) the trace dual $\{g\in
R_\mathbb{Q}:\ \operatorname{Tr}_{R_\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Q}}(gR)\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\}$ of $R$ is $\varphi'^{-1}R$. For $g\in R_\mathbb{Q}$, Lemma~\ref{lem:form} shows that $\iota(g)\in C^*$ if and
only if $\operatorname{Tr}_{R_\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Q}}(gf\psi/\varphi')\in\mathbb{Z}$ for all $f\in R$, that is, if and only if $g\psi/\varphi'\in\varphi'^{-1}R$, or equivalently
$g\psi\in R$. Hence $C^*=\iota(\psi^{-1}R)$, and $f\mapsto\iota(f/\psi)+C$ maps $R$ onto $D$ with kernel $\psi R$. As $R/\psi R=\mathcal T$
and $\iota$ commutes with multiplication by $x$, this is the asserted isomorphism. Finally $y\mapsto W^{\top}y$ maps
$C^*=(W^{\top})^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^n$ onto $\mathbb{Z}^n$ and $C$ onto $W^{\top}W\mathbb{Z}^n$, so $|D|=\det(W^{\top}W)=(\det W)^2$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:ideals}
Let $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$. The lattice $\Lambda_Q:=Q\mathbb{Z}^n$ is $A$-stable and unimodular, and $C\subseteq\Lambda_Q\subseteq C^*$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
We have $e=Qe\in\Lambda_Q$. The matrix $B:=Q^{\top}AQ$ is integral and $AQ=QB$, so $A\Lambda_Q=QB\mathbb{Z}^n\subseteq\Lambda_Q$, and hence
$C=\mathbb{Z}[A]e\subseteq\Lambda_Q$. As $Q$ is orthogonal, $\Lambda_Q^*=(Q^{\top})^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^n=\Lambda_Q$, and dualizing $C\subseteq\Lambda_Q$ gives
$\Lambda_Q\subseteq C^*$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:loc-lagr}
The discriminant pairing $b(y+C,y'+C):=y^{\top}y'\bmod\mathbb{Z}$ is a well-defined nondegenerate symmetric pairing on $D$ with values in $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$,
because $C^{**}=C$, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:D} and Lemma~\ref{lem:form} it corresponds on $\mathcal T$ to
$b(f,g)=\operatorname{Tr}_{R_\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Q}}\bigl(fg/(\psi\varphi')\bigr)\bmod\mathbb{Z}$. As $b(f,g)$ only depends on $fg$, nondegeneracy shows that the orthogonal of an
ideal $\mathfrak a$ of $\mathcal T$ is its annihilator. For a lattice $C\subseteq\Lambda\subseteq C^*$, the orthogonal of $\Lambda/C$ for $b$ is
$\Lambda^*/C$. So Lemma~\ref{lem:ideals} says that $\Lambda_Q/C$ is a \emph{Lagrangian ideal} of $\mathcal T\cong D$, that is, an ideal
equal to its orthogonal, or equivalently to its annihilator, and the identity matrix gives the Lagrangian ideal $\mathbb{Z}^n/C=\operatorname{coker} W$. We shall
not use the pairing, only the consequence $|\Lambda/C|^2=|D|$ of~\eqref{eq:loc-index} for unimodular $\Lambda$, in the local form of
Lemma~\ref{lem:loccomp}(b) and of Step~1 of the proof of Proposition~\ref{lem:levellocal}.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:loccomp}
Let $p$ be a prime, and for each irreducible factor $\beta$ of $\bar\varphi$ put $N_\beta:=\ker\Phi_\beta(A)\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_p^n$ and
$V_\beta:=N_\beta\otimes\mathbb{Q}_p\subseteq\mathbb{Q}_p^n$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item $\mathbb{Z}_p^n=\bigoplus_\beta N_\beta$ is an orthogonal decomposition into $A$-stable unimodular sublattices, $N_\beta$ has rank
$a_\beta\deg\beta$, and the reduction of $N_\beta$ modulo $p$ is $\bar N_\beta=\ker\beta(\bar A)^{a_\beta}$. The orthogonal projection
$\pi_\beta$ of $\mathbb{Q}_p^n$ onto $V_\beta$ is a polynomial in $A$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}_p$.
\item Put $e_\beta:=\pi_\beta e$ and $C_\beta:=\mathbb{Z}_p[A]e_\beta$, and let $C_\beta^*$ be the dual of $C_\beta$ in $V_\beta$. Then
$C_\beta\subseteq N_\beta\subseteq C_\beta^*$, and for $\mathfrak{m}:=(p,\tilde\beta)$
\[
\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m}=N_\beta/C_\beta,\qquad D_\mathfrak{m}=C_\beta^*/C_\beta\cong\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m},\qquad |D_\mathfrak{m}|=|\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m}|^2 .
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
(a) For $\beta\ne\beta'$ the finitely generated $\mathbb{Z}_p$-module $\mathbb{Z}_p[x]/(\Phi_\beta,\Phi_{\beta'})$ (finitely generated as $\Phi_\beta$ is
monic) vanishes modulo $p$, because $\beta^{a_\beta}$ and $\beta'^{a_{\beta'}}$ are coprime. By Nakayama's lemma it vanishes, so the
$\Phi_\beta$ are pairwise comaximal. By the Chinese remainder theorem there are $f_\beta\in\mathbb{Z}_p[x]$ with $f_\beta\equiv1\pmod{\Phi_\beta}$
and $f_\beta\equiv0\pmod{\Phi_{\beta'}}$ for $\beta'\ne\beta$. Then $\sum_\beta f_\beta\equiv1$ and $f_\beta f_{\beta'}\equiv0$ for
$\beta\ne\beta'$, modulo every $\Phi_{\beta''}$ and hence modulo $\varphi$. As $\varphi(A)=0$, the matrices $\pi_\beta:=f_\beta(A)$ are
pairwise orthogonal idempotents with $\sum_\beta\pi_\beta=I$, and they are symmetric, as polynomials in $A$. So they are the orthogonal
projections onto the pairwise orthogonal subspaces $\pi_\beta\mathbb{Q}_p^n$, whose direct sum is $\mathbb{Q}_p^n$, so that the form is
nondegenerate on each of them. Since $\Phi_\beta f_\beta\equiv0\pmod\varphi$ and
$\Phi_\beta\mid f_{\beta'}$ for $\beta'\ne\beta$, a vector $y\in\mathbb{Z}_p^n$ satisfies $\Phi_\beta(A)y=0$ if and only if $y=\pi_\beta y$. Hence
$N_\beta=\pi_\beta\mathbb{Z}_p^n$, $V_\beta=\pi_\beta\mathbb{Q}_p^n$, and $\mathbb{Z}_p^n=\bigoplus_\beta N_\beta$ orthogonally. Each $N_\beta$ is $A$-stable, and
it is unimodular as an orthogonal direct summand of the unimodular lattice $\mathbb{Z}_p^n$. Over an algebraic closure of $\mathbb{Q}_p$, $A$ is
diagonalizable with the $n$ distinct roots of $\varphi$ as eigenvalues, and $\ker\Phi_\beta(A)$ is spanned by the eigenvectors for the
roots of $\Phi_\beta$, so $N_\beta$ has rank $\deg\Phi_\beta=a_\beta\deg\beta$. Reducing modulo $p$, we get $\mathbb{F}_p^n=\bigoplus_\beta\bar N_\beta$
with $\bar N_\beta\subseteq\ker\beta(\bar A)^{a_\beta}$. As $\mathbb{F}_p^n=\bigoplus_\beta\ker\beta(\bar A)^{a_\beta}$, all these inclusions are
equalities.

(b) As $\pi_\beta\in\mathbb{Z}_p[A]$, we have $C\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p=\mathbb{Z}_p[A]e=\bigoplus_\beta C_\beta$ with $C_\beta\subseteq N_\beta$, and $C_\beta$ is a
lattice in $V_\beta$ as $\mathbb{Z}_p[A]e$ spans $\mathbb{Q}_p^n$. Since $N_\beta$ is unimodular, dualizing $C_\beta\subseteq N_\beta$ gives
$N_\beta\subseteq C_\beta^*$. The dual of $C\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p$ in $\mathbb{Q}_p^n$ is $C^*\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p$, since the dual basis of a basis of $C$ is a
basis of both, and it equals $\bigoplus_\beta C_\beta^*$, because the decomposition $\mathbb{Q}_p^n=\bigoplus_\beta V_\beta$ is orthogonal. Hence
\[
\mathfrak M_{(p)}=\mathbb{Z}_p^n/(C\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p)=\bigoplus_\beta N_\beta/C_\beta,\qquad D_{(p)}=\bigoplus_\beta C_\beta^*/C_\beta .
\]
The summands at $\beta$ are finite $p$-groups killed by $\Phi_\beta(A)$, which vanishes on $V_\beta$. As
$\Phi_\beta\equiv\tilde\beta^{a_\beta}\pmod{p\mathbb{Z}_p[x]}$, the matrix $\tilde\beta(A)^{a_\beta}$ maps each of these summands into $p$ times
itself, so they are killed by a power of $\tilde\beta(A)$ and by a power of $p$, hence by a power of $\mathfrak{m}$. Thus the summands at $\beta$ lie
in the $\mathfrak{m}$-parts, and since distinct $\beta$ give distinct $\mathfrak{m}$, they are the $\mathfrak{m}$-parts $\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m}$ and $D_\mathfrak{m}$. Finally
$D_\mathfrak{m}\cong\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:D}, and~\eqref{eq:loc-index} with $\Lambda_1=C_\beta$ and $\Lambda_2=N_\beta=N_\beta^*$
gives $|C_\beta^*/N_\beta|=|N_\beta/C_\beta|$, so that $|D_\mathfrak{m}|=|\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m}|^2$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:levellocal}
Let $G$ be controllable, $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$ and $p$ a prime.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item We have $p\mid\ell(Q)$ if and only if $\mathcal F(Q,p)\ne\emptyset$, and
\[
v_p(\ell(Q))\le\max_{\mathfrak{m}\in\mathcal F(Q,p)}\log_p\exp(\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m})\ \le\ v_p(d_n),
\]
the maximum over the empty set being $0$.
\item Let $\mathfrak{m}=(p,\tilde\beta)\in\mathcal F(Q,p)$. Then $\Lambda_\beta/C_\beta$ and $\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m}=N_\beta/C_\beta$ are two distinct ideals
of $\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}\cong D_\mathfrak{m}$ of order $|\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}|^{1/2}$. Consequently $\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$ is not a chain ring, and $\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m}\ne0$.
\item Let $\mathfrak{m}=(p,\tilde\beta)\in\mathcal F(Q,p)$. Then some simple $\bar A$-submodule $U\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p^n$ of type $\beta$ is
totally isotropic and orthogonal to $\bar e$. In particular, if $p$ is odd, then $E_p^{(\deg\beta)}$ holds.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1.}\ We decompose $\Lambda_p$ into unimodular summands $\Lambda_\beta$ between $C_\beta$ and $C_\beta^*$, and we compare them with the
summands $N_\beta$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces By Lemma~\ref{lem:ideals}, the lattice $\Lambda_p=\mathbb{Z}_p\Lambda_Q$ in $\mathbb{Q}_p^n$ is unimodular, contains $e$ and is
$A$-stable. As the $\pi_\beta$ are polynomials in $A$ with $\sum_\beta\pi_\beta=I$, we get $\Lambda_p=\bigoplus_\beta\Lambda_\beta$ with
$\Lambda_\beta=\Lambda_p\cap V_\beta$. Each $\Lambda_\beta$ is $A$-stable and contains $e_\beta$, hence $C_\beta$. Like $N_\beta$ in
Lemma~\ref{lem:loccomp}(a), it is unimodular in $V_\beta$, since it is an orthogonal direct summand of the unimodular lattice $\Lambda_p$.
Dualizing $C_\beta\subseteq\Lambda_\beta$ gives $\Lambda_\beta\subseteq C_\beta^*$, and~\eqref{eq:loc-index} gives
$|C_\beta^*/\Lambda_\beta|=|\Lambda_\beta/C_\beta|$, so that $|\Lambda_\beta/C_\beta|^2=|D_\mathfrak{m}|$ for $\mathfrak{m}=(p,\tilde\beta)$. The same holds for
$N_\beta$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:loccomp}(b). Finally, if $\Lambda_\beta\subseteq N_\beta$, then
$N_\beta=N_\beta^*\subseteq\Lambda_\beta^*=\Lambda_\beta$, so $\Lambda_\beta=N_\beta$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}\ We prove (i) by computing the $p$-part of $\ell(Q)$ summand by summand.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces For an integer $t\ge1$, $tQ$ is integral if and only if
$tQ\mathbb{Z}^n\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n$, so $\ell(Q)$ is the exponent of ${(Q\mathbb{Z}^n+\mathbb{Z}^n)/\mathbb{Z}^n}$. Hence $p^{v_p(\ell(Q))}$ is the exponent of its $p$-primary part
\[
(\Lambda_p+\mathbb{Z}_p^n)/\mathbb{Z}_p^n=\bigoplus_\beta(\Lambda_\beta+N_\beta)/N_\beta .
\]
By Step~1 the summand at $\beta$ is nonzero if and only if $\Lambda_\beta\ne N_\beta$, that is, $(p,\tilde\beta)\in\mathcal F(Q,p)$. For
$\mathfrak{m}=(p,\tilde\beta)$ let $p^k:=\exp(\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m})=\exp(N_\beta/C_\beta)$. Then $p^kN_\beta\subseteq C_\beta$, and dualizing gives
$C_\beta^*\subseteq p^{-k}N_\beta^*=p^{-k}N_\beta$. As $\Lambda_\beta\subseteq C_\beta^*$, the summand at $\beta$ is killed by $p^k$. This
proves (i), as $\exp(\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m})\le\exp(\mathfrak M_{(p)})=p^{v_p(d_n)}$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 3.}\ We prove (ii) by comparing the two ideals of $\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$ given by $\Lambda_\beta$ and by $N_\beta$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces The $A$-stable subgroups
$\Lambda_\beta/C_\beta$ and $N_\beta/C_\beta=\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m}$ of $D_\mathfrak{m}=C_\beta^*/C_\beta$ correspond to ideals of $\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}\cong D_\mathfrak{m}$.
They have order $|D_\mathfrak{m}|^{1/2}=|\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}|^{1/2}$ by Step~1, and they are distinct as $\mathfrak{m}\in\mathcal F(Q,p)$. Two distinct ideals of the
same order are not comparable, so $\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$ is not a chain ring. If $\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m}=0$, then $|\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}|=1$ and both ideals
vanish, which is impossible. So $\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m}\ne0$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 4.}\ We prove (iii) by reducing a suitable multiple of $\Lambda_\beta$ modulo $p$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces By Steps~1 and~2,
$(\Lambda_\beta+N_\beta)/N_\beta$ is a nonzero finite $p$-group. Let $p^s$ be its exponent, so that $s\ge1$ and
$p^s\Lambda_\beta\subseteq N_\beta$, and let $U_0\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p^n$ be the reduction modulo $p$ of $p^s\Lambda_\beta$. Then $U_0\ne0$, since
otherwise $p^{s-1}\Lambda_\beta\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_p^n\cap V_\beta=N_\beta$, contrary to the choice of $s$. Moreover
$U_0\subseteq\bar N_\beta=\ker\beta(\bar A)^{a_\beta}$, so every simple $\bar A$-submodule of $U_0$ has type $\beta$. The subspace $U_0$
is $\bar A$-stable as $A\Lambda_\beta\subseteq\Lambda_\beta$. It is totally isotropic, since
$(p^sy)^{\top}(p^sy')=p^{2s}y^{\top}y'\in p\mathbb{Z}_p$ for $y,y'\in\Lambda_\beta$, as $\Lambda_\beta$ is integral. And $U_0\perp\bar e$, since
$e\in\Lambda_p$ and $\Lambda_p$ is integral, so that $(p^sy)^{\top}e=p^s\,y^{\top}e\in p\mathbb{Z}_p$ for $y\in\Lambda_\beta\subseteq\Lambda_p$.
Hence every simple $\bar A$-submodule $U\subseteq U_0$ has the asserted properties, and for odd $p$ the event $E_p^{(\deg\beta)}$ holds,
as $\dim U=\deg\beta$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:chain}
Let $\mathfrak{m}=(p,\tilde\beta)\supseteq(\varphi,\psi)$ be a maximal ideal.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item If the maximal ideal of $\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$ is principal, then $\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$ is a chain ring, and $\mathfrak{m}\notin\mathcal F(Q,p)$ for every
$Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$.
\item If some element of the ideal $(\varphi,\psi)$ of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ does not lie in $\mathfrak{m}^2$, that is, if $\varphi\notin\mathfrak{m}^2$ or
$\psi\notin\mathfrak{m}^2$, then the maximal ideal of $\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$ is principal.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Let $\mathfrak n:=\mathfrak{m}\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$ be the maximal ideal of $\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$ and $k:=\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak n$ its residue field.

(a) Write $\mathfrak n=t\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$. As $\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$ is finite, $\mathfrak n$ is nilpotent. Let $\mathfrak a\ne0$ be an ideal, and
let $j$ be the largest integer with $\mathfrak a\subseteq t^j\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$. Choose $u\in\mathfrak a$ with $u\notin t^{j+1}\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$
and write $u=t^jv$. Then $v\notin\mathfrak n$, so $v$ is a unit, $t^j\in\mathfrak a$ and $\mathfrak a=t^j\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$. So the ideals of
$\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$ are the $t^j\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$, which are totally ordered by inclusion. The last assertion follows from
Proposition~\ref{lem:levellocal}(ii), by which the components at the maximal ideals in $\mathcal F(Q,p)$ are not chain rings.

(b) Since $\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}=\mathbb{Z}[x]_\mathfrak{m}/(\varphi,\psi)$, we have $\mathfrak n/\mathfrak n^2\cong\mathfrak{m}/(\mathfrak{m}^2+(\varphi,\psi))$, the localization being
harmless because this module is killed by $\mathfrak{m}$. The $k$-vector space $\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2$ is spanned by the classes of $p$ and $\tilde\beta$, and by
assumption the image of $(\varphi,\psi)$ in it is nonzero. So $\dim_k\mathfrak n/\mathfrak n^2\le1$, that is,
$\mathfrak n=t\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}+\mathfrak n^2$ for some $t\in\mathfrak n$, and $\mathfrak n=t\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$ by Nakayama's lemma.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:hensel}
Let $p$ be a prime, let $\beta$ be an irreducible factor of $\bar\varphi$, and put $\mathfrak{m}:=(p,\tilde\beta)$, $a:=a_\beta$ and $r:=a\deg\beta$.
Let $\Phi:=\Phi_\beta$ be the Hensel factor of $\varphi$ at $\beta$, and let $N:=N_\beta=\ker\Phi(A)$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:loccomp}, an
$A$-stable unimodular sublattice of $\mathbb{Z}_p^n$ of rank $r$ with $\bar N=\ker\beta(\bar A)^a$. Let $V\in\mathbb{Z}_p^{n\times r}$ be a matrix whose
columns form a basis of $N$, and define $B,\Theta\in M_r(\mathbb{Z}_p)$ and $w\in\mathbb{Q}_p^r$ by
\[
AV=VB,\qquad\Theta:=V^{\top}V,\qquad w:=\Theta^{-1}V^{\top}e .
\]
Then $\bar\Theta$ is invertible, so that $w\in\mathbb{Z}_p^r$. Moreover $\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m}\cong\mathbb{Z}_p^r/\mathcal K_r(B,w)\mathbb{Z}_p^r$, where
$\mathcal K_r(B,w):=[w,Bw,\dots,B^{r-1}w]$ is the Krylov matrix of $(B,w)$. In particular $|\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m}|=p^{v_p(\det\mathcal K_r(B,w))}$,
so that for every $E\ge1$
\[
\exp(\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m})\ge p^E\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\det\mathcal K_r(B,w)\equiv0\pmod{p^E},
\]
and the right-hand side depends only on $B$ and $w$ modulo $p^E$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
The matrix $\bar\Theta$ is invertible as $N$ is unimodular. By Lemma~\ref{lem:loccomp}(b), $\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m}=N/\mathbb{Z}_p[A]e_\beta$. As
$e_\beta=\pi_\beta e$ lies in $N$, we have $e_\beta=Vu$ for some $u\in\mathbb{Z}_p^r$, and $\Theta u=V^{\top}e_\beta=V^{\top}e$ (as
$e-e_\beta\perp N$), so that $e_\beta=Vw$. Moreover $A^je_\beta=VB^jw$. Since $V$ maps $\mathbb{Z}_p^r$ isomorphically onto $N$, this gives the
presentation by $\mathcal K_r(B,w)$, where $j<r$ suffices by the Cayley--Hamilton theorem. As $\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m}$ is finite,
$\det\mathcal K_r(B,w)\ne0$, and the Smith normal form over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ gives $|\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m}|=p^{v_p(\det\mathcal K_r(B,w))}$. Finally
$|\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m}|\ge\exp(\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m})$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:shortcol}
Let $G$ be controllable, let $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$ have level $\ell$, let $p\mid\ell$ be a prime, and put
\[
g:=\prod_{(p,\tilde\beta)\in\mathcal F(Q,p)}\beta^{a_\beta}\in\mathbb{F}_p[x],\qquad\text{where }a_\beta=v_\beta(\bar\varphi).
\]
Then some column of $\ell Q$ is an integer vector $z$ with $0<\operatorname{wt}(\bar z)\le\ell^2$ and $g(\bar A)\bar z=0$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Let $y$ be a column of $Q$, so that $y\in\Lambda_p$ and $z:=\ell y\in\mathbb{Z}^n$. For every irreducible factor $\beta$ of $\bar\varphi$ we have
$\pi_\beta z=\ell\,\pi_\beta y\in\ell\Lambda_\beta$, with the notation of Section~\ref{subsec:loc-levels}. If
$(p,\tilde\beta)\notin\mathcal F(Q,p)$, then $\Lambda_\beta=N_\beta\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_p^n$, so $\pi_\beta z\in\ell\mathbb{Z}_p^n\subseteq p\mathbb{Z}_p^n$ as
$p\mid\ell$. If $(p,\tilde\beta)\in\mathcal F(Q,p)$, then $\pi_\beta z\in\pi_\beta\mathbb{Z}_p^n=N_\beta$. Summing over $\beta$, we see that
$\bar z$ lies in $\bigoplus_{(p,\tilde\beta)\in\mathcal F(Q,p)}\bar N_\beta=
\bigoplus_{(p,\tilde\beta)\in\mathcal F(Q,p)}\ker\beta(\bar A)^{a_\beta}=\ker g(\bar A)$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:loccomp}(a) and as the
$\beta^{a_\beta}$ are pairwise coprime. Since $\ell$ is the level, $\ell Q\not\equiv0\pmod p$, so some column $z=\ell y$ has $\bar z\ne0$.
Finally $z$ is an integer vector with $\|z\|^2=\ell^2\|y\|^2=\ell^2$, so $z$ has at most $\ell^2$ nonzero entries, and
$\operatorname{wt}(\bar z)\le\ell^2$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:robust}
Let $s\ge1$. A matrix $Y\in\mathbb{F}_p^{N\times m}$ is \emph{$s$-robust} if $\operatorname{wt}(Yc)\ge s$ for every $c\in\mathbb{F}_p^m\setminus\{0\}$, that is, if its
columns are linearly independent and their span contains no nonzero vector of weight~${<s}$. A matrix $Y\in(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^{N\times m}$ is
\emph{$s$-robust} if its reduction modulo $p$ is.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:Rn}
For $\delta\in(0,\frac12)$ let $s_\delta:=\lceil n^{1-\delta}\rceil$ and
\[
\mathcal R_n(\delta):=\big\{(p,d):\ p\text{ prime},\ 1\le d\le n^{\delta}/\log^2n,\ pd\le n^{1/2-\delta}/\log n\big\}.
\]
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:special}
Let $p$ be a prime, $E\ge1$, $m\ge1$ and $s\ge16m$, and let $Y\in(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^{N\times m}$ be $s$-robust. For $X\in(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^{N\times m}$ put
\[
c_{ij}(X):=\langle X_i,Y_j\rangle+\langle X_j,Y_i\rangle\in\mathbb{Z}/p^E,\qquad \nu(X):=\#\{i<j:\ c_{ij}(X)\ne0\},
\]
\[
t(X):=\min_{K\in\mathcal A_m(p^E)}\#\{i:\ X_i\ne Y_iK\}.
\]
Then $\nu(X)\ge\min\bigl(t(X)\,s/2,\ s^2/(64m)\bigr)$. In particular $\nu(X)=0$ if and only if $X=YK$ for some $K\in\mathcal A_m(p^E)$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
For $K\in\mathcal A_m(p^E)$ we have $c_{ij}(YK)=Y_iKY_j^{\top}+Y_jKY_i^{\top}=Y_i(K+K^{\top})Y_j^{\top}=0$. Since $c_{ij}$ is additive in
$X$, it follows that $c_{ij}(X-YK)=c_{ij}(X)$. This gives the ``if'' part of the last assertion, and the ``only if'' part follows from the
inequality. Choose $K_0\in\mathcal A_m(p^E)$ attaining $t:=t(X)$, put $X':=X-YK_0$, so that
$c_{ij}(X)=\langle X'_i,Y_j\rangle+\langle X'_j,Y_i\rangle$, and let $P:=\{i:\ X'_i\ne0\}$, so that $|P|=t$. Write $\nu:=\nu(X)$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1.}\ We prove the inequality when $t\le s/2$, by counting the pairs $\{i,j\}$ with $i\in P$ and $j\notin P$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $i\in P$, and write
$X'_i=p^rX''_i$ with $0\le r<E$ and $\bar X''_i\ne0$. By robustness, $\langle\bar X''_i,\bar Y_j\rangle\ne0$ for at least $s$ indices $j$
(the nonzero coordinates of $\bar Y(\bar X''_i)^{\top}$), hence for at least $s-t$ indices $j\notin P$. For these,
$c_{ij}(X)=\langle X'_i,Y_j\rangle=p^r\langle X''_i,Y_j\rangle\ne0$. Each pair $\{i,j\}$ with $i\in P$ and $j\notin P$ is counted once, so
$\nu\ge t(s-t)\ge ts/2$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}\ We show by contradiction that $\nu\ge s^2/(64m)$ when $t>s/2$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Suppose that $\nu<s^2/(64m)$. Consider the graph on $[N]$ whose
edges are the pairs $\{i,j\}$, $i\ne j$, with $c_{ij}(X)\ne0$. It has $\nu$ edges, so at most $2\nu\cdot8m/s<s/4$ vertices have degree
$>s/(8m)$. We choose $b_1,\dots,b_m\in[N]$ of degree $\le s/(8m)$, pairwise non-adjacent, such that $\bar Y_{b_1},\dots,\bar Y_{b_m}$ are
linearly independent. Having chosen $b_1,\dots,b_{k-1}$ ($k\le m$), pick $0\ne u\in\mathbb{F}_p^m$ orthogonal to
$\bar Y_{b_1},\dots,\bar Y_{b_{k-1}}$. By robustness, at least $s$ indices $j$ satisfy $\langle\bar Y_j,u\rangle\ne0$, and then $\bar Y_j$
lies outside the span of $\bar Y_{b_1},\dots,\bar Y_{b_{k-1}}$. Fewer than $s/4$ of these indices have degree $>s/(8m)$, and at most
$(k-1)s/(8m)<s/8$ of them are adjacent to some $b_l$, $l<k$. So a valid choice of $b_k$ exists. Put $B:=\{b_1,\dots,b_m\}$, and let $\Gamma$
be the set of indices outside $B$ that are not adjacent to any element of $B$. Then $|[N]\setminus\Gamma|\le m+s/8$.

The rows $Y_b$, $b\in B$, form a basis of $(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^m$, since their reductions form a basis of $\mathbb{F}_p^m$. Hence there is a unique bilinear
form $\kappa$ on $(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^m$ with $\kappa(a,Y_b)=-\langle X'_b,a\rangle$ for all $a$ and all $b\in B$. Let $K$ be its matrix, so that
$\kappa(a,a')=aKa'^{\top}$. For $j\in\Gamma$ and $b\in B$ we have $c_{jb}(X)=0$, that is,
$\langle X'_j,Y_b\rangle=-\langle X'_b,Y_j\rangle=\kappa(Y_j,Y_b)$. The linear forms $a'\mapsto\langle X'_j,a'\rangle$ and
$a'\mapsto\kappa(Y_j,a')$ agree at the basis vectors $Y_b$, $b\in B$, so they are equal, which means that $X'_j=Y_jK$. Consequently, for
distinct $j,j'\in\Gamma$,
\[
c_{jj'}(X)=Y_jKY_{j'}^{\top}+Y_{j'}KY_j^{\top}=Y_jLY_{j'}^{\top},\qquad L:=K+K^{\top}.
\]
If $L\ne0$, write $L=p^rL'$ with $0\le r<E$ and $L'$ symmetric with $\bar L'\ne0$. By robustness applied to a nonzero row of $\bar L'$, at
least $s$ indices $j'$ satisfy $\bar L'\bar Y_{j'}^{\top}\ne0$, and at least $s-m-s/8$ of them lie in $\Gamma$. For each such $j'$,
robustness applied to $\bar L'\bar Y_{j'}^{\top}$ gives at least $s-m-s/8-1$ indices $j\in\Gamma\setminus\{j'\}$ with
$\bar Y_j\bar L'\bar Y_{j'}^{\top}\ne0$, and then $c_{jj'}(X)=p^rY_jL'Y_{j'}^{\top}\ne0$. Since $m\le s/16$ and $s\ge16$,
\[
\nu\ge\tfrac12\big(s-m-\tfrac s8\big)\big(s-m-\tfrac s8-1\big)\ge\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{13s}{16}\cdot\tfrac{3s}{4}
\ge\frac{s^2}{8}\ge\frac{s^2}{64m},
\]
a contradiction. If $L=0$, then $K\in\mathcal A_m(p^E)$ and $X_j=Y_j(K_0+K)$ for all $j\in\Gamma$, with $K_0+K\in\mathcal A_m(p^E)$. So
$t\le|[N]\setminus\Gamma|\le m+s/8<s/2$, again a contradiction. Hence $\nu\ge s^2/(64m)$ when $t>s/2$.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:fourier}
Let $A$ be the adjacency matrix of $G(n,1/2)$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Let $p$ be a prime, $E,m\ge1$, $s\ge16m$, let $Y\in(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^{n\times m}$ be $s$-robust, and let $Z\in(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^{n\times m}$. Then, with
$\tau:=\tau_{p^E}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:four-bound}
\Pr\bigl(AY\equiv Z\pmod{p^E}\bigr)\le p^{-Enm}\Big(|\mathcal A_m(p^E)|\big(1+p^{Em}\tau^{s/2}\big)^n+p^{Enm}\tau^{s^2/(64m)}\Big).
\end{equation}
\item Fix $\delta\in(0,\frac12)$. There are $\varepsilon_n=\varepsilon_n(\delta)\to0$ such that
\[
\Pr\bigl(AY\equiv Z\pmod{p^E}\bigr)\le(1+\varepsilon_n)\,p^{-Enm}\,|\mathcal A_m(p^E)|
\]
for all primes $p$ and all $E,m\ge1$ with $m\le n^{\delta}/\log^2n$ and $p^Em\le n^{1/2-\delta}/\log n$, all $s_\delta$-robust
$Y\in(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^{n\times m}$ and all $Z\in(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^{n\times m}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
(a) By the orthogonality of the additive characters of $(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^{n\times m}$,
\[
\Pr(AY\equiv Z)=p^{-Enm}\sum_{X\in(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^{n\times m}}\mathbb{E}\exp\Bigl(\frac{2\pi i\operatorname{tr}(X^{\top}(AY-Z))}{p^E}\Bigr).
\]
Since $A=(a_{ij})$ is symmetric with zero diagonal,
$\operatorname{tr}(X^{\top}AY)=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\langle X_i,Y_j\rangle=\sum_{i<j}a_{ij}c_{ij}(X)$, and the $a_{ij}$, $i<j$, are independent
and uniform on $\{0,1\}$. By~\eqref{eq:four-cos} the term of $X$ has modulus at most $\tau^{\nu(X)}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:special},
$\tau^{\nu(X)}\le\tau^{t(X)s/2}+\tau^{s^2/(64m)}$ (with $0^0=1$). Every $X$ with $t(X)=t$ has the form $YK+X'$ with $K\in\mathcal A_m(p^E)$
and $X'$ having exactly $t$ nonzero rows, so there are at most $|\mathcal A_m(p^E)|\binom ntp^{Emt}$ such $X$. Hence
\[
\sum_X\tau^{\nu(X)}\le|\mathcal A_m(p^E)|\sum_{t=0}^n\binom nt\big(p^{Em}\tau^{s/2}\big)^t+p^{Enm}\tau^{s^2/(64m)},
\]
which is~\eqref{eq:four-bound}.

(b) Put $s:=s_\delta$ and $\tau:=\tau_{p^E}$, and let $n$ be large. Then $s\ge n^{1-\delta}\ge16n^{\delta}\ge16m$, so (a) applies, and
$\tau\le e^{-4/p^{2E}}$ by~\eqref{eq:four-cos}. Since $p^E\le p^Em\le n^{1/2-\delta}/\log n$ and $s\ge n^{1-\delta}$, we have
$s/p^{2E}\ge n^{\delta}\log^2n$, and as $E\log p=\log p^E\le\log n$, also $mE\log p\le n^{\delta}/\log n$. Hence
\[
p^{Em}\tau^{s/2}\le\exp\bigl(mE\log p-2s/p^{2E}\bigr)\le\exp\bigl(-n^{\delta}\log^2n\bigr),
\]
and $(1+p^{Em}\tau^{s/2})^n\le\exp(n\,e^{-n^{\delta}\log^2n})$, which tends to $1$. Next,
$nm^2p^{2E}E\log p\le n\cdot n^{1-2\delta}\log^{-2}n\cdot\log n\le s^2/\log n$, so
\[
p^{Enm}\tau^{s^2/(64m)}\le\exp\bigl(nmE\log p-s^2/(16mp^{2E})\bigr)\le\exp\bigl(nmE\log p\,(1-\tfrac1{16}\log n)\bigr),
\]
which tends to $0$, as $nmE\log p\ge n\log2$ and $\log n>16$. Both bounds are uniform in $p$, $E$ and $m$. As $|\mathcal A_m(p^E)|\ge1$,
the bracket in~\eqref{eq:four-bound} is at most $(1+\varepsilon_n)|\mathcal A_m(p^E)|$ for suitable $\varepsilon_n\to0$, which proves (b).
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{prop:shortany}
Fix $\delta\in(0,\frac14]$, and let $A$ be the adjacency matrix of $G(n,1/2)$. For all large $n$ (depending only on $\delta$), with
probability at least $1-e^{-n/8}$, for every prime $p$ (including $p=2$) and every monic $g\in\mathbb{F}_p[x]$ with
$(p,\deg g)\in\mathcal R_n(\delta)$ there is no $z\in\mathbb{F}_p^n$ with $0<\operatorname{wt}(z)<s_\delta$ and $g(\bar A)z=0$.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Let $n$ be large, and let $p$ and $g$ be as in the statement, with $d:=\deg g$. As $(p,d)\in\mathcal R_n(\delta)$ and $\delta\le\frac14$, we
have $p\le n^{1/2}\le e^{n^{1/8}}$, $d\le n^{1/4}$ and $n/(4(d+1))\ge n^{1-\delta}\log^2n/8\ge s_\delta$. So the lemma follows from
Proposition~\ref{lem:suppd} with $M=A$, $m=n$ and $\{a,b\}=\{0,1\}$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:gram}
Let $p$ be a prime, $E,r\ge1$, and let $V$ be uniform in $(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^{n\times r}$. Put $\mathcal G:=\mathrm{Sym}_r(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)\times(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^r$,
let $\mathcal G_r(p^E):=\mathcal G$ if $p$ is odd, and
\[
\mathcal G_r(2^E):=\big\{(\Theta,u)\in\mathcal G:\ \Theta_{ii}\equiv u_i\pmod2\ \text{for all }i\big\}.
\]
Let $\mu$ be the uniform distribution on $\mathcal G_r(p^E)$, viewed as a probability measure on $\mathcal G$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item There is $c=c(p,E,r)<1$ such that $\lvert\Pr((V^{\top}V,V^{\top}e)=(\Theta,u))-\mu(\Theta,u)\rvert\le c^n$ for all $n\ge1$ and all
$(\Theta,u)\in\mathcal G$. In particular $(V^{\top}V,V^{\top}e)$ converges in total variation, exponentially fast in $n$, to $\mu$, and
$V^{\top}V$ converges to the uniform distribution on $\mathrm{Sym}_r(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)$.
\item If $p$ is odd and $E=1$, then (a) holds with $c=p^{-1/2}$, for every $r\ge1$. In particular, with $k_r:=r(r+3)/2$, the number of
$V\in\mathbb{F}_p^{n\times r}$ with $V^{\top}V=0$ and $V^{\top}\bar e=0$ differs from $p^{nr-k_r}$ by at most $p^{nr-n/2}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
The characters of $\mathcal G$ are $\chi_{\sigma,t}(\Theta,u)=\exp\bigl(2\pi i\,(\sum_{i\le j}\sigma_{ij}\Theta_{ij}+t^{\top}u)/p^E\bigr)$,
for $\sigma=(\sigma_{ij})_{i\le j}$ and $t$ with entries in $\mathbb{Z}/p^E$. Since the rows of $V$ are independent and uniform in $(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^r$,
\[
\mathbb{E}\big(\chi_{\sigma,t}(V^{\top}V,V^{\top}e)\big)=\Big(\mathbb{E}\,e^{2\pi i\,F_{\sigma,t}(v)/p^E}\Big)^n,\qquad
F_{\sigma,t}(y):=\sum_{i\le j}\sigma_{ij}y_iy_j+t^{\top}y ,
\]
where $v$ is uniform in $(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^r$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1.}\ We show that $F_{\sigma,t}$ vanishes identically if and only if $\chi_{\sigma,t}$ is trivial on $\mathcal G_r(p^E)$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces If
$F_{\sigma,t}\equiv0$, then evaluating at $y=e_i$, $y=2e_i$ and $y=e_i+e_j$ gives $\sigma_{ij}=0$ for $i<j$, $2\sigma_{ii}=0$ and
$t_i=-\sigma_{ii}$. For odd $p$ this means $(\sigma,t)=0$. For $p=2$ it means that $\sigma$ is diagonal with
$\sigma_{ii}=t_i\in\{0,2^{E-1}\}$, and conversely these $(\sigma,t)$ give $F_{\sigma,t}(y)=\sum_i\sigma_{ii}y_i(y_i+1)\equiv0$. The
corresponding characters $\chi(\Theta,u)=\prod_{i:\,\sigma_{ii}\ne0}(-1)^{\Theta_{ii}+u_i}$ are exactly the characters trivial on
$\mathcal G_r(2^E)$, since $(\Theta,u)\mapsto(\Theta_{ii}+u_i\bmod2)_{i\le r}$ identifies $\mathcal G/\mathcal G_r(2^E)$ with $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^r$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}\ We prove (a) by comparing the Fourier coefficients of the law of $(V^{\top}V,V^{\top}e)$ with those of $\mu$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces If
$F_{\sigma,t}\not\equiv0$, the mean $\mathbb{E}\,e^{2\pi i\,F_{\sigma,t}(v)/p^E}$ is an average of roots of unity that are not all equal (as
$F_{\sigma,t}(0)=0$), so it has modulus less than $1$. Let $c<1$ be the largest of these moduli. The Fourier coefficients of $\mu$ are $1$
at the characters trivial on $\mathcal G_r(p^E)$ and $0$ at all others. By Step~1, those of the law of $(V^{\top}V,V^{\top}e)$ are the same,
up to errors of modulus at most $c^n$. Fourier inversion on $\mathcal G$ gives
$\lvert\Pr((V^{\top}V,V^{\top}e)=(\Theta,u))-\mu(\Theta,u)\rvert\le c^n$, and summing over $(\Theta,u)\in\mathcal G$ bounds the total variation
distance by $\frac12|\mathcal G|c^n$. The image of $\mu$ under $(\Theta,u)\mapsto\Theta$ is uniform on $\mathrm{Sym}_r(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)$, since every
$\Theta$ has the same number of compatible $u$, and projecting does not increase the total variation distance.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 3.}\ We prove (b) by bounding the Gauss sums that arise when $p$ is odd and $E=1$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $p$ be odd, $E=1$ and $(\sigma,t)\ne0$. If
$\sigma=0$, then $t\ne0$ and $\mathbb{E}\,e^{2\pi i\,t^{\top}v/p}=0$. If $\sigma\ne0$, then $\sum_{i\le j}\sigma_{ij}y_iy_j=y^{\top}My$ for a
nonzero symmetric matrix $M$, as $p$ is odd, and we bound the Gauss sum in the standard way (see Lidl--Niederreiter
(1997)~\cite[Ch.~5]{LN97}). The substitution $y=z+h$ gives
\[
\Bigl|\sum_{y\in\mathbb{F}_p^r}e^{2\pi i\,F_{\sigma,t}(y)/p}\Bigr|^2=\sum_he^{2\pi i\,F_{\sigma,t}(h)/p}\sum_ze^{4\pi i\,h^{\top}Mz/p}
\le p^r\,\lvert\ker M\rvert\le p^{2r-1},
\]
because the inner sum equals $p^r$ if $Mh=0$ and vanishes otherwise. So $|\mathbb{E}\,e^{2\pi i\,F_{\sigma,t}(v)/p}|\le p^{-1/2}$, and Step~2
applies with $c=p^{-1/2}$. For the count, note that $\mu(0,0)=|\mathcal G|^{-1}=p^{-k_r}$, and multiply by $p^{nr}$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:firstmoment}
Fix $\delta\in(0,\frac14]$. There are $\varepsilon_n=\varepsilon_n(\delta)\to0$ and $n_0(\delta)$ such that for all $n\ge n_0(\delta)$
and all $(p,d)\in\mathcal R_n(\delta)$ with $p$ odd,
\[
\Pr\bigl(E_p^{(d)}\bigr)\le c_p^{(d)}\,(1+\varepsilon_n)+e^{-n/8}.
\]
In particular $\limsup_n\Pr(E_p^{(d)})\le c_p^{(d)}$ for every fixed odd prime $p$ and every fixed $d\ge1$, and
\[
\lim_{q_0\to\infty}\ \limsup_{n\to\infty}\ \Pr\bigl(E_p^{(d)}\text{ holds for some }(p,d)\in\mathcal R_n(\delta)
\text{ with $p$ odd and }p^d>q_0\bigr)=0 .
\]
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Let $n$ be large and $(p,d)\in\mathcal R_n(\delta)$ with $p$ odd. All error terms $o(1)$ below are uniform in such $(p,d)$. Let
$\mathcal N$ be the event of Lemma~\ref{prop:shortany} for this $\delta$, so that $\Pr(\mathcal N^c)\le e^{-n/8}$, and let $\mathcal V$ be
the (deterministic) set of $s_\delta$-robust $V\in\mathbb{F}_p^{n\times d}$ with $V^{\top}V=0$ and $V^{\top}\bar e=0$. Suppose that $\mathcal N$
holds and that some simple $\bar A$-submodule $U$ of some type $\beta$ of degree $d$ is totally isotropic and orthogonal to $\bar e$. As
$\beta(\bar A)$ kills $U$, the event $\mathcal N$ shows that $U$ contains no nonzero vector of weight $<s_\delta$. So the $q-1$
$\beta$-frames with column space $U$ are $s_\delta$-robust and admissible, that is, they lie in $\mathcal V$. Hence
\[
\mathbf 1_{E_p^{(d)}}\le\mathbf 1_{\mathcal N^c}+\frac1{q-1}\sum_\beta\sum_{V\in\mathcal V}\mathbf 1\big\{\bar AV=VM_\beta\big\},
\]
where $\beta$ runs over the irreducible polynomials of degree $d$. For $V\in\mathcal V$, Proposition~\ref{lem:fourier}(b) with $E=1$,
$m=d$, $Y=V$ and $Z=VM_\beta$ applies, as $(p,d)\in\mathcal R_n(\delta)$, and since $|\mathcal A_d(p)|=p^{d(d-1)/2}$ for odd $p$ it gives
\[
\Pr\bigl(\bar AV=VM_\beta\bigr)\le p^{-nd+d(d-1)/2}\big(1+o(1)\big).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:gram}(b) with $r=d$, and with $k_d=d(d+3)/2$,
\[
|\mathcal V|\le p^{nd-k_d}\big(1+p^{k_d-n/2}\big)=p^{nd-k_d}\big(1+o(1)\big),
\]
because $k_d\le2d^2\le n^{2\delta}\le n/4$ for large $n$. Since $k_d-d(d-1)/2=2d$, each of the $\pi_p(d)$ polynomials $\beta$ contributes at
most $p^{-2d}(p^d-1)^{-1}(1+o(1))$ to the expectation of the last term. This gives the first assertion, with $1+\varepsilon_n$ the product
of the two factors $1+o(1)$ above. The second assertion follows, since $(p,d)\in\mathcal R_n(\delta)$ for all large $n$ when $p$ and $d$ are
fixed.

For the tail statement, note that $c_p^{(d)}\le p^d/(p^{2d}(p^d-1))\le2q^{-2}$, and that distinct pairs $(p,d)$ give distinct prime powers
$q=p^d$. As the event $\mathcal N$ does not depend on $(p,d)$, the bound on $\mathbf 1_{E_p^{(d)}}$ above gives
\[
\Pr\bigl(E_p^{(d)}\text{ for some }(p,d)\in\mathcal R_n(\delta),\ p\text{ odd},\ p^d>q_0\bigr)\le(1+\varepsilon_n)\sum_{t>q_0}\frac2{t^2}
+e^{-n/8},
\]
where $t$ runs over the integers $t>q_0$. The $\limsup$ of the right-hand side is at most $\sum_{t>q_0}2t^{-2}$, a tail of a convergent
series, which tends to $0$ as $q_0\to\infty$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:tight}
Let $p$ be a prime (possibly $p=2$) and $d\ge1$, both fixed.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item For every $k\ge1$,
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\Pr\bigl(\beta^k\mid\bar\varphi\text{ for some irreducible }\beta\in\mathbb{F}_p[x]\text{ of degree }d\bigr)
\le(k+1)\,\pi_p(d)\,p^{-\lfloor k/2\rfloor d}.
\]
\item Let $\mathcal X_E$ be the event that $G$ is controllable and $\exp(\mathfrak M_{(p,\beta)})\ge p^E$ for some irreducible
$\beta\in\mathbb{F}_p[x]$ of degree $d$. Then $\lim_{E\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\Pr(\mathcal X_E)=0$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Throughout the proof, $p$ and $d$ are fixed, as are the parameters $k$, $E$ and $a$ introduced below, and $o(1)$ refers to $n\to\infty$ with
all of them fixed. Put $s:=s_{1/4}=\lceil n^{3/4}\rceil$. Let $\mathcal N$ be the event of Lemma~\ref{prop:shortany} with $\delta=\frac14$,
so that $\Pr(\mathcal N^c)\le e^{-n/8}$ for large $n$. As $p$, $d$ and $k$ are fixed, $(p,jd)\in\mathcal R_n(\frac14)$ for $1\le j\le k$ and
large $n$. So on $\mathcal N$, for every irreducible $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_p[x]$ of degree $d$ and every $j\le k$, the space $\ker\beta(\bar A)^j$
contains no nonzero vector of weight $<s$. We also use Proposition~\ref{lem:fourier}(b) with $\delta=\frac14$ (so that $s=s_\delta$) and a
fixed $m$. Its hypotheses hold for large $n$, as $p$, $E$ and $m$ are fixed. So, uniformly over $s$-robust $Y\in(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^{n\times m}$ and
all $Y'\in(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^{n\times m}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fourierfixed}
