\Pr\bigl(AY\equiv Y'\pmod{p^E}\bigr)\le p^{-Enm}\,|\mathcal A_m(p^E)|\,\big(1+o(1)\big).
\end{equation}

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1.}\ We bound, on the event $\mathcal N$, the expected number of vectors with annihilator $\beta^j$ in terms of the size of a
set $\mathcal S_j$ of Gram matrices.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces
Fix an irreducible $\beta$ of degree $d$ (there are $\pi_p(d)$ of them), and let $\beta^b\,\|\,\bar\varphi$. The $\beta$-primary component
of the $\mathbb{F}_p[x]$-module $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ is $\bigoplus_i\mathbb{F}_p[x]/(\beta^{b_i})$ with $\sum_ib_i=b$, so $\dim\ker\beta(\bar A)^k=d\sum_i\min(b_i,k)$,
which is at least $kd$ if and only if $b\ge k$. Thus $\beta^k\mid\bar\varphi$ if and only if $\lvert\ker\beta(\bar A)^k\rvert\ge p^{kd}$.

The annihilator of a vector $z\in\mathbb{F}_p^n$ is the monic generator of the ideal of the polynomials $f$ with $f(\bar A)z=0$. Every
$z\in\ker\beta(\bar A)^k$ has annihilator $\beta^j$ for some $0\le j\le k$. Let $Z_j$ be the set of these $z$, so that $Z_0=\{0\}$. For
$j\ge1$ put $R_j:=\mathbb{F}_p[x]/(\beta^j)$, and let $C_j\in M_{jd}(\mathbb{F}_p)$ be the companion matrix of $\beta^j$, that is, the matrix of
multiplication by $x$ on $R_j$ in the basis $1,x,\dots,x^{jd-1}$. Then $z\mapsto V_z:=[z,\bar Az,\dots,\bar A^{jd-1}z]$ is a
bijection from $Z_j$ onto the set of matrices $V\in\mathbb{F}_p^{n\times jd}$ of rank $jd$ with $\bar AV=VC_j$: the identity $\bar AV_z=V_zC_j$
means $\beta^j(\bar A)z=0$, every $V$ with $\bar AV=VC_j$ equals $V_z$ for $z=Ve_1$, and $V_z$ has rank $jd$ if and only if the
annihilator of $z$ has degree $jd$. On $\mathcal N$ these matrices are $s$-robust, as they have full rank and their column spaces lie in
$\ker\beta(\bar A)^k$. Moreover, $\bar AV=VC_j$ implies that $V^{\top}VC_j=V^{\top}\bar AV$ is symmetric, and alternating if $p=2$ (as
$\bar A$ is then alternating). Let $\mathcal S_j$ be the set of symmetric $\Theta\in M_{jd}(\mathbb{F}_p)$ such that $\Theta C_j$ is symmetric,
and alternating if $p=2$. Then
\[
|Z_j|\,\mathbf 1_{\mathcal N}\le\sum_V\mathbf 1\big\{\bar AV=VC_j\big\},
\]
the sum over the $s$-robust $V\in\mathbb{F}_p^{n\times jd}$ with $V^{\top}V\in\mathcal S_j$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:gram}(a) (with $E=1$ and $r=jd$, for
$V^{\top}V$ alone), and as $\mathcal S_j$ is nonempty (it contains $0$), the number of $V\in\mathbb{F}_p^{n\times jd}$ with
$V^{\top}V\in\mathcal S_j$ is $p^{njd}\,|\mathcal S_j|\,|\mathrm{Sym}_{jd}(\mathbb{F}_p)|^{-1}(1+o(1))$. With~\eqref{eq:fourierfixed} for $E=1$ and
$m=jd$ we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Zj}
\mathbb{E}\big(|Z_j|\,\mathbf 1_{\mathcal N}\big)\le\frac{|\mathcal S_j|\,|\mathcal A_{jd}(p)|}{|\mathrm{Sym}_{jd}(\mathbb{F}_p)|}\big(1+o(1)\big).
\end{equation}

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}\ We bound the size of $\mathcal S_j$ and prove (a) by Markov's inequality.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces
Identify $\mathbb{F}_p^{jd}$ with $R_j$ through the basis $1,x,\dots,x^{jd-1}$, so that $C_j$ becomes multiplication by $x$. A symmetric $\Theta$
defines the symmetric bilinear form $\langle y,y'\rangle_\Theta:=y^{\top}\Theta y'$ on $R_j$, and $\Theta C_j$ is symmetric if and only if
$\langle y,xy'\rangle_\Theta=\langle xy,y'\rangle_\Theta$ for all $y,y'$. In that case
$\langle fy,y'\rangle_\Theta=\langle y,fy'\rangle_\Theta$ for every polynomial $f$, so $\langle y,y'\rangle_\Theta=\lambda(yy')$ with
$\lambda:=\langle1,\cdot\rangle_\Theta$ in the dual space $R_j^*$ of $R_j$. Conversely, every $\lambda\in R_j^*$ defines such a form.
Hence, for odd $p$, $|\mathcal S_j|=p^{jd}$, and as $|\mathcal A_{jd}(p)|/|\mathrm{Sym}_{jd}(\mathbb{F}_p)|=p^{-jd}$, the right-hand side
of~\eqref{eq:Zj} is $1+o(1)$. For $p=2$ we have $|\mathcal A_{jd}(2)|=2^{jd(jd+1)/2}=|\mathrm{Sym}_{jd}(\mathbb{F}_2)|$, and $\Theta C_j$ is
moreover alternating if and only if $\lambda(xy^2)=0$ for all $y\in R_j$. The map $y\mapsto xy^2$ is $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear on $R_j$, so the
$\lambda$ satisfying this condition are those that vanish on its image, and they form a space whose dimension equals that of its kernel.
If $xy^2\equiv0\pmod{\beta^j}$, then $\beta^{j-1}\mid y^2$, as $\beta^2\nmid x$, so that $\beta^{\lceil(j-1)/2\rceil}\mid y$. Hence the
kernel lies in $\beta^{\lceil(j-1)/2\rceil}R_j$, which has dimension $(j-\lceil(j-1)/2\rceil)d=\lceil j/2\rceil d$, and
$|\mathcal S_j|\le2^{\lceil j/2\rceil d}\le2^{\lceil k/2\rceil d}$ for $j\le k$.

Since $|Z_0|=1$, summing~\eqref{eq:Zj} over $1\le j\le k$ gives $\mathbb{E}\big(\lvert\ker\beta(\bar A)^k\rvert\,\mathbf 1_{\mathcal N}\big)\le k+1+o(1)$
for odd $p$, and $\le(k+1)\,2^{\lceil k/2\rceil d}+o(1)$ for $p=2$. By Markov's inequality,
\[
\Pr\bigl(\beta^k\mid\bar\varphi\bigr)\le\Pr\bigl(\mathcal N^c\bigr)+p^{-kd}\,\mathbb{E}\big(\lvert\ker\beta(\bar A)^k\rvert\,\mathbf 1_{\mathcal N}\big),
\]
which is at most $(k+1)p^{-kd}+o(1)$ for odd $p$, and at most $(k+1)2^{-\lfloor k/2\rfloor d}+o(1)$ for $p=2$. Summing over the $\pi_p(d)$
polynomials $\beta$ gives (a), since $p^{-kd}\le p^{-\lfloor k/2\rfloor d}$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 3.}\ We reduce (b) to events $\mathcal Y_{a,E}$ on which $\beta^a$ exactly divides $\bar\varphi$, for a fixed $\beta$ and a fixed $a$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces
Let $\eta>0$, and choose $k$ with $(k+1)\pi_p(d)p^{-\lfloor k/2\rfloor d}<\eta$. Then $\mathcal X_E$ is contained in the union of the
event of (a) for this $k$ and the event that $G$ is controllable and $\exp(\mathfrak M_{(p,\beta)})\ge p^E$ for some irreducible $\beta$
of degree $d$ with $\beta^k\nmid\bar\varphi$. Since $\mathfrak M_{(p,\beta)}=0$ unless $\beta\mid\bar\varphi$, and
$\Pr(\mathcal N^c)\le e^{-n/8}$, it therefore suffices to show, for each irreducible $\beta$ of degree $d$ and each $1\le a<k$, that
$\lim_E\limsup_n\Pr(\mathcal Y_{a,E})=0$, where $\mathcal Y_{a,E}$, or $\mathcal Y$ for short, is the event that $G$ is controllable,
$\beta^a\,\|\,\bar\varphi$, $\mathcal N$ holds and $\exp(\mathfrak M_{(p,\beta)})\ge p^E$. Put $r:=ad$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 4.}\ We bound $\Pr(\mathcal Y)$ by the mean of a function of the Gram data of a uniformly random matrix modulo $p^E$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces
On $\mathcal Y$ let $\Phi:=\Phi_\beta$ be the Hensel factor of $\varphi$ at $\beta$, so that $\bar\Phi=\beta^a$, and let
$N:=N_\beta=\ker\Phi(A)\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_p^n$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:hensel}: $N$ is $A$-stable and unimodular of rank $r$, and its reduction
modulo $p$ is $\bar N=\ker\beta(\bar A)^a$. As $N$ is a direct summand of $\mathbb{Z}_p^n$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:loccomp}(a)), $N/p^EN$ is a submodule of
$(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^n$. Call $V\in(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^{n\times r}$ a \emph{basis of $N$ modulo $p^E$} if its columns form a basis of $N/p^EN$. There are
$|GL_r(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)|=p^{Er^2}\prod_{i=1}^r(1-p^{-i})$ of them, and each such $V$ has the following properties. It is the reduction of a
$\mathbb{Z}_p$-basis of $N$ (lift its columns and apply Nakayama's lemma). It is $s$-robust, since its reduction modulo $p$ has rank $r$ and column
space $\ker\beta(\bar A)^a$, and $\mathcal N$ holds. Its Gram matrix $\Theta_V:=V^{\top}V$ is invertible modulo $p$, since $N$ is
unimodular. Finally, ${AV\equiv VB_V\pmod{p^E}}$ for a unique $B_V\in M_r(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)$, since $N$ is $A$-stable and $V$ maps $(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^r$
isomorphically onto $N/p^EN$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:hensel}, applied to a basis of $N$ lifting $V$, and since
$\exp(\mathfrak M_{(p,\beta)})\ge p^E$, we have $\det\mathcal K_r(B_V,\Theta_V^{-1}V^{\top}e)\equiv0\pmod{p^E}$.

If $AV\equiv VB\pmod{p^E}$, then $\Theta_VB\equiv V^{\top}AV$ is symmetric, with even diagonal if $p=2$ (the diagonal entries
$y^{\top}Ay=2\sum_{i<l}a_{il}y_iy_l$ are even). For $V$ with $\Theta_V$ invertible modulo $p$, call $B\in M_r(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)$
\emph{compatible with $V$} if $\Theta_VB$ is symmetric, with even diagonal if $p=2$. As $B\mapsto\Theta_VB$ is a bijection, the number of
compatible $B$ is $p^{Er(r+1)/2}$ for odd $p$ and $2^{Er(r+1)/2-r}$ for $p=2$. In both cases it equals $p^{Er^2}/|\mathcal A_r(p^E)|$.
Therefore
\[
\mathbf 1_{\mathcal Y}\le\frac1{|GL_r(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)|}\sum_V\sum_B\mathbf 1\big\{AV\equiv VB\pmod{p^E}\big\}\,
\mathbf 1\bigl\{\det\mathcal K_r(B,\Theta_V^{-1}V^{\top}e)\equiv0\pmod{p^E}\bigr\},
\]
where $V$ runs over the $s$-robust matrices in $(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^{n\times r}$ with $\Theta_V$ invertible modulo $p$, and $B$ over the matrices
compatible with $V$. For $(\Theta,u)\in\mathrm{Sym}_r(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)\times(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^r$ let $h(\Theta,u):=0$ if $\Theta$ is not invertible modulo
$p$, and otherwise let $h(\Theta,u)$ be the proportion of the matrices $B$ with $\Theta B$ symmetric (with even diagonal if $p=2$) for which
$\det\mathcal K_r(B,\Theta^{-1}u)\equiv0\pmod{p^E}$. Taking expectations with~\eqref{eq:fourierfixed} for $m=r$, and dropping the robustness
condition, which only increases the sum, we get
\[
\Pr(\mathcal Y)\le c_{p,r}\,\mathbb{E}\big(h(\Theta_V,V^{\top}e)\big)\big(1+o(1)\big),\qquad c_{p,r}:=\prod_{i=1}^r\big(1-p^{-i}\big)^{-1},
\]
where $V$ is uniform in $(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^{n\times r}$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 5.}\ We identify the limit of this mean as the Haar measure of a set $\Omega_E$ of $p$-adic data.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces
By Lemma~\ref{lem:gram}(a), $(\Theta_V,V^{\top}e)$ converges in total variation to the uniform distribution on $\mathcal G_r(p^E)$, which is
$\mathrm{Sym}_r(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)\times(\mathbb{Z}/p^E)^r$ for odd $p$ and $\{(\Theta,u):\ \Theta_{ii}\equiv u_i\pmod2\ \text{for all }i\}$ for $p=2$. We
describe the limit $p$-adically, by a Haar measure, as for the random $p$-adic matrices of Friedman--Washington (1989)~\cite{FW89} in
connection with the heuristics of Cohen--Lenstra (1984)~\cite{CL84}. Let
$X_r:=\mathrm{Sym}_r(\mathbb{Z}_p)\times\mathbb{Z}_p^r\times\mathrm{Sym}_r(\mathbb{Z}_p)$, with points denoted $(\Theta,u,H)$. For $p=2$ we replace $X_r$ by its
open subset on which $\Theta_{ii}\equiv u_i$ and $H_{ii}\equiv0\pmod2$ for all $i$. Let $\mu_r$ be the normalized Haar measure on $X_r$,
and put
\[
\Omega_E:=\big\{(\Theta,u,H)\in X_r:\ \bar\Theta\text{ is invertible and }\det\mathcal K_r(\Theta^{-1}H,\Theta^{-1}u)\equiv0
\pmod{p^E}\big\}.
\]
The reduction of $\mu_r$ modulo $p^E$ is the product of the uniform distribution on $\mathcal G_r(p^E)$ and the uniform distribution on the
symmetric matrices $H$ modulo $p^E$ (with even diagonal if $p=2$). Moreover, for fixed $\Theta$ invertible modulo $p$, $B=\Theta^{-1}H$ is
uniform among the $B$ with $\Theta B$ symmetric (with even diagonal if $p=2$) when $H$ is uniform. As $\Omega_E$ depends only on
reductions modulo $p^E$, it follows that $\mathbb{E}(h(\Theta_V,V^{\top}e))\to\mu_r(\Omega_E)$, and hence
$\limsup_n\Pr(\mathcal Y_{a,E})\le c_{p,r}\,\mu_r(\Omega_E)$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 6.}\ We show that $\mu_r(\Omega_E)\to0$ as $E\to\infty$, which completes the proof of (b).\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces
The sets $\Omega_E$ decrease in $E$, and for $(\Theta,u,H)\in\bigcap_E\Omega_E$ the determinant of
$\mathcal K_r(\Theta^{-1}H,\Theta^{-1}u)$ is divisible by every power of $p$, so it vanishes. Hence $\bigcap_E\Omega_E$ is contained in the
zero set of
\begin{align*}
F(\Theta,u,H)&:=\det\Bigl(\bigl(\operatorname{adj}(\Theta)H\bigr)^i\operatorname{adj}(\Theta)\,u\Bigr)_{0\le i<r}\\
&=\det(\Theta)^{r(r+1)/2}\det\mathcal K_r\big(\Theta^{-1}H,\Theta^{-1}u\big),
\end{align*}
the determinant of the matrix with columns $(\operatorname{adj}(\Theta)H)^i\operatorname{adj}(\Theta)u$, $0\le i<r$. It is a polynomial in
the entries of $(\Theta,u,H)$, and it is not the zero polynomial: at $\Theta=I$, $u=(1,\dots,1)^{\top}$ and
$H=\operatorname{diag}(0,2,4,\dots,2r-2)$ it is a nonzero Vandermonde determinant. The zero set of a nonzero polynomial in $t$ variables has
Haar measure $0$ in $\mathbb{Z}_p^{t}$ (by induction on $t$ and Fubini's theorem, since a nonzero polynomial in one variable has finitely many zeros
and Haar measure on $\mathbb{Z}_p$ has no atoms), and $\mu_r$ is a multiple of the restriction of Haar measure to an open set. Hence
$\mu_r(\bigcap_E\Omega_E)=0$, so $\mu_r(\Omega_E)\to0$ as $E\to\infty$. With Steps~3 and~5, $\limsup_n\Pr(\mathcal X_E)<2\eta$ for all
large $E$, and as $\eta>0$ was arbitrary, this proves (b).
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:par}
For every graph and every $i\ge1$ we have $\langle\bar e,\bar A^i\bar e\rangle=0$ in $\mathbb{F}_2$, that is, $e^{\top}A^ie$ is even. Consequently,
for all $i,j\ge0$, $\langle\bar A^i\bar e,\bar A^j\bar e\rangle=0$ unless $i=j=0$.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
We prove the first assertion by induction on $i$. If $i=2l+1$ is odd, then $\langle\bar e,\bar A^i\bar e\rangle=y^{\top}\bar Ay=0$ for
$y:=\bar A^l\bar e$. If $i=2l$ with $l\ge1$, then $\langle\bar e,\bar A^i\bar e\rangle=\langle y,y\rangle=\langle\bar e,y\rangle$ for
$y:=\bar A^l\bar e$, which vanishes by induction, as $l<i$. The last assertion follows from
$\langle\bar A^i\bar e,\bar A^j\bar e\rangle=\langle\bar e,\bar A^{i+j}\bar e\rangle$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:Ttwo}
Let $G$ be any graph on $n$ vertices, and write $\varphi=\sum_{i=0}^nc_ix^{n-i}$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item $c_i$ is even for every odd $i$. Hence $\bar\varphi=\gamma^2$ if $n$ is even and $\bar\varphi=x\gamma^2$ if $n$ is odd, for a unique
monic $\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_2[x]$ of degree $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, namely $\gamma=\sum_j\bar c_{2j}x^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor-j}$.
\item $\bar\psi=0$ if $n$ is even and $\bar\psi=\gamma^2$ if $n$ is odd. Consequently
$\mathcal T/2\mathcal T=\mathbb{F}_2[x]/(\bar\varphi,\bar\psi)=\mathbb{F}_2[x]/(\gamma^2)$.
\item If $G$ is controllable, $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_2[x]$ is irreducible and $\mathfrak{m}:=(2,\tilde\beta)$, then $D_\mathfrak{m}\ne0$ if and only if $\beta\mid\gamma$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
(a) The number $(-1)^ic_i$ is the sum of the principal minors of order $i$ of $A$. A principal submatrix of odd order $i$ is symmetric with
zero diagonal, so its reduction modulo $2$ is alternating. Alternating matrices have even rank, so this reduction is singular and the minor
is even. (Equivalently, each elementary subgraph on an odd number of vertices contains a cycle, which contributes a factor $2$ to its
term in Sachs' theorem, see Cvetkovi\'c--Doob--Sachs (1980)~\cite{CDS80}.) Hence $\bar\varphi=\sum_j\bar c_{2j}x^{n-2j}$. As squaring
is additive on $\mathbb{F}_2[x]$ and fixes $\mathbb{F}_2$, this equals $\bigl(\sum_j\bar c_{2j}x^{n/2-j}\bigr)^2$ for even $n$ and
$x\bigl(\sum_j\bar c_{2j}x^{(n-1)/2-j}\bigr)^2$ for odd $n$. The polynomial $\gamma$ is monic since $c_0=1$, and unique since squaring is
injective on $\mathbb{F}_2[x]$. (The evenness of the odd-index coefficients is used in the same way by Wang (2017)~\cite{W17}.)

(b) By~\eqref{eq:walkgf} and $N_0=n$, the Laurent series $\psi-nx^{-1}\varphi=\varphi\sum_{k\ge1}N_kx^{-k-1}$ has even coefficients, that
is, $x\bar\psi=\bar n\,\bar\varphi$ in $\mathbb{F}_2[x]$. For even $n$ this gives $\bar\psi=0$, and for odd $n$ it gives $x\bar\psi=x\gamma^2$, that
is, $\bar\psi=\gamma^2$. Finally
$\mathcal T/2\mathcal T=\mathbb{Z}[x]/(2,\varphi,\psi)=\mathbb{F}_2[x]/(\bar\varphi,\bar\psi)$, and both $(\gamma^2,0)$ and $(x\gamma^2,\gamma^2)$ generate the
ideal $(\gamma^2)$.

(c) By Proposition~\ref{prop:D}, $D_\mathfrak{m}\cong\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$, which is nonzero if and only if $\mathfrak{m}\supseteq(\varphi,\psi)$, that is, if and only if
$\beta$ divides $\bar\varphi$ and $\bar\psi$. By (a) and (b) this means $\beta\mid\gamma$.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:loc-wang}
Let $G$ be controllable. By Lemma~\ref{lem:Ttwo}(b), $\mathcal T/2\mathcal T\cong\mathbb{F}_2[x]/(\gamma^2)$ has order $2^{2\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$.
Since $\mathcal T/2\mathcal T=\mathcal T_{(2)}/2\mathcal T_{(2)}$ and $|\mathcal T_{(2)}|=2^{2v_2(\det W)}$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:D}, we
get $v_2(\det W)\ge\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, with equality if and only if $2\mathcal T_{(2)}=0$. This recovers the divisibility
$2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\mid\det W$ of Wang (2013)~\cite{W13}. If equality holds, that is, if $2^{-\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\det W$ is odd, then
$\mathcal T_{(2)}=\mathcal T/2\mathcal T\cong\mathbb{F}_2[x]/(\gamma^2)$, so every nonzero local component above $2$ is isomorphic to
$\mathbb{F}_2[x]/(\beta^{2c})$ for some $\beta\mid\gamma$, with $c:=v_\beta(\gamma)$, and its maximal ideal is generated by $\beta$. By
Corollary~\ref{cor:chain}(a) for the nonzero components, and by Proposition~\ref{lem:levellocal}(ii) for the others, $\mathcal F(Q,2)$ is
then empty for every $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$, so that every level is odd by Proposition~\ref{lem:levellocal}(i). This is the $2$-adic part of the main
theorem of Wang (2017)~\cite{W17}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:krylov}
Let $k\ge1$. Conditionally on $(v_0,\dots,v_{k-1})$, on the event $\dim K_k=k$, the vector $v_k$ is uniformly distributed on $K_k^{\perp}$.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Fix the values of $v_0=e,v_1,\dots,v_{k-1}$, linearly independent. The conditioning event is $\{\bar A:\ \bar Av_i=v_{i+1},\ 0\le i\le k-2\}$,
a coset $\bar A_0+\mathrm{Alt}_{K_{k-1}}$ (with $K_0=0$), on which $\bar A$ is uniformly distributed, and
$v_k=\bar Av_{k-1}=\bar A_0v_{k-1}+Bv_{k-1}$ with $B$ uniform on $\mathrm{Alt}_{K_{k-1}}$. The values of $v_k$ lie in $K_k^{\perp}$:
$\langle\bar Av_{k-1},v_i\rangle=\langle v_{k-1},v_{i+1}\rangle=0$ for $i\le k-2$ by~\eqref{eq:vorth}, and $\langle\bar Av_{k-1},v_{k-1}\rangle=0$
as $\bar A$ is alternating. The linear map $B\mapsto Bv_{k-1}$ maps $\mathrm{Alt}_{K_{k-1}}$ onto $K_k^{\perp}$: given $z\in K_k^{\perp}$, choose
$y$ with $\langle y,v_{k-1}\rangle=1$ and $\langle y,v_i\rangle=0$ for $i\le k-2$, and take $B=zy^{\top}+yz^{\top}$, which is alternating,
kills $K_{k-1}$ and maps $v_{k-1}$ to $z$. Hence $v_k$ is uniform on $K_k^{\perp}$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:krylovlaw}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item If $n$ is even, then $K\subseteq K^{\perp}$. If $n$ is odd, then $\mu=x\mu_1$, where $\mu_1$ (of degree $k_0-1$) is the minimal
polynomial of $v_1=\bar Ae$, and $K\cap K^{\perp}=\bar AK=\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_{k_0-1})$. In both cases $j\ge0$, and there is a
monic $\gamma'\in\mathbb{F}_2[x]$ of degree $j$ with
\[
\bar\varphi=\mu^2\gamma'^2,\quad\gamma=\mu\gamma'\quad(n\text{
even}),\qquad\qquad\bar\varphi=x\mu_1^2\gamma'^2,\quad\gamma=\mu_1\gamma'\quad(n\text{ odd}).
\]
In both cases $\gamma_\circ=\mu\gamma'$.
\item $\Pr(j\ge r)\le\frac43\,4^{-r}$ for every integer $r\ge0$.
\item Conditionally on $(k_0,v_0,\dots,v_{k_0-1})$, the polynomial $\mu$ is uniformly distributed among the monic polynomials of degree
$k_0$ if $n$ is even, and $\mu_1$ is uniformly distributed among the monic polynomials of degree $k_0-1$ if $n$ is odd.
\item Let $P:=e^{\perp}/\mathbb{F}_2e$ and $K^{\circ}:=K/\mathbb{F}_2e$ if $n$ is even, and $P:=e^{\perp}$ and $K^{\circ}:=\bar AK$ if $n$ is odd. Then
$\langle\,,\rangle$ induces a nondegenerate alternating form on $P$, which has dimension $2(\kappa-1)$, and $K^{\circ}$ is a totally isotropic
subspace of $P$ of dimension $k_0-1$. Conditionally on $k_0$, $K^{\circ}$ is uniformly distributed among the totally isotropic subspaces of
$P$ of dimension $k_0-1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
(a) If $n$ is even, all $\langle v_i,v_l\rangle$ vanish by~\eqref{eq:vorth}, so $K\subseteq K^{\perp}$. If $n$ is odd, a vector
$y=\sum_{i<k_0}c_iv_i$ satisfies $\langle y,v_0\rangle=c_0$ and $\langle y,v_l\rangle=0$ for $l\ge1$, so
$K\cap K^{\perp}=\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_{k_0-1})$. Moreover $v_{k_0}\in K$, and $v_{k_0}\perp v_i$ for all $i<k_0$
by~\eqref{eq:vorth}, so $v_{k_0}\in K\cap K^{\perp}$. Writing $v_{k_0}=\sum_{i=1}^{k_0-1}a_iv_i$ shows that $x\mid\mu$, that
$\bar AK=\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_{k_0})=K\cap K^{\perp}$, and that $\mu_1=\mu/x$ is the minimal polynomial of $v_1$ (it kills $v_1$,
and $v_1,\dots,v_{k_0-1}$ are independent).

All the subspaces below are $\bar A$-stable ($\bar A$ is symmetric). Let $n$ be even. The characteristic polynomial of $\bar A$ on the cyclic
space $K$ is $\mu$. The pairing identifies $\mathbb{F}_2^n/K^{\perp}$ with the dual of $K$, the action of $\bar A$ becoming the transpose, so the
characteristic polynomial on $\mathbb{F}_2^n/K^{\perp}$ is also $\mu$. Let $\chi'$ be the characteristic polynomial on $K^{\perp}/K$, of degree
$n-2k_0\ge0$. Then $\gamma^2=\bar\varphi=\mu^2\chi'$, so $\mu\mid\gamma$, and $\chi'=\gamma'^2$ with $\gamma':=\gamma/\mu$ of degree
$n/2-k_0=j$. Now let $n$ be odd, and put $K':=\bar AK$. In the filtration $0\subseteq K'\subseteq K^{\perp}\subseteq K'^{\perp}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n$
the characteristic polynomials of $\bar A$ on the successive quotients are $\mu_1$ (on the cyclic space $K'$ generated by $v_1$), some
$\chi'$ of degree $n+1-2k_0\ge0$, $x$ (the pairing identifies $K'^{\perp}/K^{\perp}$ with the dual of $K/K'$, on which $\bar A$ acts as $0$
because $\bar AK=K'$), and $\mu_1$ (on $\mathbb{F}_2^n/K'^{\perp}$, dual to $K'$). Hence $x\gamma^2=\bar\varphi=x\mu_1^2\chi'$, so $\mu_1\mid\gamma$, and
$\chi'=\gamma'^2$ with $\gamma':=\gamma/\mu_1$ of degree $(n+1)/2-k_0=j$. Then $\gamma_\circ=x\mu_1\gamma'=\mu\gamma'$.

(b), (c) Fix $k\ge1$ and values $v_0=e,v_1,\dots,v_{k-1}$ with $\dim K_k=k$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:krylov}, $v_k$ is then uniform on
$K_k^{\perp}$, a space of size $2^{n-k}$, and $k_0=k$ if and only if $v_k\in K_k\cap K_k^{\perp}$. By the computation in (a) (with $k$ in
place of $k_0$), $K_k\cap K_k^{\perp}$ is $K_k$ if $n$ is even and $\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_{k-1})$ if $n$ is odd. Hence the
conditional probability that $k_0=k$ is $2^{2k-n}$ for even $n$ and $2^{2k-1-n}$ for odd $n$, that is, $4^{k-\kappa}$ in both cases.
Conditionally on $k_0=k$, the vector
$v_k=\sum_{i<k}a_iv_i$ is uniform on $K_k\cap K_k^{\perp}$, that is, $(a_0,\dots,a_{k-1})$ is uniform on $\mathbb{F}_2^k$ for even $n$, while $a_0=0$
and $(a_1,\dots,a_{k-1})$ is uniform on $\mathbb{F}_2^{k-1}$ for odd $n$. As $\mu=x^k+\sum_{i<k}a_ix^i$, this proves (c). For (b), $j\ge r$ means
$k_0\le\kappa-r$, and summing the conditional probabilities of stopping at the steps $k\le\kappa-r$ gives
\[
\Pr(j\ge r)\le\sum_{k=1}^{\kappa-r}4^{k-\kappa}\le\sum_{i\ge r}4^{-i}=\tfrac43\,4^{-r}.
\]

(d) If $n$ is even, then $e\in e^{\perp}$ and the radical of the restriction of $\langle\,,\rangle$ to $e^{\perp}$ is
$e^{\perp}\cap(e^{\perp})^{\perp}=\mathbb{F}_2e$. If $n$ is odd, then $e\notin e^{\perp}$ and the restriction to $e^{\perp}$ is nondegenerate. In both
cases the induced form on $P$ is alternating, since $\langle y,y\rangle=\langle e,y\rangle=0$ for $y\in e^{\perp}$, and $\dim P=2(\kappa-1)$.
By (a), $K^{\circ}$ is totally isotropic of dimension $k_0-1$ (for odd $n$, $K'=\bar AK\subseteq e^{\perp}$ by~\eqref{eq:vorth}).

Let $1\le k\le\kappa$ and let $U$ be a totally isotropic subspace of $P$ of dimension $k-1$. Let $U'$ be the preimage of $U$ in $e^{\perp}$
if $n$ is even, and $U':=U$ if $n$ is odd. For a sequence $w=(w_1,\dots,w_{k-1})$ with
$w_i\in U'\setminus\operatorname{span}(e,w_1,\dots,w_{i-1})$ for all $i$, let $F(w)$ be the event that $v_i=w_i$ for $1\le i<k$ and
$v_k\in K_k$. The event $\{k_0=k,\ K^{\circ}=U\}$ is the disjoint union of the events $F(w)$. Indeed, on this event $v_1,\dots,v_{k-1}$
lie in $U'$ (by (a) if $n$ is odd) and form such a sequence. Conversely, on $F(w)$ we have $k_0=k$, and $K^{\circ}$ is spanned by the
images of $w_1,\dots,w_{k-1}$ in $P$ (by (a) if $n$ is odd), which are linearly independent and lie in $U$, so that $K^{\circ}=U$. For
each such $w$, the vector $w_i$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname{span}(e,w_1,\dots,w_{i-1})$, because $U'$ is totally isotropic and, if $n$
is odd, contained in $e^{\perp}$. Hence Lemma~\ref{lem:krylov}, applied successively, and the
stopping probability computed in (b) give $\Pr(F(w))=4^{k-\kappa}\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}2^{-(n-i)}$ for both parities of $n$.
The number of sequences $w$ is $\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}(2^k-2^i)$ for even $n$ and
$\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}(2^{k-1}-2^{i-1})$ for odd $n$. Neither depends on $U$, which proves (d).
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:wangfails}
By the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:krylovlaw}(b), the conditional probability of stopping at step $k$ is $4^{k-\kappa}$ for both parities
of $n$. Hence
$\Pr(k_0=\kappa)=\prod_{i=1}^{\kappa-1}(1-4^{-i})$, which tends to $\prod_{i\ge1}(1-4^{-i})<0.69$. By the Smith normal form,
$2^{n-\operatorname{rank}_2W}$ divides $\det W$, so the hypothesis of Wang (2017)~\cite{W17} that $2^{-\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\det W$ is odd forces
$k_0\ge\lceil n/2\rceil$, that is, $k_0=\kappa$. So this hypothesis fails for $G(n,1/2)$ with probability at least $0.31$ for large $n$ (compare
the heuristics of Lvov--Van Werde (2026)~\cite{LVW26}), whereas, for every $d_0\ge2$, Proposition~\ref{prop:twolarge} shows that its
$2$-adic conclusion holds at all local components above $2$ of degree at least $d_0$, except with probability $O(2^{-d_0})+o(1)$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:wangLC}
Let $G$ be controllable, let $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_2[x]$ be irreducible with $\beta\mid\gamma$, and let $\mathfrak{m}:=(2,\tilde\beta)$. If $\omega$ does not
vanish identically on $(\gamma_\circ^2/\beta)\mathbb{F}_2[x]$, then $\mathcal T_\mathfrak{m}$ is a chain ring.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:Ttwo}(a),(b), $\beta$ divides $\bar\varphi$ and $\bar\psi$, so $\mathfrak{m}\supseteq(\varphi,\psi)$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:chain} it
suffices to show that $\varphi\notin\mathfrak{m}^2$ or $\psi\notin\mathfrak{m}^2$, that is, to find an element of the ideal $(\varphi,\psi)$ that does not lie
in $\mathfrak{m}^2$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1.}\ We find a polynomial $h$ with $2h\in(\varphi,\psi)$ that encodes $\omega$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Multiplying~\eqref{eq:walkgf} by
$x^{\epsilon_n}\varphi$ and using $N_0=n$, we obtain
\[
x^{\epsilon_n}\psi-\epsilon_nn\varphi=\varphi\sum_{k\ge\epsilon_n}N_kx^{\epsilon_n-k-1}.
\]
The numbers $N_k$ in this sum are even (for even $n$ also $N_0=n$), so the right-hand side has even coefficients. Hence
$h:=(x^{\epsilon_n}\psi-\epsilon_nn\varphi)/2$ lies in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$, and $2h\in(\varphi,\psi)$. Dividing the last identity by
$2x^{\epsilon_n}\varphi$ in $\mathbb{Z}((x^{-1}))$ and reducing modulo $2$, with $x^{\epsilon_n}\bar\varphi=\gamma_\circ^2$, we get
$\bar h/\gamma_\circ^2=\sum_{k\ge\epsilon_n}\omega(x^k)x^{-k-1}$. As
$\omega(1)=0$ for odd $n$, it follows that, for every $g\in\mathbb{F}_2[x]$, $\omega(g)$ is the coefficient of $x^{-1}$ in the Laurent series
$g\bar h/\gamma_\circ^2\in\mathbb{F}_2((x^{-1}))$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}\ We show that $2h\notin\mathfrak{m}^2$, which proves the lemma by Corollary~\ref{cor:chain}.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces For $g=(\gamma_\circ^2/\beta)t$ with
$t\in\mathbb{F}_2[x]$, Step~1 shows that $\omega(g)$ is the coefficient of $x^{-1}$ in $t\bar h/\beta$. If $\beta$ divided $\bar h$, then
$t\bar h/\beta$ would be a polynomial, without a term in $x^{-1}$, and $\omega$ would vanish on $(\gamma_\circ^2/\beta)\mathbb{F}_2[x]$. Hence
$\beta\nmid\bar h$, that is, $h\notin\mathfrak{m}$. Suppose that $2h=4a+2\tilde\beta b+\tilde\beta^2c$ with $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$, that is, $2h\in\mathfrak{m}^2$.
Reducing modulo $2$ gives $\beta^2\bar c=0$, so $c=2c'$ with $c'\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$, and then $h=2a+\tilde\beta b+\tilde\beta^2c'\in\mathfrak{m}$, a
contradiction.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:Lambda}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item The restrictions of $q_A$ and $q_J$ to $K$ are $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear, and so is the restriction of $q_B$ to $K$ for every
$B\in\mathrm{Alt}_K$.
\item Let $f=f_0^2+xf_1^2$ with $f_0,f_1\in\mathbb{F}_2[x]$, and if $n$ is odd assume that $f(0)=0$. Then
$\omega(f)=q_J\big(f_0(\bar A)e\big)+q_A\big(f_1(\bar A)e\big)$.
\item $\omega$ vanishes on $\mu^2\mathbb{F}_2[x]$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
(i) A quadratic form is additive on every subspace on which its polar form vanishes. By Lemma~\ref{lem:par},
$\langle e,g(\bar A)e\rangle=g(0)n$ in $\mathbb{F}_2$ for $g\in\mathbb{F}_2[x]$. Hence, for $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_2[x]$,
$\langle a(\bar A)e,\bar Ab(\bar A)e\rangle=\langle e,(xab)(\bar A)e\rangle=0$, and
\[
\langle a(\bar A)e,b(\bar A)e\rangle+\langle e,a(\bar A)e\rangle\langle e,b(\bar A)e\rangle=(ab)(0)\,n+a(0)b(0)\,n^2=0 .
\]
These are the polar forms of $q_A$ and $q_J$ on $K$. For $B\in\mathrm{Alt}_K$ the polar form $\langle y,Bz\rangle$ vanishes for $z\in K$.

(ii) For $y\in\mathbb{Z}^n$ we have $\frac12y^{\top}Ay=\sum_{i<l}a_{il}y_iy_l\equiv q_A(\bar y)\pmod2$. Moreover $y_i^2\equiv1$ or $0\pmod4$
according as $y_i$ is odd or even, so $\|y\|^2\equiv\operatorname{wt}(\bar y)\pmod4$. If $\operatorname{wt}(\bar y)$ is even, then
$\frac12\|y\|^2\equiv\frac12\operatorname{wt}(\bar y)\equiv\binom{\operatorname{wt}(\bar y)}2=q_J(\bar y)\pmod2$. Let $\tilde f_0,\tilde f_1$ be the $0/1$ lifts of
$f_0,f_1$. Then $\tilde f:=\tilde f_0^2+x\tilde f_1^2$ is a lift of $f$, with $\tilde f(0)=0$ if $n$ is odd (as then $f_0(0)=f(0)=0$). With
$u_0:=\tilde f_0(A)e$ and $u_1:=\tilde f_1(A)e$ we get $e^{\top}\tilde f(A)e=\|u_0\|^2+u_1^{\top}Au_1$, and
$\operatorname{wt}(\bar u_0)\equiv\langle\bar u_0,\bar u_0\rangle=\langle e,f_0^2(\bar A)e\rangle=f_0(0)n\equiv0\pmod2$. Hence
$\omega(f)=\frac12\|u_0\|^2+\frac12u_1^{\top}Au_1\equiv q_J(\bar u_0)+q_A(\bar u_1)$, where $\bar u_i=f_i(\bar A)e$.

(iii) For $h=h_0^2+xh_1^2$ we have $\mu^2h=(\mu h_0)^2+x(\mu h_1)^2$ and $(\mu h_i)(\bar A)e=0$. If $n$ is odd, then $(\mu^2h)(0)=0$ since
$x\mid\mu$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:krylovlaw}(a)). So $\omega(\mu^2h)=0$ by (ii).
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:condlaw}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Conditionally on $\mathcal D$, $\bar A$ is uniformly distributed on a coset of $\mathrm{Alt}_K$, and the linear form $q_A|_K$ is
uniformly distributed on a coset of the subspace
\[
\Psi(\mathrm{Alt}_K)=\big\{\langle z,\cdot\rangle|_K:\ z\in\operatorname{span}(K^{\perp}*K^{\perp})\big\}\subseteq K^*,
\qquad\text{where }\Psi(B):=q_B|_K ,
\]
and $K^*$ is the dual space of $K$.
\item The event $\mathcal B$ that $\operatorname{span}(K^{\perp}*K^{\perp})\not\supseteq e^{\perp}$ is determined by $\mathcal D$, and
$\Pr(\mathcal B)=O(n^22^{-n/2})$ with an absolute implied constant.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
(i) The event that the Krylov data equals a given value $(w_0,\dots,w_r)$ is $\{\bar A:\ \bar Aw_i=w_{i+1},\ 0\le i<r\}$, a coset
$\bar A_0+\mathrm{Alt}_K$, on which $\bar A$ is uniformly distributed. The map $B\mapsto q_B$ is linear, $q_{\bar A_0+B}=q_{\bar A_0}+q_B$, and
the restrictions to $K$ are linear (Lemma~\ref{lem:Lambda}(i)). So $q_A|_K$ is uniform on the coset $q_{\bar A_0}|_K+\Psi(\mathrm{Alt}_K)$.
The space $\mathrm{Alt}_K$ is the space of alternating bilinear forms on $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ that vanish on $K\times\mathbb{F}_2^n$, that is, of alternating
forms on $\mathbb{F}_2^n/K$,
so its dimension is $\binom m2$ with $m:=n-k_0$. If $z_1,\dots,z_m$ is a basis of $K^{\perp}$, the matrices $z_az_b^{\top}+z_bz_a^{\top}$
($a<b$) lie in $\mathrm{Alt}_K$, and they are linearly independent (evaluate the corresponding forms at $(y_c,y_d)$, where
$\langle z_a,y_c\rangle=\delta_{ac}$). Hence they span $\mathrm{Alt}_K$. For $B=uu'^{\top}+u'u^{\top}$ with $u,u'\in K^{\perp}$ and $h\in K$,
using $h_i^2=h_i$ and $\langle u,h\rangle=0$,
\[
q_B(h)=\sum_{i\ne l}u_iu'_lh_ih_l=\langle u,h\rangle\langle u',h\rangle+\sum_iu_iu'_ih_i=\langle u*u',h\rangle .
\]
Since the matrices $uu'^{\top}+u'u^{\top}$ with $u,u'\in K^{\perp}$ lie in $\mathrm{Alt}_K$ and span it, and $\Psi$ is linear, this gives
the formula for $\Psi(\mathrm{Alt}_K)$.

(ii) The event $\mathcal B$ is determined by $K$, hence by $\mathcal D$. Put $\theta_t:=\prod_{i=1}^t(2^i+1)$, so that $\theta_0=1$. We use
two standard facts about a nondegenerate alternating (that is, symplectic) space $Y$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$ of dimension $2t$, for which we refer to
Taylor (1992)~\cite{Tay92}. First, for a totally isotropic subspace $U$, the map $L\mapsto L/U$ is a bijection from the Lagrangian (that is,
totally isotropic $t$-dimensional) subspaces containing $U$ onto the Lagrangian subspaces of the nondegenerate alternating space
$U^{\perp}/U$ of dimension $2t-2\dim U$. Second, $Y$ has exactly $\theta_t$ Lagrangian subspaces. (The second fact follows from the first by
counting the pairs $(y,L)$ with $0\ne y\in L$, every vector being isotropic: $\theta_t(2^t-1)=(2^{2t}-1)\theta_{t-1}$.)

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1.}\ We count the totally isotropic subspaces of maximal dimension in $\mathbb{F}_2^m$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces For $m\ge1$ let $e\in\mathbb{F}_2^m$ also denote the all-ones
vector. A totally isotropic subspace of $\mathbb{F}_2^m$ (for the standard form) has dimension at most $\lfloor m/2\rfloor$ and lies in $e^{\perp}$.
If $m$ is odd, $e^{\perp}$ is nondegenerate alternating of dimension $m-1$. If $m$ is even, a totally isotropic subspace $L$ of dimension
$m/2$ satisfies $L=L^{\perp}\ni e$, and $L\mapsto L/\mathbb{F}_2e$ identifies these subspaces with the Lagrangians of $e^{\perp}/\mathbb{F}_2e$, of
dimension $m-2$. In both cases $\mathbb{F}_2^m$ has exactly $\theta_{\lceil m/2\rceil-1}$ totally isotropic subspaces of dimension
$\lfloor m/2\rfloor$. In particular, for $m=n$ these subspaces correspond bijectively to the Lagrangians of the space $P$ of
Lemma~\ref{lem:krylovlaw}(d), via $L\mapsto L/\mathbb{F}_2e$ for even $n$ and $L\mapsto L$ for odd $n$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}\ We find inside $K^{\perp}$ a uniformly random totally isotropic subspace $L$ of maximal dimension, and reduce (ii) to a statement
about $L$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Conditionally on $G$, let $L^{\circ}$ be a uniformly random Lagrangian of $P$ containing $K^{\circ}$, and let $L\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n$
be the corresponding totally isotropic subspace of dimension $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. Then $L\subseteq K^{\perp}$. Indeed, $L^{\circ}$ is
orthogonal to $K^{\circ}$ in $P$, as $L^{\circ}\supseteq K^{\circ}$ is totally isotropic. For even $n$ this gives $\langle L,K\rangle=0$, and
for odd $n$ it gives $L=L^{\circ}\subseteq e^{\perp}\cap(\bar AK)^{\perp}=K^{\perp}$, as $K=\mathbb{F}_2e+\bar AK$. Conditionally on $k_0$,
$L^{\circ}$ is uniformly distributed among all Lagrangians of $P$: for a Lagrangian $L_1$ of $P$,
\[
\Pr\bigl(L^{\circ}=L_1\bigm|k_0\bigr)=\sum_U\frac{\Pr(K^{\circ}=U\mid k_0)}{\theta_{\kappa-k_0}},
\]
the sum over the $(k_0-1)$-dimensional subspaces $U$ of $L_1$ (all of them totally isotropic). Here $\theta_{\kappa-k_0}$ is the number of
Lagrangians of $P$ that contain a given totally isotropic subspace of dimension $k_0-1$, by the two facts above. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:krylovlaw}(d) all summands are equal, and their number depends only on $k_0$ and $\kappa$. Hence $L$ is uniformly
distributed among the $\theta_{\kappa-1}$ totally isotropic subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ of dimension $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. Since
$L\subseteq K^{\perp}$, we have
$\operatorname{span}(L*L)\subseteq\operatorname{span}(K^{\perp}*K^{\perp})$, and it suffices to show that
$\Pr(\operatorname{span}(L*L)\not\supseteq e^{\perp})=O(n^22^{-n/2})$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 3.}\ We show that if $\operatorname{span}(L*L)\ne e^{\perp}$, then $L$ splits along a nontrivial partition of the coordinates, and we
count such $L$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces For $y,z\in L$ we have $\langle y*z,e\rangle=\langle y,z\rangle=0$, so $\operatorname{span}(L*L)\subseteq e^{\perp}$.
Suppose $\operatorname{span}(L*L)\ne e^{\perp}$. Then some $w\notin(e^{\perp})^{\perp}=\{0,e\}$ is orthogonal to $L*L$. Let $S$ be its
support, so that $\emptyset\ne S\ne[n]$. For $y,z\in L$ we get $\sum_{i\in S}y_iz_i=\langle w,y*z\rangle=0$ and
$\sum_{i\notin S}y_iz_i=\langle y,z\rangle-\sum_{i\in S}y_iz_i=0$, so the coordinate projections $\pi_S(L)\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^S$ and
$\pi_{S^c}(L)\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^{S^c}$ are totally isotropic, and
$\dim\pi_S(L)+\dim\pi_{S^c}(L)\le\lfloor|S|/2\rfloor+\lfloor|S^c|/2\rfloor\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor=\dim L$. As $L$ embeds into
$\pi_S(L)\oplus\pi_{S^c}(L)$, it follows that $L$ splits along $S$, that is, $L=\pi_S(L)\oplus\pi_{S^c}(L)$, with both summands
totally isotropic of the maximal dimensions $\lfloor|S|/2\rfloor$ and $\lfloor|S^c|/2\rfloor$, whose sum is $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. Hence,
for $|S|=m$, the number of such $L$ is at most $\theta_{a-1}\theta_{b-1}$ with $a:=\lceil m/2\rceil$ and $b:=\lceil(n-m)/2\rceil$, and
it is $0$ unless $a+b=\kappa$ (if $n$ is even and $m$ is odd, the dimensions add up to $n/2-1$).

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 4.}\ We sum the bound of Step~3 over the possible supports $S$ and conclude the proof of (ii).\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces With $c:=\prod_{i\ge1}(1+2^{-i})<3$ we
have $2^{t(t+1)/2}\le\theta_t\le c\,2^{t(t+1)/2}$. If $a+b=\kappa$, then
\[
\frac{\theta_{a-1}\theta_{b-1}}{\theta_{\kappa-1}}\le c^2\,2^{\frac12\left((a-1)a+(b-1)b-(a+b-1)(a+b)\right)}=c^2\,2^{-ab}.
\]
As $L$ is uniform among $\theta_{\kappa-1}$ subspaces, the probability that $L$ splits along some $S$ of size $m$ is at most
$\binom nmc^22^{-ab}$, and this bound is symmetric under $m\mapsto n-m$. For $1\le m\le n/2$ we have
$a\ge1$, $m\le2a$ and $b\ge(n-m)/2\ge\max(n/4,(n-2a)/2)$, so $ab=b+(a-1)b\ge\frac n2-a+(a-1)\frac n4$. With $\binom nm\le n^{2a}$ this gives
\[
\binom nm\,c^2\,2^{-ab}\le c^2\,2^{-n/2}\cdot2n^2\cdot\big(2n^22^{-n/4}\big)^{a-1}.
\]
Each $a\ge1$ arises from at most two values of $m$. Hence, if $2n^22^{-n/4}\le\frac12$, the probability that $L$ splits along some $S$ is at
most $2\cdot2\cdot c^2\,2^{-n/2}\cdot2n^2\cdot\sum_{i\ge0}2^{-i}=16c^2n^22^{-n/2}$. For the finitely many remaining $n$ the bound
$O(n^22^{-n/2})$ holds trivially.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:socle}
Let $\mu\in\mathbb{F}_2[x]$ be nonzero, let $\beta$ be an irreducible factor of $\mu$, and put $c:=v_\beta(\mu)$. If $f=(\mu^2/\beta)t$ with
$t\in\mathbb{F}_2[x]$, $\beta\nmid t$, and $f=f_0^2+xf_1^2$ with $f_0,f_1\in\mathbb{F}_2[x]$, then $v_\beta(f_1)=c-1$.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Differentiating $f=f_0^2+xf_1^2$ gives $f'=f_1^2$, since squares have derivative $0$ in characteristic $2$. Write
$\mu^2/\beta=\beta^{2c-1}g$ with $\beta\nmid g$. Then $f=\beta^{2c-1}gt$ and, as $2c-1$ is odd, $f'=\beta^{2c-2}\big(\beta'gt+\beta(gt)'\big)$.
Here $\beta'\ne0$, because $\beta$ is irreducible and hence not a square, and $\deg\beta'<\deg\beta$, so $\beta\nmid\beta'gt$. Hence
$2v_\beta(f_1)=v_\beta(f')=2c-2$.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:twolarge}
For all $n\ge3$ and $d_0\ge2$,
\[
\Pr\bigl(\mathcal E_2(d_0)\bigr)\le2^{2-d_0}+O\big(n^22^{-n/2}\big),
\]
with an absolute implied constant. If $G$ is controllable and $\mathcal E_2(d_0)$ does not hold, then $(2,\tilde\beta)\notin\mathcal F(Q,2)$
for every $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$ and every irreducible $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_2[x]$ with $\deg\beta\ge d_0$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:krylovlaw}(a), $\gamma_\circ=\mu\gamma'$ with $\deg\gamma'=j$, and $x\mid\mu$ if $n$ is odd. Let $\mathcal B$ be the event
of Lemma~\ref{lem:condlaw}(ii). For an irreducible $\beta\ne x$ let $\mathcal Z_\beta$ be the event that $\beta\mid\mu$ and that $\omega$
vanishes identically on the space
\[
S_\beta:=\big\{(\mu^2/\beta)r:\ r\in\mathbb{F}_2[x],\ \deg r<\deg\beta\big\}.
\]
Only polynomials $\beta$ of degree at least $d_0\ge2$ occur below, so $\beta\ne x$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1.}\ We show that $\mathcal E_2(d_0)\subseteq\{j\ge d_0\}\cup\bigcup_{\deg\beta\ge d_0}\mathcal Z_\beta$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Suppose that
$\mathcal E_2(d_0)$ holds through $\beta$ of degree $d\ge d_0$, and that $j<d_0$. As $D_{(2,\beta)}\ne0$, $\beta$ divides $\gamma$ and hence
$\gamma_\circ=\mu\gamma'$, and $\beta\nmid\gamma'$ because $\deg\gamma'=j<d$. So $\beta\mid\mu$. As $\mathcal T_{(2,\beta)}$ is not a chain
ring, Lemma~\ref{lem:wangLC} shows that $\omega$ vanishes on $(\gamma_\circ^2/\beta)\mathbb{F}_2[x]$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:Lambda}(iii) it also
vanishes on $\mu^2\mathbb{F}_2[x]$, hence on the ideal generated by $\gamma_\circ^2/\beta=(\mu^2/\beta)\gamma'^2$ and $\mu^2$, which is
$(\mu^2/\beta)\gcd(\gamma'^2,\beta)\mathbb{F}_2[x]=(\mu^2/\beta)\mathbb{F}_2[x]$. This ideal contains $S_\beta$, so $\mathcal Z_\beta$ holds.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}\ We show that $\Pr(\mathcal Z_\beta\mid\mathcal D)\le2^{1-\deg\beta}$ whenever the Krylov data $\mathcal D$ is such that
$\beta\mid\mu$ and $\mathcal B$ fails.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $d:=\deg\beta$, so that $\dim S_\beta=d$, and $c:=v_\beta(\mu)$. For $f\in S_\beta$ write
$f=f_0^2+xf_1^2$. If $n$ is odd,
then $f(0)=0$, as $x\mid\mu$ and $\beta\ne x$. So Lemma~\ref{lem:Lambda}(ii) gives $\omega(f)=q_J(f_0(\bar A)e)+q_A(f_1(\bar A)e)$. The
maps $f\mapsto f_0$ and $f\mapsto f_1$ are $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear, the vectors $f_i(\bar A)e\in K$ are determined by $\mathcal D$, and $q_J$, $q_A$
are linear on $K$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:Lambda}(i)). Hence $\omega|_{S_\beta}=\lambda_{\mathcal D}+\varpi\circ\iota$, where
$\lambda_{\mathcal D}(f):=q_J(f_0(\bar A)e)$ is determined by $\mathcal D$, $\varpi:=q_A|_K\in K^*$, and $\iota:S_\beta\to K$,
$f\mapsto f_1(\bar A)e$, is linear and determined by $\mathcal D$. If $f=(\mu^2/\beta)r\in S_\beta$ is nonzero, then $\beta\nmid r$ as
$\deg r<d$, so $v_\beta(f_1)=c-1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:socle}. Then $\mu\nmid f_1$ and $\iota(f)\ne0$, as $\mu$ is the minimal polynomial of
$e$. So $\iota$ is injective, and $\mathcal Z_\beta$ is the event that $\lambda_{\mathcal D}+\varpi\circ\iota=0$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:condlaw}(i), conditionally on $\mathcal D$, $\varpi$ is uniform on a coset of $\Psi(\mathrm{Alt}_K)$. As $\mathcal B$ fails,
this subspace contains $\{\langle z,\cdot\rangle|_K:\ z\in e^{\perp}\}=\{\vartheta\in K^*:\ \vartheta(e)=0\}$ (the map
$z\mapsto\langle z,\cdot\rangle|_K$ is onto $K^*$, and $e\in K$). The image of this hyperplane under the surjection
$\vartheta\mapsto\vartheta\circ\iota$ of $K^*$ onto $S_\beta^*$ has codimension at most $1$. Hence, conditionally on $\mathcal D$,
$\varpi\circ\iota$ is uniform on a coset of a subspace of $S_\beta^*$ of dimension at least $d-1$, and
$\Pr(\mathcal Z_\beta\mid\mathcal D)\le2^{1-d}$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 3.}\ We sum the bounds of Steps~1 and~2 over $\beta$ and obtain the bound on $\Pr(\mathcal E_2(d_0))$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces By Lemma~\ref{lem:krylovlaw}(c),
conditionally on $k_0$ the polynomial $\mu$ is uniformly distributed among the monic polynomials of degree $k_0$ if $n$ is even, and
$\mu=x\mu_1$ with $\mu_1$ uniformly distributed among the monic polynomials of degree $k_0-1$ if $n$ is odd. A uniformly random monic
polynomial of degree at least $\deg\beta$ is divisible by $\beta$ with probability $2^{-\deg\beta}$, and one of smaller degree is not
divisible by $\beta$. As $\beta\ne x$, we get $\Pr(\beta\mid\mu)\le2^{-\deg\beta}$ in both cases. The events $\{\beta\mid\mu\}$ and
$\mathcal B$ are determined by $\mathcal D$. By Steps~1 and~2, Lemma~\ref{lem:krylovlaw}(b), Lemma~\ref{lem:condlaw}(ii) and the bound
$\pi_2(d)\le2^d/d$ of Section~\ref{sec:small},
\begin{align*}
\Pr\bigl(\mathcal E_2(d_0)\bigr)&\le\Pr(j\ge d_0)+\Pr(\mathcal B)
+\sum_{\deg\beta\ge d_0}\mathbb{E}\Big(\mathbf 1\{\beta\mid\mu\}\,\mathbf 1_{\mathcal B^c}\,\Pr\bigl(\mathcal Z_\beta\bigm|\mathcal D\bigr)\Big)\\
&\le\tfrac43\,4^{-d_0}+O\big(n^22^{-n/2}\big)+\sum_{d\ge d_0}\frac{2^d}d\,2^{-d}\,2^{1-d}.
\end{align*}
The last sum is at most $2^{2-d_0}/d_0\le2^{1-d_0}$, and $\frac43\,4^{-d_0}\le2^{-d_0}$. So
$\Pr(\mathcal E_2(d_0))\le3\cdot2^{-d_0}+O(n^22^{-n/2})\le2^{2-d_0}+O(n^22^{-n/2})$.

Finally, let $G$ be controllable, suppose that $\mathcal E_2(d_0)$ fails, and let $\beta$ be irreducible with $\deg\beta\ge d_0$. Then
$D_{(2,\beta)}=0$ or $\mathcal T_{(2,\beta)}$ is a chain ring. In both cases Proposition~\ref{lem:levellocal}(ii) shows that
$(2,\tilde\beta)\notin\mathcal F(Q,2)$ for every $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Fix $\varepsilon\in(0,\frac12)$, put $\delta:=\varepsilon/2\in(0,\frac14)$, and let $\eta>0$. In this proof, limits are taken as
$n\to\infty$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1.}\ We choose the parameters $q_0$, $d_0$, $a_*$ and $h$, together with a finite set $\mathcal P$ of pairs $(p,\beta)$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces By
Theorem~\ref{thm:firstmoment} (with this $\delta$) choose $q_0\ge2$ such that
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\Pr\bigl(E_p^{(d)}\text{ holds for some }(p,d)\in\mathcal R_n(\delta)\text{ with $p$ odd and }p^d>q_0\bigr)<\eta,
\]
and choose $d_0\ge2$ with $2^{2-d_0}<\eta$. Let $\mathcal P$ be the finite set of pairs $(p,\beta)$, with $p$ prime and $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_p[x]$
irreducible, such that either $p$ is odd and $p^{\deg\beta}\le q_0$, or $p=2$ and $\deg\beta<d_0$. Only finitely many pairs $(p,\deg\beta)$
occur in $\mathcal P$, so by Proposition~\ref{prop:tight}(a) there is $a_*\ge1$ such that
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\Pr\bigl(\beta^{a_*}\mid\bar\varphi\text{ for some }(p,\beta)\in\mathcal P\bigr)<\eta,
\]
and by Proposition~\ref{prop:tight}(b) there is $h\ge1$ such that
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\Pr\bigl(G\text{ is controllable and }\exp(\mathfrak M_{(p,\beta)})\ge p^h
\text{ for some }(p,\beta)\in\mathcal P\bigr)<\eta .
\]
Put $L_0:=\prod_{p\le q_0}p^{h-1}$, the product over the primes $p\le q_0$, and $d_*:=a_*\sum_{(p,\beta)\in\mathcal P}\deg\beta$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}\ We define an exceptional event $\mathcal X$ and bound its probability.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $\mathcal X$ be the union of the following events.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(X\arabic*)]
\item $G$ is not controllable.
\item $E_p^{(d)}$ holds for some $(p,d)\in\mathcal R_n(\delta)$ with $p$ odd and $p^d>q_0$.
\item $E_p^{(d)}$ holds for some odd prime $p$ and some $d\ge3\log_2n$.
\item $G$ is controllable, and $D_{(2,\beta)}\ne0$ while $\mathcal T_{(2,\beta)}$ is not a chain ring, for some irreducible
$\beta\in\mathbb{F}_2[x]$ with $\deg\beta\ge d_0$.
\item $\beta^{a_*}\mid\bar\varphi$ for some $(p,\beta)\in\mathcal P$, or $G$ is controllable and $\exp(\mathfrak M_{(p,\beta)})\ge p^h$
for some $(p,\beta)\in\mathcal P$.
\item The conclusion of Proposition~\ref{lem:suppd} fails for $M=A$ and $m=n$, the entries of $A$ above the diagonal being uniform on
$\{0,1\}$.
\end{enumerate}
The probability of (X1) tends to $0$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:OT}. That of (X2) has $\limsup$ less than $\eta$ by the choice of $q_0$, and that
of (X3) tends to $0$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:largedegrees}. The event (X4) is the event $\mathcal E_2(d_0)$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:twolarge},
of probability at most $2^{2-d_0}+O(n^22^{-n/2})$, so its $\limsup$ is less than $\eta$ by the choice of $d_0$. By the choices of $a_*$ and
$h$, the probability of (X5) has $\limsup$ less than $2\eta$. Finally, (X6) has probability at most $e^{-n/8}$ for large $n$ by
Proposition~\ref{lem:suppd}. Hence
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\Pr(\mathcal X)\le4\eta .
\]

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 3.}\ We show that, outside $\mathcal X$, a matrix in $\mathcal{Q}_G$ whose level has only small prime factors can differ from the identity only at
components given by $\mathcal P$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $n$ be large, let $G\notin\mathcal X$, and suppose that some $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$ which is not a permutation
matrix has a level $\ell:=\ell(Q)$ all of whose prime factors are at most $n^{1/2-\varepsilon}$. Since (X1) fails, $G$ is controllable.
Moreover $\ell\ge2$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:wangxu}, as $Q$ is not a permutation matrix. Let $p$ be a prime factor of $\ell$. By
Proposition~\ref{lem:levellocal}(i) the set $\mathcal F(Q,p)$ is nonempty. Let $\mathfrak{m}=(p,\tilde\beta)\in\mathcal F(Q,p)$ and put
$d:=\deg\beta$.

If $p$ is odd, then $E_p^{(d)}$ holds by Proposition~\ref{lem:levellocal}(iii). Since (X3) fails, $d<3\log_2n$. For large $n$ (depending
only on $\varepsilon$) we have $3\log_2n\le n^{\delta}/\log^2n$ and $3n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\log_2n\le n^{1/2-\delta}/\log n$. As
$p\le n^{1/2-\varepsilon}$, it follows that $(p,d)\in\mathcal R_n(\delta)$. Since (X2) fails, we get $p^d\le q_0$, that is,
$(p,\beta)\in\mathcal P$.

If $p=2$, then $d<d_0$ by the last assertion of Proposition~\ref{prop:twolarge}, as $G$ is controllable and (X4) fails. Hence
$(2,\beta)\in\mathcal P$.

Thus $\mathcal F(Q,p)\subseteq\{(p,\tilde\beta):\ (p,\beta)\in\mathcal P\}$ for every prime $p\mid\ell$. In particular every prime factor of
$\ell$ is at most $q_0$ (recall that $q_0\ge2$).

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 4.}\ We show that the level of such a matrix $Q$ divides $L_0$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $p\mid\ell$. For $\mathfrak{m}=(p,\tilde\beta)\in\mathcal F(Q,p)$ we have
$(p,\beta)\in\mathcal P$ and $\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m}=\mathfrak M_{(p,\beta)}$. As $G$ is controllable and (X5) fails, $\exp(\mathfrak M_\mathfrak{m})$ is a
power of $p$ smaller than $p^h$, so Proposition~\ref{lem:levellocal}(i) gives $v_p(\ell)\le h-1$. Hence $\ell$ divides $L_0$, and
$\ell\le L_0$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 5.}\ We derive a contradiction from the short columns of $\ell Q$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $p\mid\ell$, and put
\[
g:=\prod_{(p,\tilde\beta)\in\mathcal F(Q,p)}\beta^{a_\beta}\in\mathbb{F}_p[x],\qquad\text{where }\beta^{a_\beta}\,\|\,\bar\varphi .
\]
By Step~3, $(p,\beta)\in\mathcal P$ for all these $\beta$, so $a_\beta<a_*$ as (X5) fails, and $\deg g\le d_*$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:shortcol}, some column $z$ of $\ell Q$ satisfies $0<\operatorname{wt}(\bar z)\le\ell^2\le L_0^2$ and $g(\bar A)\bar z=0$. In particular
$\deg g\ge1$, as $\bar z\ne0$. For large $n$ we have $p\le q_0\le e^{n^{1/8}}$, $d_*\le n^{1/4}$ and
$L_0^2<n/(4(d_*+1))\le n/(4(\deg g+1))$, so $\bar z$ violates the conclusion of Proposition~\ref{lem:suppd}, and (X6) holds, which
contradicts $G\notin\mathcal X$.

Consequently, for all large $n$, the event that some $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_G$ other than a permutation matrix has a level whose prime factors are all at
most $n^{1/2-\varepsilon}$ is contained in $\mathcal X$. Its probability therefore has $\limsup$ at most $4\eta$, and as $\eta>0$ was
arbitrary, it tends to $0$.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{lem:gauss}
Let $p$ be an odd prime, $0<c\le10^{-5}$ and $\sigma:=1/(2cp^2)$. Then
\[
\theta_0:=\sum_{z\in p\mathbb{Z}}e^{-\sigma z^2}\le1.001,\qquad \mu_0:=\sum_{z\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus p\mathbb{Z}}e^{-\sigma z^2}\le\sqrt{2\pi c}\,p\ \ (\le p),
\]
and $\theta_0+\mu_0\le1+\sqrt{2\pi c}\,p$. Moreover, the image on $\mathbb{F}_p^\times$ of the probability law proportional to $e^{-\sigma z^2}$ on
$\mathbb{Z}\setminus p\mathbb{Z}$ has largest atom $\nu_{\max}$ with $\mu_0\nu_{\max}\le1.001$ (and, trivially, $\nu_{\max}\ge1/(p-1)$).
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Note that $\sigma p^2=1/(2c)\ge5\cdot10^4$. Then
$\theta_0=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{-k^2/(2c)}\le1+2\sum_{k\ge1}e^{-k/(2c)}\le1+3e^{-1/(2c)}\le1.001$.
As $z\mapsto e^{-\sigma z^2}$ is decreasing on $[0,\infty)$,
\[
\theta_0+\mu_0=\sum_{z\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{-\sigma z^2}\le1+2\int_0^\infty e^{-\sigma z^2}\,dz=1+\sqrt{\pi/\sigma}=1+\sqrt{2\pi c}\,p ,
\]
and as $\theta_0\ge1$ (the term $z=0$), $\mu_0\le\sqrt{2\pi c}\,p$, where $\sqrt{2\pi c}<1$. The image law gives $a\in\mathbb{F}_p^\times$ the
mass $\mu_0^{-1}\sum_{z\equiv a}e^{-\sigma z^2}$. Let $z_0\in(-\frac p2,\frac p2)$ represent $a$. The other elements of its residue class
are $z_0+jp$, $j\ne0$, and $|z_0+jp|\ge(|j|-\frac12)p$. Using $(k+\frac12)^2\ge k+\frac14$,
\[
\sum_{z\equiv a\ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)}e^{-\sigma z^2}\le1+2\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-(k+\frac12)^2/(2c)}\le1+2\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-(k+\frac14)/(2c)}
\le1+3e^{-1/(8c)}\le1.001 .
\]
So $\mu_0\nu_{\max}\le1.001$. Finally $\nu_{\max}\ge1/(p-1)$, as the image law lives on $p-1$ points.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{lem:seqexp}
Let $T$ be a uniformly random Seidel matrix of order $m$, let $G$ be an abelian group (for instance $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Z}/N$ or $\mathbb{F}_p^d$), and let
$w,t\in G^m$ be fixed. Write $Tw=t$ for the system $\sum_{j}T_{ij}w_j=t_i$, $i\in[m]$ (for $G=\mathbb{F}_p^d$ this is the system $\bar Tw=t$). Then
\[
\Pr(Tw=t)\ \le\ \prod_{i=1}^{m-1}\rho_G\big(w_{(i,m]}\big),\qquad w_{(i,m]}:=(w_{i+1},\dots,w_m).
\]
The same bound holds after any reordering of the coordinates, that is, with $(w_{\pi(i+1)},\dots,w_{\pi(m)})$ in place of $w_{(i,m]}$ for
any permutation $\pi$ of $[m]$. Consequently, $\Pr(Tw=t)\le\rho_G(w_b)^{m-|b|}$ for every $b\subseteq[m]$.
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
Reveal the upper triangle of $T$ one row at a time, at step $i$ the entries $T_{ij}$, $j>i$. The $i$th equation reads
$\sum_{j>i}T_{ij}w_j=t_i-\sum_{j<i}T_{ij}w_j$. Its right side is determined by the entries revealed before step $i$ (as $T_{ij}=T_{ji}$ for
$j<i$ and $T_{ii}=0$), and its left side has the law of $\sum_{j>i}\xi_jw_j$, since the signs $T_{ij}$, $j>i$, are independent of the
entries revealed before step $i$. So, conditionally on these entries, the $i$th equation holds with probability at most
$\rho_G(w_{(i,m]})$. Multiplying these bounds over $i\le m-1$ gives the first claim (the last equation is not used). The law of $T$ is
invariant under simultaneous permutations of rows and columns, and $Tw=t$ is equivalent to $T'w'=t'$ for the permuted matrix $T'$ and
the permuted vectors $w',t'$, which gives the second claim.
For the third, order the coordinates so that $b$ comes last. Then $w_{(i,m]}$ contains $w_b$ for $i\le m-|b|$, so the corresponding factors
are at most $\rho_G(w_b)$, and we bound the other factors by $1$.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{lem:dilates}
Let $p$ be an odd prime, $b$ a finite set, and $\mu$ as in Section~\ref{subsec:toolsnotation} (so $\mu(0)=0$). Then for all $w\in\mathbb{F}_p^b$ and
$c\in\mathbb{F}_p^\times$
\[
\prod_{j\in b}\Bigl|\cos\frac{2\pi cw_j}p\Bigr|\le e^{-2\mu(w)/p^2},\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
\rho_p(w)\le\hat\rho_p(w)\le\frac1p+e^{-2\mu(w)/p^2}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
On $[-\frac12,\frac12]$, where $\cos(\pi\theta)\ge0$, we have $\lvert\cos(\pi\theta)\rvert\le1-2\theta^2\le e^{-2\theta^2}$: the function
${1-2\theta^2-\cos(\pi\theta)}$ is even, vanishes at $0$, and its derivative $\pi\sin(\pi\theta)-4\theta$ is nonnegative on $[0,\frac12]$, as
$\sin(\pi\theta)\ge2\theta$ there. By periodicity, $\lvert\cos(\pi\theta)\rvert\le e^{-2\|\theta\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}^2}$ for all real $\theta$. For $c\ne0$
apply this with $\theta=2cw_j/p$. As $\|2cw_j/p\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}=|(\widetilde{2cw})_j|/p$ and $2c\ne0$ in $\mathbb{F}_p$,
\[
\prod_{j\in b}\Bigl|\cos\frac{2\pi cw_j}p\Bigr|\le\exp\Bigl(-\frac2{p^2}\big\|\widetilde{2cw}\big\|^2\Bigr)\le e^{-2\mu(w)/p^2}.
\]
Finally $\hat\rho_p(w)=\frac1p\sum_{c\in\mathbb{F}_p}\prod_j|\cos(2\pi cw_j/p)|$, where the term $c=0$ equals $\frac1p$ and each of the other
$p-1$ terms is at most $\frac1pe^{-2\mu(w)/p^2}$.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:halasz}
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of odd order $N$, let $m,l\ge1$, and let $w\in G^m$ be such that every proper subgroup $K<G$ satisfies
$\#\{j:\ w_j\notin K\}\ge0.18m/l$. Then
\[
\hat\rho_G(w)\ \le\ \frac1N+8\sqrt{\frac{\pi l}m}\;r_l(w)+e^{-m/(16l)} .
\]
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Since $\log\cos z\le-z^2/2$ for $|z|<\pi/2$, we have $\lvert\cos(\pi\theta)\rvert\le e^{-c\|\theta\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}^2}$ for all $\theta$, with
$c:=\pi^2/2$. Hence $\prod_j|\cos(2\pi\chi(w_j))|\le e^{-cf(\chi)}$, where $f(\chi):=\sum_j\|2\chi(w_j)\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}^2$. For $x\ge0$ let
$\mathcal L(x):={\{\chi\in\widehat G:\ f(\chi)\le x\}}$. Then
\[
N\hat\rho_G(w)\le\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}e^{-cf(\chi)}=\int_0^\infty ce^{-cx}\,|\mathcal L(x)|\,dx .
\]

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1.}\ We show that sums of level sets are contained in level sets.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces The map $\phi:\widehat G\to(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})^m$, $\chi\mapsto(2\chi(w_j))_j$,
is a homomorphism, and $f(\chi)=\operatorname{dist}(\phi(\chi),0)^2$ for the translation-invariant metric
$\operatorname{dist}(u,v):=(\sum_j\|u_j-v_j\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}^2)^{1/2}$ on $(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})^m$. Hence
$\sqrt{f(\chi+\chi')}\le\sqrt{f(\chi)}+\sqrt{f(\chi')}$, and the $h$-fold sumset satisfies $h\mathcal L(x)\subseteq\mathcal L(h^2x)$.
Also $0\in\mathcal L(x)=-\mathcal L(x)$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}\ We bound the size of one level set by a moment computation.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces As $N$ is odd, $\sum_{\chi}e^{4\pi i\chi(g)}=\sum_\chi
e^{2\pi i\chi(2g)}=N\,\mathbf 1\{g=0\}$
for $g\in G$. Writing $\sum_j\cos(4\pi\chi(w_j))=\frac12\sum_{j,\sigma}e^{4\pi i\sigma\chi(w_j)}$ with $\sigma\in\{\pm1\}$ and expanding the
$2l$th power, we get
\[
\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^m\cos\bigl(4\pi\chi(w_j)\bigr)\Bigr)^{2l}=4^{-l}N\,R_l(w)=N\,m^{2l}\,r_l(w).
\]
For $\chi\in\mathcal L(x)$, the bound $\cos(2\pi\theta)\ge1-2\pi^2\|\theta\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}^2$ gives $\sum_j\cos(4\pi\chi(w_j))\ge m-2\pi^2x$. For
$x_0:=m/(8\pi^2l)$ this is at least $m(1-\frac1{4l})>0$, and all terms of the sum above are nonnegative, so
$|\mathcal L(x_0)|\le N\,r_l(w)(1-\frac1{4l})^{-2l}\le2N\,r_l(w)$ by Bernoulli's inequality.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 3.}\ We show that $\mathcal L(x_0)$ contains no nonzero subgroup of $\widehat G$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $H\le\widehat G$ be a nonzero subgroup. For each
$j$, $\chi\mapsto\chi(w_j)$ maps $H$ homomorphically onto a cyclic group $k_j^{-1}\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}$, whose order $k_j$ divides $|H|$ and is therefore
odd, and it takes each value $|H|/k_j$ times. As $k_j$ is odd, the same holds for $\chi\mapsto2\chi(w_j)$. So the average of
$\|2\chi(w_j)\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}^2$ over $\chi\in H$ is
\[
\frac1{k_j}\sum_{u\in\mathbb{Z}/k_j}\Big\|\frac u{k_j}\Big\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}^2=\frac{k_j^2-1}{12k_j^2},
\]
which vanishes if $k_j=1$, that is, if $w_j\in H^\perp:=\{g\in G:\ \chi(g)=0\text{ for all }\chi\in H\}$, and is at least $\frac2{27}$
otherwise. Now $H^\perp$ is a proper subgroup of $G$, since only the zero character vanishes on $G$. By hypothesis at least $0.18m/l$
indices have $w_j\notin H^\perp$, so the average of $f$ over $H$ is at least $\frac2{27}\cdot\frac{0.18m}l>\frac m{8\pi^2l}=x_0$.
Hence $H\not\subseteq\mathcal L(x_0)$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 4.}\ We show with Kneser's theorem that the level sets below $x_0$ are small.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $0<x\le x_0$, $h:=\lfloor\sqrt{x_0/x}\rfloor\ge1$ and
$\Lambda:=\mathcal L(x)$. By Step~1, $h\Lambda\subseteq\mathcal L(x_0)$, and $(j+1)\Lambda\subseteq h\Lambda$ for $1\le j<h$ as
$0\in\Lambda$. The stabilizer $\{\chi:\ \chi+(j+1)\Lambda=(j+1)\Lambda\}$ of $(j+1)\Lambda$ is a subgroup, and it is contained in
$(j+1)\Lambda\subseteq\mathcal L(x_0)$ as $0\in(j+1)\Lambda$. Hence it is trivial by Step~3. Kneser's theorem~\cite{Kne53} (see also Tao--Vu
(2006)~\cite[Theorem~5.5]{TVbook}) states that $|X+Y|\ge|X+K|+|Y+K|-|K|$ for nonempty finite subsets $X,Y$ of an abelian group, where $K$ is
the stabilizer of $X+Y$. So $|(j+1)\Lambda|\ge|j\Lambda|+|\Lambda|-1$ for $1\le j<h$. Hence $h|\Lambda|-(h-1)\le|h\Lambda|\le2N\,r_l(w)$,
and since $h\ge\frac12\sqrt{x_0/x}$,
\[
|\mathcal L(x)|\le1+4N\,r_l(w)\sqrt{x/x_0}\qquad(0<x\le x_0).
\]

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 5.}\ We integrate the bounds of Step~4 for the level sets and conclude the proof.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Using Step~4 on $(0,x_0]$ and $|\mathcal L(x)|\le N$
for $x>x_0$,
\[
N\hat\rho_G(w)\le1+\frac{4N\,r_l(w)}{\sqrt{x_0}}\int_0^\infty c\sqrt x\,e^{-cx}\,dx+Ne^{-cx_0}
=1+\frac{4N\,r_l(w)}{\sqrt{2\pi x_0}}+Ne^{-m/(16l)},
\]
since $\int_0^\infty c\sqrt x\,e^{-cx}\,dx=\Gamma(\frac32)c^{-1/2}=(2\pi)^{-1/2}$ and $cx_0=m/(16l)$. As
$4/\sqrt{2\pi x_0}=8\sqrt{\pi l/m}$, the proposition follows.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{lem:chains}
Let $G$ be a finite set, $k>s\ge0$ integers, and $\nu=\nu_1\otimes\dots\otimes\nu_k$ a product probability measure on $G^k$. A
\emph{witness} at $b\subseteq[k]$ is an object $\omega$ together with an index $i(\omega)\in b$ and a map $A_\omega$ from
$G^{b\setminus\{i(\omega)\}}$ to the set of subsets of $G$. It is \emph{valid} for $y\in G^k$ if
$y_{i(\omega)}\in A_\omega(y_{b\setminus\{i(\omega)\}})$. (For instance, if $G$ is an abelian group, a vanishing-sum witness
$\omega=(i,r,\iota,\sigma)$ of Section~\ref{subsec:toolsnotation} has $i(\omega)=i$ and
$A_\omega(z)=\{-\sigma_r\sum_{r'\ne r}\sigma_{r'}z_{\iota_{r'}}\}$.) Let $\tau_0\ge1$, $\kappa_1,\dots,\kappa_{\tau_0}\ge0$, and
$\lambda_\tau(j)>0$ for $\tau\le\tau_0$ and $s<j\le k$. Suppose that to every $b\subseteq[k]$ with $|b|>s$ there are assigned pairwise
disjoint finite sets $\mathcal W_1(b),\dots,\mathcal W_{\tau_0}(b)$ of witnesses at $b$ such that
$\nu_{i(\omega)}(A_\omega(z))\le\kappa_\tau$ for every $\omega\in\mathcal W_\tau(b)$ and every $z\in G^{b\setminus\{i(\omega)\}}$. Let
$\mathcal B\subseteq G^k$ be such that for every $y\in\mathcal B$ and every
$b\subseteq[k]$ with $|b|=j>s$, some $\mathcal W_\tau(b)$ contains at least $\lambda_\tau(j)$ witnesses that are valid for $y$. Then
\[
\nu(\mathcal B)\ \le\ \prod_{j=s+1}^k\ \max_{|b|=j}\ \sum_{\tau=1}^{\tau_0}\frac{\kappa_\tau\,|\mathcal W_\tau(b)|}{\lambda_\tau(j)}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Put $\mathcal W(b):=\bigcup_\tau\mathcal W_\tau(b)$, and write $\tau(\omega):=\tau$ for $\omega\in\mathcal W_\tau(b)$. For $|b|=j\ge s$,
a \emph{chain} from $b$ is a sequence $(\omega_j,\omega_{j-1},\dots,\omega_{s+1})$ with $\omega_{j'}\in\mathcal W(b_{j'})$, where
$b_j:=b$ and $b_{j'-1}:=b_{j'}\setminus\{i(\omega_{j'})\}$ (the empty sequence if $j=s$). Its weight is
$\prod_{j'=s+1}^j1/\lambda_{\tau(\omega_{j'})}(j')$, and it is valid for $y$ if all its witnesses are. Fix $y\in\mathcal B$, and let
$F(b)$ be the total weight of the chains from $b$ that are valid for $y$. Then $F(b)=1$ if $|b|=s$. If $|b|=j>s$, choose $\tau$
such that $\mathcal W_\tau(b)$ contains at least $\lambda_\tau(j)$ witnesses valid for $y$. By induction on $j$,
\[
F(b)\ \ge\ \sum_{\substack{\omega\in\mathcal W_\tau(b)\\ \omega\text{ valid for }y}}\frac{F(b\setminus\{i(\omega)\})}{\lambda_\tau(j)}\
\ge\ 1 .
\]
So the chains from $[k]$ that are valid for $y$ have total weight $F([k])\ge1$. Now fix a chain from $[k]$. The validity of $\omega_j$
is the event $y_{i(\omega_j)}\in A_{\omega_j}(y_{b_{j-1}})$, and the validity of $\omega_{j'}$ for $j'<j$ depends only on $y_{b_{j'}}$,
which does not involve $y_{i(\omega_j)}$. Integrating out $y_{i(\omega_k)}$, then $y_{i(\omega_{k-1})}$, and so on (this uses that $\nu$
is a product measure), we find that the chain is valid on a set of $\nu$-measure at most $\prod_j\kappa_{\tau(\omega_j)}$. Hence
\[
\nu(\mathcal B)\le\int\ \sum_{\text{chains valid for }y}\operatorname{weight}\ d\nu(y)
\le\sum_{\text{chains from }[k]}\ \prod_{j=s+1}^k\frac{\kappa_{\tau(\omega_j)}}{\lambda_{\tau(\omega_j)}(j)} ,
\]
and summing first over $\omega_{s+1}\in\mathcal W(b_{s+1})$ for fixed $\omega_k,\dots,\omega_{s+2}$, then over $\omega_{s+2}$, and so
on, gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:fjls}
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of order $N$, $\nu$ a probability measure on $G$ with largest atom $\nu_{\max}$, and let $l\ge1$,
$1\le s<k$ and $t>0$. Let $\mathcal B$ be the set of $y\in G^k$ such that $R'_l(y_b)\ge t(2|b|)^{2l}/N$ for every $b\subseteq[k]$
with $|b|>s$. Then
\[
\nu^{k}(\mathcal B)\ \le\ \Big(\frac{2N\nu_{\max}}t\Big)^{k-s}.
\]
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:chains} with $\tau_0:=1$, the family $\mathcal W_1(b)$ of all vanishing-sum witnesses at $b$, $\kappa_1:=\nu_{\max}$
(each $A_\omega(z)$ is a single point) and the function $\lambda_1$ of~\eqref{eq:witnesses}. By the discussion
before~\eqref{eq:witnesses}, every $y\in\mathcal B$ has at least $\lambda_1(|b|)$ valid vanishing-sum witnesses at every $b$
with $|b|>s$, and by~\eqref{eq:witnesses} every factor of the product in Lemma~\ref{lem:chains} is at most $2N\nu_{\max}/t$.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:blockdelta}
Let $N\ge3$ be odd, $l\ge1$, $\delta\in(0,1]$, and let $s\le k$ be integers with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scondsdelta}
s\ge16l\log(2N/\delta)\qquad\text{and}\qquad s^{(l+1)/2}\ge\frac{32(1+\delta)}{\delta}\,\sqrt{\pi l}\,N\,(1.5l)^{2l}.
\end{equation}
Let $\rho_0\ge(1+\delta)/N$ and $t:=N\delta\rho_0\sqrt s/(32(1+\delta)\sqrt{\pi l})$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=*]
\item Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of order $N$, and let $w\in G^b$ with $|b|=j\ge s$ and $\hat\rho_G(w)\ge\rho_0$ be such that
every proper subgroup of $G$ misses at least $0.18j/l$ of the $w_i$. Then $R'_l(w)\ge t(2j)^{2l}/N$.
\item Let $\nu$ be a probability measure on $(\mathbb{Z}/N)^{\times}$ with largest atom $\nu_{\max}$. Then
\[
\nu^k\big(\{y:\ \rho_N(y)\ge\rho_0\}\big)\ \le\ \nu^k\big(\{y:\ \hat\rho_N(y)\ge\rho_0\}\big)\ \le\
\Big(\frac{64(1+\delta)\sqrt{\pi l}\,\nu_{\max}}{\delta\,\rho_0\sqrt s}\Big)^{k-s}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
(a) As $j\ge s\ge16l\log(2N/\delta)$, we have $e^{-j/(16l)}\le\delta/(2N)$. So Proposition~\ref{lem:halasz}, applied with $m=j$, gives,
as $1/N\le\rho_0/(1+\delta)$,
\[
8\sqrt{\frac{\pi l}j}\,r_l(w)\ge\rho_0-\frac{1+\delta/2}N\ge\frac{\delta\rho_0}{2(1+\delta)}.
\]
By the second condition in~\eqref{eq:scondsdelta}, $j\ge s$ and $\rho_0\ge1/N$, the degenerate pairs form a fraction at most
\[
j^{-l/2}(1.5l)^{2l}\le\frac{\delta\sqrt j}{32(1+\delta)\sqrt{\pi l}\,N}\le\frac{\delta\rho_0\sqrt j}{32(1+\delta)\sqrt{\pi l}} .
\]
The first display says that $r_l(w)\ge\delta\rho_0\sqrt j/(16(1+\delta)\sqrt{\pi l})$, so~\eqref{eq:degen} gives
$R'_l(w)\ge\frac{\delta\rho_0\sqrt j}{32(1+\delta)\sqrt{\pi l}}(2j)^{2l}\ge t(2j)^{2l}/N$, where the last step uses $j\ge s$.

(b) The first inequality holds as $\rho_N\le\hat\rho_N$. For the second, let $s<k$ (otherwise there is nothing to prove), and note
that $s\ge16\log6>1$. If $y\in((\mathbb{Z}/N)^{\times})^k$ and $\hat\rho_N(y)\ge\rho_0$, then for every $b\subseteq[k]$ with $|b|\ge s$ we
have $\hat\rho_N(y_b)\ge\rho_0$, and the coordinates of $y_b$ are units, which lie in no proper subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}/N$ (a unit generates
$\mathbb{Z}/N$). So (a) gives $R'_l(y_b)\ge t(2|b|)^{2l}/N$, and Corollary~\ref{lem:fjls} for $G=\mathbb{Z}/N$ gives the bound
$(2N\nu_{\max}/t)^{k-s}$, which is the claim, as $2N\nu_{\max}/t=64(1+\delta)\sqrt{\pi l}\,\nu_{\max}/(\delta\rho_0\sqrt s)$.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{lem:lineheavy}
Let $d\ge1$, let $L\le\mathbb{F}_p^d$ be a subspace of dimension $g$, $\theta\in[0,1)$, $l\ge1$, and let $w\in(\mathbb{F}_p^d)^b$ with
$\operatorname{out}_L(w)\le\theta|b|$. Then $r_l(w)\ge(1-\theta)^{2l}p^{-g}$.
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
Let $b':=\{i\in b:\ w_i\in L\}$, so that $|b'|\ge(1-\theta)|b|>0$. The pairs $(i,\sigma)$ with all indices in $b'$ form a fraction
$(|b'|/|b|)^{2l}\ge(1-\theta)^{2l}$ of all pairs, and among them the vanishing ones form the fraction $r_l(w_{b'})$. By Fourier inversion
on $L$, with $i_1,\dots,i_{2l}$ independent and uniform in $b'$ and independent signs $\sigma_r$,
\[
r_l(w_{b'})=\frac1{p^g}\sum_{\chi\in\widehat L}\mathbb{E}\exp\Bigl(2\pi i\,\chi\Bigl(\sum_r\sigma_rw_{i_r}\Bigr)\Bigr)
=\frac1{p^g}\sum_{\chi\in\widehat L}\Big(\frac1{|b'|}\sum_{i\in b'}\cos\bigl(2\pi\chi(w_i)\bigr)\Big)^{2l}\ge\frac1{p^g},
\]
as the term $\chi=0$ equals $1$ and the others are nonnegative. Hence $r_l(w)\ge(1-\theta)^{2l}r_l(w_{b'})\ge(1-\theta)^{2l}p^{-g}$.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:blockd}
Let $2\le d\le4$, so that $G=\mathbb{F}_p^d$ and $N=p^d$, let $\delta:=\frac1{100}$, and let $l\ge50$ and $s<k$ be integers that
satisfy~\eqref{eq:scondsdelta} (with this $N$), $s^{l/2}\ge100p^{d-1}(1.5l)^{2l}$, $s\ge1400\,l$ and, if $d\ge3$, $p\ge\sqrt{s/l}$. Put
$\varpi:=6(1+\delta)\sqrt{\pi l}/(\delta\sqrt s)$
and $W^{(g)}:=(\varpi p^{-g},1.1p^{-g})$ for $1\le g<d$. These intervals are pairwise disjoint. Let $\nu$ be a probability measure on
$G\setminus\{0\}$ with largest atom $\nu_{\max}$, and $\kappa_g:=\max\{\nu(L):\ L\le G,\ \dim L=g\}$. Then for every
$\rho_0\ge(1+\delta)/N$,
\[
\nu^k\big(\{w\in G^k:\ \hat\rho_G(w)\ge\rho_0\}\big)\ \le\ \big(\gamma_1(\rho_0)+1.1\,\kappa(\rho_0)\big)^{k-s},
\]
where $\gamma_1(\rho_0):=64(1+\delta)\sqrt{\pi l}\,\nu_{\max}/(\delta\rho_0\sqrt s)$, and $\kappa(\rho_0):=\kappa_g$ if
$\rho_0\in W^{(g)}$ and $\kappa(\rho_0):=0$ if $\rho_0$ lies in no window.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
We first check that the windows are disjoint. For $d=2$ there is only one window. For $d\ge3$, the window $W^{(g+1)}$ lies to the left
of $W^{(g)}$ because $1.1p^{-g-1}\le\varpi p^{-g}$,
that is, $p\ge1.1/\varpi$, and $1.1/\varpi\le0.0011\sqrt{s/l}\le p$. This is the only use of the hypothesis $p\ge\sqrt{s/l}$. (The windows
are empty if $\varpi\ge1.1$, and then Step~5 is never used.) Note that
$\vartheta_g\le\vartheta_1\le0.18\cdot2.1^2/l\le0.794/l\le0.016$ for every $g$, and put
$t:=N\delta\rho_0\sqrt s/(32(1+\delta)\sqrt{\pi l})$, so that $\gamma_1(\rho_0)=2N\nu_{\max}/t$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1.}\ We apply Hal\'asz's inequality in a subspace.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $L\le G$ have dimension $g\ge1$, and let $w\in(L\setminus\{0\})^b$ satisfy
$\operatorname{out}_{L''}(w)\ge0.18|b|/l$ for every hyperplane $L''$ of $L$. The subgroups of $L$ are its subspaces, and every proper
subspace of $L$ lies in a hyperplane of $L$, so every proper subgroup of $L$ misses at least $0.18|b|/l$ of the $w_i$. As
$\hat\rho_G(w)=\hat\rho_L(w)$, Proposition~\ref{lem:halasz}, applied to the group $L$ of order $p^g$, gives
$\hat\rho_G(w)\le{p^{-g}+8\sqrt{\pi l/|b|}\,r_l(w)+\exp(-|b|/(16l))}$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}\ We bound the vanishing sums of heavy blocks from below.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces If $\operatorname{out}_L(w)<\vartheta|b|$ with $\dim L=g$ and
$\vartheta\le\vartheta_1$, then $r_l(w)\ge(1-\vartheta)^{2l}p^{-g}\ge0.2p^{-g}$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:lineheavy} and since
$(1-0.794/l)^{2l}\ge(1-0.794/50)^{100}\ge0.2$ for $l\ge50$ ($(1-c/l)^l$ increases with $l$).

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 3.}\ We show that a block satisfies the hypothesis of Step~1 on a minimal heavy subspace.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $|b|=j\ge s$,
$w\in(G\setminus\{0\})^b$, $g^*=g^*(w)<d$, let $L^*$ be a subspace of dimension $g^*$ on which $w$ is heavy, and
$b^*:=\{i\in b:\ w_i\in L^*\}$, so that $|b^*|>(1-\vartheta_{g^*})j\ge0.98j$. Then $\operatorname{out}_{L''}(w_{b^*})\ge0.18|b^*|/l$ for
every hyperplane $L''$ of $L^*$. For $L''=\{0\}$ this holds as all $w_i\ne0$. Otherwise $\dim L''=g^*-1\ge1$, and
$\operatorname{out}_{L''}(w)\le\operatorname{out}_{L^*}(w)+\operatorname{out}_{L''}(w_{b^*})$. If
$\operatorname{out}_{L''}(w_{b^*})<0.18|b^*|/l$, this would be less than $(\vartheta_{g^*}+0.18/l)j\le\vartheta_{g^*-1}j$, and $w$ would
be heavy on $L''$, contradicting the minimality of $g^*$ (note $\vartheta_{g-1}=2.1\vartheta_g\ge\vartheta_g+0.18/l$).

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 4.}\ We show that, outside the window of dimension $g^*(w)$, a block has many valid vanishing-sum witnesses.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $|b|=j>s$,
$w\in(G\setminus\{0\})^b$ and $\hat\rho_G(w)\ge\rho_0$, and suppose that $g^*=g^*(w)=d$, or that $g^*<d$ and $\rho_0\notin W^{(g^*)}$. It
suffices to show that $R'_l(w)\ge t(2j)^{2l}/N$, because by the discussion before~\eqref{eq:witnesses} $w$ then has at least
$\lambda_1(j)=l\,t(2j)^{2l}/N$ valid vanishing-sum witnesses at $b$. The degenerate pairs form a fraction at most
$j^{-l/2}(1.5l)^{2l}\le0.01p^{1-d}$, by $s^{l/2}\ge100p^{d-1}(1.5l)^{2l}$.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
\item $g^*=d$: then $\operatorname{out}_{L''}(w)\ge\vartheta_{d-1}j=0.18j/l$ for every hyperplane $L''$ of $G$, so every proper subgroup of
$G$ misses at least $0.18j/l$ of the $w_i$, and Proposition~\ref{lem:blockdelta}(a) applies.
\item $g^*<d$ and $\rho_0\le\varpi p^{-g^*}$: by Step~2 for a subspace of dimension $g^*$ on which $w$ is heavy, $r_l(w)\ge0.2p^{-g^*}$,
and the degenerate pairs form a fraction at most $0.01p^{1-d}\le0.01p^{-g^*}$. So $R'_l(w)\ge0.19p^{-g^*}(2j)^{2l}$, and
$0.19p^{-g^*}\ge\delta\rho_0\sqrt s/(32(1+\delta)\sqrt{\pi l})=t/N$, since $\rho_0\le\varpi p^{-g^*}$ and $0.19\cdot32>6$.
\item $g^*<d$ and $\rho_0\ge1.1p^{-g^*}$: let $L^*$ and $b^*$ be as in Step~3. By Steps~3 and~1 for $L^*$ and $w_{b^*}$, and as
$\hat\rho_G(w_{b^*})\ge\hat\rho_G(w)\ge\rho_0$,
\[
\rho_0\le p^{-g^*}+8\sqrt{\frac{\pi l}{|b^*|}}\,r_l(w_{b^*})+\exp\Bigl(-\frac{|b^*|}{16l}\Bigr).
\]
Here $\rho_0-p^{-g^*}\ge\rho_0/11$ and $\exp(-|b^*|/(16l))\le\exp(-0.98s/(16l))\le\frac1{20}p^{-g^*}\le\rho_0/22$, because
$s\ge16l\log(200p^d)\ge16.4\,l\log(20p^{d-1})$. So $r_l(w_{b^*})\ge\rho_0\sqrt{|b^*|}/(176\sqrt{\pi l})$, and since vanishing signed sums of
$w_{b^*}$ are vanishing signed sums of $w$,
\[
r_l(w)\ge\Big(\frac{|b^*|}j\Big)^{2l}r_l(w_{b^*})\ge\frac{0.2\sqrt{0.98}\,\rho_0\sqrt s}{176\sqrt{\pi l}}\ge0.00112\,\frac{\rho_0\sqrt
s}{\sqrt{\pi l}},
\]
using $(|b^*|/j)^{2l}\ge(1-\vartheta_{g^*})^{2l}\ge0.2$ as in Step~2. The degenerate pairs form a fraction at most
$0.01p^{1-d}\le0.0091\rho_0$. Finally $\sqrt{s/(\pi l)}\ge\sqrt{1400/\pi}>21$, so that
$0.00112\sqrt{s/(\pi l)}-0.0091\ge0.00031\sqrt{s/(\pi l)}\ge\delta\sqrt{s/(\pi l)}/(32(1+\delta))$, and~\eqref{eq:degen} gives
$R'_l(w)\ge t(2j)^{2l}/N$.
\end{itemize}

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 5.}\ We introduce membership witnesses for the levels inside a window.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $\rho_0\in W^{(g)}$. For $|b|=j>s$ and $i\in b$ let
$\omega_{b,i}$ be a witness at $b$, distinct from the vanishing-sum witnesses, with $i(\omega_{b,i})=i$ and $A_{\omega_{b,i}}(z)$, for
$z\in G^{b\setminus\{i\}}$, equal to $L$ if $L$ is the only $g$-dimensional subspace with $\operatorname{out}_L(z)<\vartheta_gj$, and
$A_{\omega_{b,i}}(z)=\emptyset$ otherwise. So $A_{\omega_{b,i}}(z)$ depends only on $z$ (and $b$), and
$\nu(A_{\omega_{b,i}}(z))\le\kappa_g$. Suppose that $w\in(G\setminus\{0\})^b$ has $\hat\rho_G(w)\ge\rho_0$ and that neither case of
Step~4 applies, that is, $g^*(w)<d$ and $\rho_0\in W^{(g^*(w))}$. As the windows are disjoint, this means $g^*(w)=g$. Let $L^*$ and
$b^*$ be as in Step~3, and let $i\in b^*$ and $z:=w_{b\setminus\{i\}}$. Then
$\operatorname{out}_{L^*}(z)=\operatorname{out}_{L^*}(w)<\vartheta_gj$, and by minimality
$\operatorname{out}_{L'}(z)\ge\operatorname{out}_{L'}(w)-1\ge\vartheta_{\dim L'}j-1$ whenever $1\le\dim L'<g$. If some $L\ne L^*$ of
dimension $g$ had $\operatorname{out}_L(z)<\vartheta_gj$, then $L':=L\cap L^*$ would have $\operatorname{out}_{L'}(z)<2\vartheta_gj$. This
is impossible if $L'=\{0\}$, as then $\operatorname{out}_{L'}(z)=j-1\ge2\vartheta_gj$. If $\dim L'\ge1$, then $\dim L'\le g-1$, as
$L\ne L^*$. Since
$\vartheta_{g'}$ decreases in $g'$ and $j>s\ge1400l>10/\vartheta_g$, this contradicts
$\operatorname{out}_{L'}(z)\ge\vartheta_{\dim L'}j-1\ge\vartheta_{g-1}j-1=2.1\vartheta_gj-1>2\vartheta_gj$. So
$A_{\omega_{b,i}}(z)=L^*\ni w_i$, and $\omega_{b,i}$ is valid for each of the more than $\lambda_M(j):=(1-\vartheta_g)j$ indices
$i\in b^*$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 6.}\ We combine Steps~4 and~5 by means of Lemma~\ref{lem:chains} and conclude the proof.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $\mathcal B$ be the set of
$w\in(G\setminus\{0\})^k$ with $\hat\rho_G(w)\ge\rho_0$. It has the $\nu^k$-measure of the set in the statement. We use the following
families at a block $b$: the vanishing-sum witnesses at $b$ (with $\kappa_\tau=\nu_{\max}$ and $\lambda_\tau=\lambda_1$) and, if
$\rho_0\in W^{(g)}$, the witnesses $\omega_{b,i}$, $i\in b$, of Step~5 (with $\kappa_\tau=\kappa_g$ and $\lambda_\tau=\lambda_M$). For every
$w\in\mathcal B$ and every $b\subseteq[k]$ with $|b|>s$ we have $\hat\rho_G(w_b)\ge\hat\rho_G(w)\ge\rho_0$, so by Steps~4 and~5, applied
to $w_b$, one of these families contains at least $\lambda_\tau(|b|)$ witnesses that are valid for $w$. At each size $j$, the witnesses
of Step~4 contribute at most $2N\nu_{\max}/t=\gamma_1(\rho_0)$ by~\eqref{eq:witnesses}, and those of Step~5 at most
$\kappa_gj/((1-\vartheta_g)j)\le1.1\kappa_g$. So Lemma~\ref{lem:chains} bounds
$\nu^k(\mathcal B)$ by $(\gamma_1(\rho_0)+1.1\,\kappa(\rho_0))^{k-s}$, which is the claim.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{lem:squaring}
Let $p$ be an odd prime, $B\in\mathbb{F}_p^{m\times m}$ symmetric, $t\in\mathbb{F}_p$, and $\xi$ uniform in $\{\pm1\}^m$. Let
$u\in\{-1,0,1\}^m$ have independent coordinates with $\Pr(u_j=0)=\frac12$ and $\Pr(u_j=1)=\Pr({u_j=-1})=\frac14$, and let $U:=\operatorname{supp} u$. Then
\[
\Big|\mathbb{E}\exp\Bigl(\frac{2\pi i\,t\,\xi^{\top}B\xi}p\Bigr)\Big|^2\ \le\
\mathbb{E}_u\prod_{j\notin U}\Bigl|\cos\frac{8\pi t\,(Bu)_j}p\Bigr| .
\]
Consequently, if $t\ne0$ and $\Pr\bigl(\mu((Bu)_{U^c})\le cmp^2\bigr)\le e^{-m/100}$ for some $c\in(0,\frac1{200}]$, where $(Bu)_{U^c}$
is the restriction of $Bu$ to the coordinates outside $U$, then the left side is at most $2e^{-2cm}$.
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
Let $\xi'$ be an independent copy of $\xi$, and put $u:=(\xi-\xi')/2$ and $v:=(\xi+\xi')/2$. The pairs $(u_j,v_j)$ are independent and
uniform on $\{(\pm1,0),(0,\pm1)\}$. So $u$ has the stated law, and given $u$, $v$ vanishes on $U$ and its coordinates outside $U$ are
independent uniform signs. With $Q(y):=t\,y^{\top}By$ and $B=B^{\top}$,
\[
Q(\xi)-Q(\xi')=t\,(\xi-\xi')^{\top}B(\xi+\xi')=4t\,(Bu)^{\top}v .
\]
Hence
\[
\big|\mathbb{E}\,e^{2\pi iQ(\xi)/p}\big|^2=\mathbb{E}\,e^{2\pi i(Q(\xi)-Q(\xi'))/p}=\mathbb{E}_u\prod_{j\notin U}\cos\bigl(8\pi t\,(Bu)_j/p\bigr),
\]
and the first claim follows. For the second, Lemma~\ref{lem:dilates}, applied with the nonzero multiplier $4t$, bounds the product on
the right by $e^{-2\mu((Bu)_{U^c})/p^2}$, which is less than $e^{-2cm}$ unless $\mu((Bu)_{U^c})\le cmp^2$. So the right side is at most
$e^{-m/100}+e^{-2cm}\le2e^{-2cm}$, as $2c\le\frac1{100}$.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- lemma-33: body_md -->
\label{lem:LOp}
Let $p$ be an odd prime and $t\ge2$ an integer. Then
\[
\frac1p\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{F}_p}\Bigl|\cos\frac{2\pi\sigma}p\Bigr|^t\ \le\ \frac1p\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{F}_p}\Bigl(\cos\frac{2\pi\sigma}p\Bigr)^{2\lfloor
t/2\rfloor}
\ \le\ \frac1p+\big(\pi\lfloor t/2\rfloor\big)^{-1/2}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-33 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
The first inequality holds termwise, as $\lvert\cos\rvert\le1$ and $2\lfloor t/2\rfloor\le t$. Let $h:=\lfloor t/2\rfloor\ge1$ and
$S:=\xi_1+\dots+\xi_{2h}$. Since $\cos(2\pi\sigma/p)^{2h}=\mathbb{E}\,e^{2\pi i\sigma S/p}$ and
$\frac1p\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{F}_p}e^{2\pi i\sigma S/p}=\mathbf 1\{p\mid S\}$,
the middle term equals $\Pr(S\in p\mathbb{Z})$. The law of $S$ is supported on $2\mathbb{Z}$, symmetric, and unimodal: $\Pr(S=2i)=\binom{2h}{h+i}4^{-h}$ is
nonincreasing in $i\ge0$. As $p$ is odd and $S$ is even, $S\in p\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ means $S=2jp$ with $j\ne0$. For $j\ge1$ the interval
