$p^{\lceil t\rceil}$ divides $a-a'$. So these $a$ lie in one residue class modulo $p^{\lceil t\rceil}$, and
$C(t)\le N/p^{\lceil t\rceil}+1$. Hence, as $\lceil t\rceil=k$ for $k-1<t\le k$,
\[
\sum_{a=1}^Nv(a-\gamma_i)=\int_0^\tau C(t)\,dt\ \le\ \sum_{k=1}^{\lceil\tau\rceil}\Big(\frac N{p^k}+1\Big)\ <\ \frac N{p-1}+\tau+1.
\]

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 3.}\ We sum the bounds of Step~2 over the roots and conclude the proof.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces By Step~1,
$\sum_{a=1}^Nv_p(g(a))=\sum_{i=1}^j\sum_{a=1}^Nv(a-\gamma_i)$, and by Step~2 each of the $j$ inner sums is less than
$\frac N{p-1}+\tau+1$ with $\tau=\log X/\log p$, which gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-76 -->
<!-- proposition-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:schur}
There is an absolute constant $A_0\ge2$ with the following property. Let $g\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be monic and irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ of degree $j\ge2$,
suppose that all complex roots of $g$ have absolute value at most $R$, where $R\ge1$, and let $A\ge\max(A_0,R+1,j)$. Then there are an
integer $a$ with $1\le a\le\lceil A^3\rceil$ and a prime $p$ with
\[
p\mid g(a)\qquad\text{and}\qquad A\le p\le A^{4j} .
\]
<!-- end proposition-23 -->
<!-- proof-77: body_md -->
Put $N:=\lceil A^3\rceil$, $X:=A^{4j}$ and $P:=\prod_{a=1}^Ng(a)$. Since $g$ is irreducible of degree at least $2$, it has no rational
root, so $g(a)\ne0$ for every integer $a$. Let $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_j$ be the complex roots of $g$. For $1\le a\le N$ we have
$|g(a)|=\prod_i|a-\alpha_i|\le(a+R)^j\le(A^3+1+A)^j\le X$, as $N\le A^3+1$, $R\le A$ and $A^3+A+1\le A^4$. So if a prime $p\ge A$ divides
$P$, then it divides some $g(a)$ with $1\le a\le N$, and $p\le|g(a)|\le X$, as claimed. Suppose, for a contradiction, that every prime
factor of $P$ is less than $A$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1.}\ We bound $\log|P|$ from above, using that all prime factors of $P$ are less than $A$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces By Lemma~\ref{lem:valuations}, applied to
each prime $p<A$, and by $\frac1{p-1}\le\frac2p$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log|P|&=\sum_{p<A}\log p\sum_{a=1}^Nv_p\big(g(a)\big)\le j\sum_{p<A}\Big(\frac{N\log p}{p-1}+\log X+\log p\Big)\\
&\le j\Big(2N\sum_{p\le A}\frac{\log p}p+A\log X+\vartheta(A)\Big),
\end{aligned}
\]
since there are at most $A$ primes below $A$. As $A\ge2$, Lemma~\ref{lem:chebyshev} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Pupper}
\log|P|<j\big(2N(\log A+\log4)+A\log X+A\log4\big).
\end{equation}

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}\ We bound $\log|P|$ from below, using that the roots of $g$ are small.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Put $R':=\lceil R\rceil$, so that $R'\le R+1\le A<N$. For
$a\ge R'+1$ we have $|a-\alpha_i|\ge a-R'\ge1$ for all $i$, so $|g(a)|\ge(a-R')^j$. For $1\le a\le R'$ we have $|g(a)|\ge1$, as $g(a)$ is a
nonzero integer. Hence, with $M:=N-R'$,
\[
\log|P|\ \ge\ j\sum_{a=R'+1}^N\log(a-R')=j\log(M!)\ \ge\ j\,(M\log M-M),
\]
by $\log M!=\sum_{t=2}^M\log t\ge\int_1^M\log t\,dt=M\log M-M+1$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 3.}\ We compare the two bounds and obtain a contradiction for large $A$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces As $M\ge A^3-A\ge1$ and $t\mapsto t\log t-t$ is increasing on
$[1,\infty)$, Step~2 gives $\log|P|\ge j(A^3-A)\bigl(\log(A^3-A)-1\bigr)$. On the other hand $N\le A^3+1$ and
$\log X=4j\log A\le4A\log A$, as $j\le A$, so by~\eqref{eq:Pupper}
\[
\log|P|\ <\ j\big(2(A^3+1)(\log A+\log4)+4A^2\log A+A\log4\big).
\]
After division by $j$, both bounds depend only on $A$. As $A\to\infty$, the lower bound is $(3+o(1))A^3\log A$, while the upper bound is
$(2+o(1))A^3\log A$. So the two bounds contradict each other for all $A\ge A_0$, where $A_0$ is a suitable absolute constant. This
contradiction shows that some prime $p\ge A$ divides $P$, which proves the proposition.
<!-- end proof-77 -->
<!-- lemma-42: body_md -->
\label{lem:candidates}
Let $j\ge1$ and $R\ge6$. The number of monic polynomials $g\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ of degree $j$ all of whose complex roots have absolute value at most
$R$ is at most $R^{2j^2}$.
<!-- end lemma-42 -->
<!-- proof-78: body_md -->
Write $g(x)=\prod_{i=1}^j(x-\alpha_i)=x^j+\sum_{k=1}^j(-1)^k\sigma_k\,x^{j-k}$, where $\sigma_k$ is the $k$th elementary symmetric
polynomial in the roots $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_j$. As $\sigma_k$ is a sum of $\binom jk\le2^j$ products of $k$ roots, we have
$|\sigma_k|\le2^jR^k\le2^jR^j$. So each of the $j$ coefficients of $x^{j-1},\dots,x^0$ is an integer of absolute value at most $2^jR^j$,
and there are at most $2^{j+1}R^j+1\le3\cdot2^jR^j\le6^jR^j\le R^{2j}$ choices for it, as $R\ge6$. Multiplying over the $j$ coefficients
gives at most $R^{2j^2}$ polynomials.
<!-- end proof-78 -->
<!-- proof-79: body_md -->
Fix $\eta\in(0,\frac1{27})$, let $m$ be large, and put $K:=\lfloor m^\eta\rfloor\ge1$. Let $\mathcal F_m$ be the event that $\chi_{S_m}$
has a monic factor in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ of degree in $[1,m^\eta]$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1.}\ We reduce $\mathcal F_m$ to irreducible candidates.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces For $j\ge1$ let $\mathcal C_j$ be the set of monic polynomials $g\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$
of degree $j$ that are irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ and all of whose complex roots have absolute value at most $m$. Suppose that $\mathcal F_m$
holds, and let $f\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be a monic factor of $\chi_{S_m}$ of degree $k\in[1,m^\eta]$, so that $1\le k\le K$. By Gauss's lemma, the
monic irreducible factors of $f$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ have integer coefficients. Let $g$ be one of them, and let $j:=\deg g$, so that $1\le j\le K$.
Then $g$ divides $\chi_{S_m}$, and since $g$ is monic, the quotient lies in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$. Every root of $g$ is an eigenvalue of the real
symmetric matrix $S_m$, so its absolute value is at most $m-1$, the largest absolute row sum of $S_m$. Hence $g\in\mathcal C_j$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:union}
\mathcal F_m\ \subseteq\ \bigcup_{j=1}^K\ \bigcup_{g\in\mathcal C_j}\big\{g\text{ divides }\chi_{S_m}\big\}.
\end{equation}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:candidates} with $R=m$, we have $|\mathcal C_j|\le m^{2j^2}$ for all $j\ge1$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}\ We attach to every candidate a large prime at which it has a root.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces For $1\le j\le K$ put $A_j:=\exp\bigl(m^{1/9}/(4j)\bigr)$, so
that $A_j^{4j}=e^{m^{1/9}}$ and $A_j\ge\exp\bigl(m^{1/9-\eta}/4\bigr)$. As $\eta<\frac19$, the exponent $\frac19-\eta$ is positive, and
$A_j$ is larger than every fixed power of $m$ for large $m$. Fix a prime $p_*$ with $A_1<p_*\le2A_1$, which exists by Bertrand's postulate
for the integer $\lfloor A_1\rfloor$, proved by Chebyshev (1852)~\cite{Che52} (see also Hardy--Wright (2008)~\cite[Chapter~XXII]{HW08}). For
$g=x-c\in\mathcal C_1$ put $p_g:=p_*$ and $a_g:=c$. For $2\le j\le K$ and $g\in\mathcal C_j$ we apply Proposition~\ref{lem:schur} with
$R=m$ and $A=A_j$, which is allowed for large $m$, as $A_j\ge\max(A_0,m+1,K)$ and $j\le K$. It provides an integer $a_g$ and a prime
$p_g$ with $p_g\mid g(a_g)$ and $A_j\le p_g\le A_j^{4j}$. As $2A_1\le A_1^4$, in both cases
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pgsize}
p_g\mid g(a_g)\qquad\text{and}\qquad A_j\ \le\ p_g\ \le\ A_j^{4j}=e^{m^{1/9}} .
\end{equation}
The pair $(p_g,a_g)$ depends only on $g$, and not on $S_m$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 3.}\ We bound the probability that a fixed candidate divides $\chi_{S_m}$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $1\le j\le K$ and $g\in\mathcal C_j$. If $g$ divides
$\chi_{S_m}$, then $g(a_g)$ divides $\chi_{S_m}(a_g)=\det(a_gI-S_m)$, as the quotient lies in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$, so $p_g$ divides $\det(a_gI-S_m)$
and the matrix $\bar S_m-\lambda I$ with $\lambda:=\bar a_g\in\mathbb{F}_{p_g}$ is singular over $\mathbb{F}_{p_g}$. As $A_j\ge23$ for large $m$, we have
$23\le p_g\le e^{m^{1/9}}$ by~\eqref{eq:pgsize}, so the bound~\eqref{eq:rankfixed} applies to the prime $p_g$ and to $\lambda=\bar a_g$, and
gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:onecand}
\Pr\bigl(g\text{ divides }\chi_{S_m}\bigr)\ \le\ \frac3{p_g}\ \le\ 3e^{-m^{1/9}/(4j)}.
\end{equation}

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 4.}\ We sum the bounds of Step~3 over all candidates and conclude the proof.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Put $y:=m^{1/9-\eta}$. For $1\le j\le K$ we have
$|\mathcal C_j|\le m^{2j^2}\le\exp(2m^{2\eta}\log m)$ and $e^{-m^{1/9}/(4j)}\le e^{-y/4}$. As $\eta<\frac1{27}$, we have
$2\eta<\frac19-\eta$, so that $2m^{2\eta}\log m\le y/8$ for large $m$. Hence, by~\eqref{eq:union} and~\eqref{eq:onecand},
\[
\Pr(\mathcal F_m)\ \le\ \sum_{j=1}^K3\,|\mathcal C_j|\,e^{-m^{1/9}/(4j)}\ \le\ 3Ke^{y/8-y/4}\ \le\ e^{-y/9}
\]
for large $m$, as $K\le m^\eta$. As $y=m^{1/9-\eta}$, this is the bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:nofactor}.
<!-- end proof-79 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:nofactor}
For Theorem~\ref{thm:huge} it suffices to exclude the factors of degree at most $(\log m)^3$ (see Proposition~\ref{lem:acinv} in
Section~\ref{sec:huge}), so any fixed exponent $\eta>0$ would do in Theorem~\ref{thm:nofactor}. The exponent $\frac1{27}$ is where the
number of candidates catches up with the size of the primes. For a candidate of degree $j$, Proposition~\ref{lem:schur} guarantees a prime
$p$ with $A\le p\le A^{4j}$ at which it has a root, which lies in the range $p\le e^{m^{1/9}}$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:rankp} when
$\log A\le m^{1/9}/(4j)$. The union bound needs $A$ to be much larger than the bound $m^{2j^2}$ for the number of candidates, and both
conditions can be met only if $j^3\log m$ is small compared with $m^{1/9}$. Better constants in Lemma~\ref{lem:candidates} and
Proposition~\ref{lem:schur} do not change the exponent. Primes of size $A^{O(1)}$ at which the candidates have roots would improve it to
$\frac1{18}$, and a larger range of primes in Theorem~\ref{thm:rankp} would improve it as well. However, the error term $e^{-c_3m}$ of
Theorem~\ref{thm:rankp}, multiplied by the number $e^{O(j^2\log m)}$ of candidates, limits the union bound to degrees
$j=O((m/\log m)^{1/2})$, whatever the range of primes. So the argument does not give the irreducibility of $\chi_{S_m}$.

The argument uses the random matrix only through a bound for its eigenvalues and through the bound~\eqref{eq:rankfixed} for each fixed
$\lambda$. Let $M_n$ be a random symmetric matrix of order $n$ with independent uniform $\pm1$ entries on and above the diagonal. Its
eigenvalues have absolute value at most $n$. The rank theorem of Ferber--Jain--Sah--Sawhney (2023)~\cite[Theorem~1.2]{FJSS}, applied with
corank $0$, gives $\Pr(\det(\bar M_n-\lambda I)=0\text{ in }\mathbb{F}_p)\le\frac2p+O(e^{-cn/\log p})$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_p$ and every prime
$2<p\le e^{cn^{1/4}}$, where $c>0$ is a constant. In this range the error term is $O(e^{-n^{3/4}})$, so that the analogue
of~\eqref{eq:rankfixed} holds for large $n$. The same argument, with $A_j:=\exp(cn^{1/4}/(4j))$, then shows that the characteristic
polynomial of $M_n$ has no factor over $\mathbb{Q}$ whose degree lies between $1$ and $n^\eta$, for every fixed $\eta\in(0,\frac1{12})$, with
probability tending to one.

Irreducibility with probability tending to one is known in several related settings. For matrices with independent entries, Eberhard
(2022)~\cite{Eb22} proved it unconditionally when the entries are uniform modulo a product of four distinct primes, and under the extended
Riemann hypothesis for every fixed nonconstant law of the entries with finite support. Ferber--Jain--Sah--Sawhney (2023)~\cite{FJSS} proved
it under the extended Riemann hypothesis for symmetric matrices with independent uniform $\pm1$ entries on and above the diagonal. For
random polynomials with independent coefficients, Breuillard--Varj\'u (2019)~\cite{BV19} proved it under the Riemann hypothesis for Dedekind
zeta functions. Unconditionally, Bary-Soroker--Kozma (2020)~\cite{BSK20} proved it for coefficients uniform on $\{1,\dots,L\}$ whenever $L$
is divisible by at least four distinct primes, and Bary-Soroker--Koukoulopoulos--Kozma (2023)~\cite{BKK23} for coefficients uniform on at
least $35$ consecutive integers. The latter authors also showed that a random monic polynomial whose other coefficients are independent with
a fixed finitely supported law that is not a point mass, conditioned on a nonzero constant term, has with probability tending to one no
factor of degree at most a small constant times its degree. This is an analogue of Theorem~\ref{thm:nofactor} with a much larger range.
Earlier, Konyagin (1999)~\cite{Kon99} showed that a proportion $\gg1/\log n$ of the $0$--$1$ polynomials of degree $n$ are irreducible.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- lemma-43: body_md -->
\label{lem:dissoc}
Let $p$ be an odd prime and $w\in\mathbb{F}_p^m$. Then there are a set $B\subseteq[m]$ with $2^{|B|}\le1/\rho_p(w)$ and vectors
$y_b\in\{-1,0,1\}^m$, $b\in B$, such that $w=\sum_{b\in B}w_b\,\bar y_b$.
<!-- end lemma-43 -->
<!-- proof-80: body_md -->
Call a set $B\subseteq[m]$ \emph{dissociated} if $\sum_{b\in B}c_bw_b\ne0$ for every nonzero $c\in\{-1,0,1\}^B$. The empty set is
dissociated, and we fix a dissociated set $B$ that is maximal for inclusion. If $\sigma\ne\sigma'$ are vectors in $\{\pm1\}^B$, then
$c:=\frac12(\sigma-\sigma')$ is a nonzero vector in $\{-1,0,1\}^B$, and $\sum_b\sigma_bw_b-\sum_b\sigma'_bw_b=2\sum_bc_bw_b\ne0$, as $p$ is
odd. So the $2^{|B|}$ sums $\sum_{b\in B}\sigma_bw_b$ with $\sigma\in\{\pm1\}^B$ are pairwise distinct. For $a\in\mathbb{F}_p$,
conditionally on the signs $\xi_j$ with $j\notin B$, the event $\sum_{j=1}^m\xi_jw_j=a$ prescribes the value of $\sum_{b\in B}\xi_bw_b$, so
it has conditional probability at most $2^{-|B|}$. Hence $\rho_p(w)\le2^{-|B|}$.

Now let $j\in[m]\setminus B$. As $B\cup\{j\}$ is not dissociated, there is a nonzero $c\in\{-1,0,1\}^{B\cup\{j\}}$ with
$c_jw_j+\sum_{b\in B}c_bw_b=0$, and $c_j\ne0$, since $B$ is dissociated. Hence $w_j=\sum_{b\in B}t_{bj}w_b$ with
$t_{bj}:=-c_jc_b\in\{-1,0,1\}$. For $j\in B$ put $t_{bj}:=1$ if $b=j$, and $t_{bj}:=0$ otherwise. Then the vectors $y_b\in\{-1,0,1\}^m$
with the coordinates $t_{bj}$, $j\in[m]$, satisfy $w=\sum_{b\in B}w_b\,\bar y_b$.
<!-- end proof-80 -->
<!-- lemma-44: body_md -->
\label{lem:liftinv}
Let $T\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times m}$ be symmetric with entries in $\{-1,0,1\}$, and let $u_1,\dots,u_D\in\{-1,0,1\}^m$ with $D<m$. Let
$U:=\operatorname{span}_\mathbb{Q}(u_1,\dots,u_D)$, and suppose that $0$ is the only $T$-invariant subspace of $\mathbb{Q}^m$ contained in $U$, which
holds, for instance, if $\chi_T$ has no monic factor in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ of degree in $[1,D]$. Then for every prime $p>m^{3D^2}$, the only
$\bar T$-invariant subspace of $\mathbb{F}_p^m$ contained in $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{F}_p}(\bar u_1,\dots,\bar u_D)$ is $0$.
<!-- end lemma-44 -->
<!-- proof-81: body_md -->
If $V\ne0$ is a $T$-invariant subspace of $\mathbb{Q}^m$ contained in $U$, the characteristic polynomial of $T|_V$ is a monic factor of
$\chi_T$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ of degree $\dim V\in[1,D]$, and it lies in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ by Gauss's lemma. This proves the sufficient condition in the
statement. Now let $p>m^{3D^2}$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1.}\ We construct an integral matrix whose kernel is $U$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{F}_p}(\bar u_1,\dots,\bar u_D)$
over $\mathbb{F}_p$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $d:=\dim U\le D$. If $d=0$ there is nothing to prove. After renumbering, $u_1,\dots,u_d$ is a basis of $U$. Let
$M:=[u_1,\dots,u_d]\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times d}$. In this proof, for a set $I\subseteq[m]$, we write $y_I$ for the restriction of a vector $y$ to the
coordinates in $I$, and $Y_I$ for the submatrix formed by the rows in $I$ of a matrix $Y$ with $m$ rows. Choose a set $I$ of $d$ rows with
$\kappa:=\det M_I\ne0$. By Hadamard's inequality $|\kappa|\le d^{d/2}\le m^{3D^2}<p$, so $p\nmid\kappa$. Let
$\pi_U\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times m}$ be the matrix of $y\mapsto\kappa y-M\operatorname{adj}(M_I)\,y_I$. Then
$\pi_UM=\kappa M-M\operatorname{adj}(M_I)M_I=0$, and $\pi_Uy=0$ implies $y=M\big(\kappa^{-1}\operatorname{adj}(M_I)y_I\big)$, over $\mathbb{Q}$
and, as $p\nmid\kappa$, also over $\mathbb{F}_p$. Hence $\ker\pi_U=U$ and $\ker\bar\pi_U=\operatorname{im}\bar M$. As $\pi_Uu_i=0$ for
$1\le i\le D$, we get $\bar u_i\in\ker\bar\pi_U$, and hence $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{F}_p}(\bar u_1,\dots,\bar u_D)=\operatorname{im}\bar M$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}\ We show that a Krylov matrix built from $\pi_U$, $T$ and $M$ has rank $d$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let $\Lambda\in\mathbb{Z}^{md\times d}$ be the
matrix of the map $a\mapsto(\pi_UT^jMa)_{1\le j\le d}$, that is, the blocks $\pi_UT^jM$, $1\le j\le d$, stacked vertically. Let
$a\in\mathbb{Q}^d$ with $\Lambda a=0$ and put $y:=Ma\in U$. Then $T^jy\in\ker\pi_U=U$ for $1\le j\le d$. Suppose $y\ne0$, and for
$0\le j\le d$ let $K_j:=\operatorname{span}(y,Ty,\dots,T^jy)$, the Krylov subspaces of $y$ (after Krylov (1931)~\cite{Kry31}), which
are contained in $U$. As $\dim K_0=1$ and $\dim K_d\le d$, we have $K_j=K_{j+1}$ for some $j<d$. Then $TK_j\subseteq K_{j+1}=K_j$, so
$K_j$ is a nonzero $T$-invariant subspace contained in $U$, a contradiction. Hence $Ma=0$ and $a=0$. So some $d\times d$ minor
$\Lambda_0$ of $\Lambda$ is nonzero.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 3.}\ We bound the nonzero minor $\Lambda_0$ by Hadamard's inequality and deduce that $p$ does not divide it.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces For $j\ge1$ the entries
of $T^j$ are at most $m^{j-1}$ in absolute value, so those of $T^jM$ are at most $m^j$. The entries of $\operatorname{adj}(M_I)$ are at
most $(d-1)!$, and $|\kappa|\le d!$. Hence, for $1\le j\le d$, the entries of $\pi_UT^jM=\kappa\,T^jM-M\operatorname{adj}(M_I)(T^jM)_I$
are at most
\[
d!\,m^j+d^2\,(d-1)!\,m^j=(d+1)!\,m^j\le m^{2d},
\]
as $(d+1)!\le(d+1)^d\le m^d$ by $d<m$. By Hadamard's inequality, $|\Lambda_0|\le(\sqrt d\,m^{2d})^d\le m^{3d^2}\le m^{3D^2}<p$,
as $\sqrt d<m$. So $p\nmid\Lambda_0$, and $\bar\Lambda$ has rank $d$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 4.}\ We deduce from Step~3 that $\operatorname{im}\bar M$ contains no nonzero $\bar T$-invariant subspace.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces Let
$V\subseteq\operatorname{im}\bar M$ be $\bar T$-invariant, and suppose that $0\ne w\in V$. Write $w=\bar Ma$ with $a\in\mathbb{F}_p^d$, $a\ne0$.
Then $\bar T^jw\in V\subseteq\operatorname{im}\bar M=\ker\bar\pi_U$, so $\bar\pi_U\bar T^j\bar Ma=0$ for $1\le j\le d$. That is,
$\bar\Lambda a=0$, contradicting $\operatorname{rank}\bar\Lambda=d$. Hence $V=0$, and since
$\operatorname{im}\bar M=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{F}_p}(\bar u_1,\dots,\bar u_D)$ by Step~1, this proves the lemma.
<!-- end proof-81 -->
<!-- proposition-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:acinv}
For all sufficiently large $m$ the following holds. Let $T$ be a Seidel matrix of order $m$ such that $\chi_T$ has no monic factor in
$\mathbb{Z}[x]$ of degree in $[1,(\log m)^3]$, and let $p>e^{(\log m)^6}$ be prime. Then every nonzero $\bar T$-invariant subspace
$V\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p^m$ satisfies $\Pr_\xi(\bar\xi\perp V)<m^{-3}$. In particular $a_\beta(T)<m^{-3}$ for every monic irreducible
$\beta\in\mathbb{F}_p[x]$.
<!-- end proposition-24 -->
<!-- proof-82: body_md -->
Let $m$ be large, so that the prime $p>e^{(\log m)^6}$ is odd, let $V\ne0$ be $\bar T$-invariant, and put $k:=\dim V$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1.}\ We treat the invariant subspaces of dimension greater than $3\log_2m$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces If $k>3\log_2m$, then
$\Pr_\xi(\bar\xi\perp V)\le2^{-k}<m^{-3}$ by Odlyzko's lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:odlyzko}).

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}\ We show that if $k\le3\log_2m$, then $V$ contains a vector $w$ with $\rho_p(w)<m^{-3}$.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces This gives the claim, as
$\bar\xi\perp V$ implies $\sum_j\xi_jw_j=0$, so that $\Pr_\xi(\bar\xi\perp V)\le\rho_p(w)$. Let $v_1,\dots,v_k$ be a basis of $V$, and
suppose, for a contradiction, that $\rho_p(v_l)\ge m^{-3}$ for $l=1,\dots,k$. As $p$ is odd, Lemma~\ref{lem:dissoc} shows that each $v_l$
is a linear combination of the reductions of at most $\log_2(m^3)=3\log_2m$ vectors in $\{-1,0,1\}^m$. Altogether $V$ is contained in the
$\mathbb{F}_p$-span of the reductions of $D$ vectors $u_1,\dots,u_D\in\{-1,0,1\}^m$, where, as $m$ is large,
\[
D\le k\cdot3\log_2m\le9\,(\log_2m)^2\le(\log m)^3<m .
\]
By the hypothesis on $\chi_T$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:liftinv}, $0$ is the only $T$-invariant subspace of $\mathbb{Q}^m$ contained in
$\operatorname{span}_\mathbb{Q}(u_1,\dots,u_D)$, and since $V\ne0$ is $\bar T$-invariant, $p\le m^{3D^2}$. Hence
\[
\log p\le3D^2\log m\le243\,(\log_2m)^4\log m<(\log m)^6 ,
\]
again as $m$ is large. This contradicts $p>e^{(\log m)^6}$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Step 3.}\ We deduce the bound for $a_\beta(T)$ from Steps~1 and~2.\par\nobreak\noindent\ignorespaces A simple $\bar T$-submodule of type $\beta$ is a nonzero
$\bar T$-invariant subspace, so the bound of Steps~1 and~2 holds for each of them, and hence for $a_\beta(T)$.
<!-- end proof-82 -->
<!-- proof-83: body_md -->
Let $\Pi_n$ be the set of pairs $(p,d)$ with $p>e^{(\log n)^6}$ an odd prime and $d\ge1$. For $m\in\{n-1,n\}$ let
$\mathcal G_m$ be the set of Seidel matrices $T$ of order $m$ with $\Delta_T\ne0$ such that $\chi_T$ has no monic factor in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ of
degree in $[1,(\log m)^3]$. Since $(\log m)^3\le m^{1/30}$ for large $m$, Theorem~\ref{lem:simplespectrum} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:nofactor} (with $\eta=\frac1{30}$) show that $\Pr(S_m\notin\mathcal G_m)\to0$ for $m\in\{n-1,n\}$. By
Proposition~\ref{prop:reduction} it suffices to show that $\mathbb{E}(N_{\Pi_n}(S_m);\ S_m\in\mathcal G_m)\to0$ for $m\in\{n-1,n\}$.

Let $n$ be large, $m\in\{n-1,n\}$ and $T\in\mathcal G_m$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:budget}(b) with $P=e^{(\log n)^6}$, the number of pairs
$(p,\beta)$ with $p>e^{(\log n)^6}$ prime and $\beta$ a repeated factor of $T$ at $p$ is at most
\[
\frac{m^2\log(2m)}{(\log n)^6}\le n^2\log(2n).
\]
For each of them $p>e^{(\log n)^6}\ge e^{(\log m)^6}$, so Proposition~\ref{lem:acinv} gives $a_\beta(T)<m^{-3}\le(n-1)^{-3}$. Hence
$N_{\Pi_n}(T)\le n^2\log(2n)\,(n-1)^{-3}$, and therefore
\[
\mathbb{E}\big(N_{\Pi_n}(S_m);\ S_m\in\mathcal G_m\big)\le n^2\log(2n)\,(n-1)^{-3}\longrightarrow0\qquad(m\in\{n-1,n\}).
\]
So the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop:reduction} hold for $\Pi_n$ and the sets $\mathcal G_m$, and the proposition proves the
theorem.
<!-- end proof-83 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:hugeAC}
Let $m$ be large. By Theorem~\ref{thm:nofactor} (with $\eta=\frac1{30}$, as $(\log m)^3\le m^{1/30}$) and Proposition~\ref{lem:acinv}, with
probability at least $1-e^{-m^{7/90}/9}$ every nonzero $\bar S_m$-invariant subspace $V\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p^m$ satisfies
$\Pr_\xi(\bar\xi\perp V)<m^{-3}$, simultaneously for all primes $p>e^{(\log m)^6}$. In particular $\Pr_\xi(\xi^{\top}w=0)<m^{-3}$ for every
eigenvector $w\in\mathbb{F}_p^m$ of $\bar S_m$ with eigenvalue in $\mathbb{F}_p$. At the primes $23\le p\le e^{m^{1/8}}$, Corollary~\ref{cor:ACplus} for
$S_m$ shows that, outside an event of probability $O(2^{-m/8})$, every such eigenvector satisfies
$\Pr_\xi(\xi^{\top}w=0)\le\frac1p+e^{-2c_1m}\le\frac1p+m^{-3}$. As $e^{m^{1/8}}>e^{(\log m)^6}$ and
$e^{-m^{7/90}/9}+O(2^{-m/8})\le e^{-m^{7/90}/10}$, with probability at least $1-e^{-m^{7/90}/10}$ every such eigenvector satisfies
$\Pr_\xi(\xi^{\top}w=0)\le\frac1p+m^{-3}$, at all primes $p\ge23$ at once.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
